methods.description: The best (lowest) change-from-baseline rule of the ASM (average of selected markers) cfDNA methylation monitoring of Barault et al. (Gut 2017, DOI 10.1136/gutjnl-2016-313372), a fixed rule on five methylation markers: markers[0..4] carry the paper's roles in its order (EYA4, GRIA4, ITGA4, MAP3K14-AS1, MSC; the package passes the main markers sorted, which is this order). Per patient: a marker is selected iff its value at the last baseline draw (on or before baseline_max_day) is above its ROC-derived per-marker positivity cutoff (0.7%, 1.02%, 2.3%, 0.24%, 0.9%; positivity_cutoffs); the ASM at a time-point is the mean of the selected markers' values there; the per-draw change is the ABSOLUTE difference ASM_t - ASM_baseline in percentage points (not a percent change); the best change is the minimum over the on-treatment draws by the landmark (the paper's 'best methylation change (lowest) over the course of treatment', with the RECIST best-response analogy); a best change below the call cutoff (0: any decrease) is clinical benefit (RECIST stable disease or partial response), at or above it (increase or stable ASM) progression. It writes the quantity it thresholds as risk (best change in percentage points, higher = worse: negative = decrease = benefit, 0 or positive = progression side) and the 0/1 call (0 = clinical benefit, 1 = progression, the contract's failure orientation; the paper's call is the inverse, and its PPV/NPV and PFS HR are cohort-level associations, not per-patient output). It writes no probability and saves a model (markers, cutoffs and the call cutoff). Where the paper is silent it is fixed as follows: the draws are truncated at the landmark (the paper's whole course becomes a time-restricted minimum); the per-draw ASM re-averages over the selected markers with a value at that draw; a non-detect value of 0 participates as 0; a patient with no marker above its cutoff at baseline, or with no on-treatment draw carrying a selected marker's value, gets no prediction with the reason in note (the paper excludes such patients).

methods.description: The Bayesian semi-parametric joint model of event time and a longitudinal marker of Zhang, Mueller & Do (Biometrics 2010, 66(2):546-553; the paper's model M1): the joint law is factored as P(T, Y) = P(T) P(Y | T), so the desired regression P(T | Y) is implied by Bayes theorem instead of being parametrized. The event-time prior is a non-parametric Pólya tree (PT) centred at a Weibull distribution plus a cure fraction: the progression time T comes either from the treatment-specific random measure G_v (susceptible patients) or equals a very long time t_c (cured, long-term survivors) with arm-specific cure probability p_v. The longitudinal marker is a mixed model whose curve contains a subject-specific line, a subject-specific exponential drop after diagnosis, a treatment-level exponential drop, a treatment-level slope change and a reverse-regression term u(T) = exp(-xi T) - 1 multiplied by the post-treatment trend, so that subjects with flatter profiles tend to take longer to progress; G_v is analytically marginalised (the PT predictive), and the model is fitted by MCMC (conjugate Gibbs for the linear coefficients, priors and variance; Metropolis steps on the non-linear parameters, the latent susceptible progression times and the latent cure indicators). Given a currently observed marker profile the wrapper obtains the posterior predictive distribution of the failure time by posterior simulation, updated as marker draws accumulate, and reports, per patient and horizon h, the posterior probability of failure by h given being event-free at the landmark (the paper reports P(cure | y_-t), E(T | cure=0, y_-t) and the predictive TTP distribution, not a conditional-on-landmark probability: the wrapper adds the ordinary landmark conditioning, see the README). Differences from the paper, in the README: the two treatment arms of the prostate trial are not modelled (the benchmark data is one treatment per unit; with one arm the model is the paper's v = 1 case); the paper's age clock svij with hinges at the age at diagnosis uvi0 and age at treatment start uvi1 is not available in the benchmark (days since the first dose only), so the wrapper measures time in years from the first dose and sets both hinges to the first dose (the diagnosis drop and the treatment drop then share the hinge and confounded curves are not both estimated: the two drops are kept with both decay constants, and the wrapper reports the confounding risk); the paper's fixed hyper-parameters are used (Weibull centering tau = 4.52, beta = 1.23; alpha = c*m^2 with c = 1; t_c = 18 years; Uniform(0,1) on p_v; the N3 / IW / Gamma(0.01, 0.01) / N(0,100) block) and the PT is truncated at 2^8 dyadic quantile cells (the paper's partition level is not stated); the outcome is the benchmark's progression or death endpoint (the paper's TTP; the paper uses event time, survival time and failure time interchangeably).

methods.description: Dynamic prediction of treatment failure by the backward joint model (BJM) with competing risks of Li, Wang, Yin, Astor, Yang, Greene and Li (Lifetime Data Analysis 2026;32(3):46, DOI 10.1007/s10985-026-09725-x; R package BJM 0.2.0, the same authors), the method of the paper's AASK kidney-disease application. The likelihood is factorized backwards: a marginal event-time sub-model (survival::coxph, ties='breslow') x, for two event types, a vertical-model binomial glm of the event type on the event time and the baseline covariates, x a per-biomarker multivariate linear mixed model of the trajectory (nlme::lme, method='ML', random intercept, conditional mean trajectory linear in visit time with varying coefficients in the event time, the event type and the baseline covariates, per the paper's equation (12)); the random-effect covariance is then refined by the package's EM update (tol.em=1e-4). From the fitted sub-models the package evaluates the paper's dynamic prediction formula (10): per patient, the conditional probability of the composite event (any of the competing causes) and of each cause within a horizon, given that no event has happened by the prediction time (the landmark) and the biomarker draws up to it. The wrapper's endpoint is the benchmark's composite progression-or-death event: the wrapper writes the model's own probability of the composite (p_progression_H<h>) and of the death cause (p_death_H<h>) for every horizon, risk (composite probability at the first horizon) and risk_death; when the training event types do not separate (no progression without death, or only one survival endpoint measured) it falls back to the basic single-cause BJM on the composite, where the composite and death risks coincide. The future-biomarker estimand of the paper (its equation (3), dynamicPredictionBio) is part of the method but is not written: the benchmark's outputs carry risks and probabilities only.

methods.description: The two-spot complement C3 change score of Michlmayr et al. (Br J Cancer 2010, DOI 10.1038/sj.bjc.6605909; neoadjuvant epirubicin/docetaxel in early or locally advanced breast cancer, 25 patients): per patient, the difference of the treatment-induced changes of the two 2D-DIGE complement C3 isoform spots between the pre-dose draw (T1) and the 24-h draw (T2) - score = (Δ529 − Δ195) with Δspot = DeCyder-2D expression value(T2) − expression value(T1), spot 529 = C3 α-chain, spot 195 = C3 group 1 (likely non-cleaved full-length C3) ('We calculated the difference of the treatment-induced expression changes of the two spots in each patient (529–195).', md:86; the per-spot change is the absolute difference T2 − T1, md:59). The paper evaluates the score as a receiver operating characteristic curve against the pathological response (WHO criteria: responder = CR or PR, non-responder = SD or PD; AUC 0.917 discovery n = 12, 0.944 validation n = 13, 0.908 over all 25 with SE 0.063, p = 0.001) and reports an operating point with sensitivity 0.80 and specificity 0.83, but the operating cutoff VALUE and the ROC direction are not published ('?'), and no per-patient probability is defined. The wrapper takes exactly two markers (markers[0] = the C3 group-1 spot 195, markers[1] = the C3 α-chain spot 529 - the package passes them sorted, which is this order, the convention of the corpus fixed-list wrappers), computes the score and writes it as risk in the failure direction, risk = Δ195 − Δ529 (higher = the non-responder side, because the spots change contrariwise: spot 195 decreased and spot 529 increased in responders, md:86; the flip of the paper's score is a monotone decreasing transform, so the ROC AUC is the paper's). It writes no call (the operating cutoff is not published - the wrapper does not invent a threshold; the roster group is response-call because the paper publishes classification sensitivity/specificity, but the wrapper cannot emit a binary call without inventing its cutoff, so the contract classification is static-risk: one risk score at the landmark, recorded as a deviation) and no probability (the paper defines no per-patient probability; the benchmark's package converts the risk per outcome). Nothing is learned from the training outcomes (fitted false, no cutoff, no model or probability fitted): the fit step only records the marker roles, the draw-pair convention and the training counts. The T1 draw is the marker's last draw on or before baseline_max_day (the paper's immediately-before-the-initial-dose sample); the T2 draw is the marker's last draw after it and at or before the landmark (the corpus convention of the fixed-pair wrappers - the paper's T2 is protocol-fixed at 24 h, which a 1-day landmark reproduces exactly; at a later landmark the wrapper evaluates the two-draw change as of the decision day, and draws after the landmark never enter; the paper's day-2/day-3 changes were stable but 'undetectable at day 14', md:91). A patient without a T1 or a T2 draw of either spot gets no prediction, with the reason in note; a non-detect value of 0 participates as 0, and no imputation is performed (the paper defines no fallback, md:57 records only a gel-level inclusion rule).

methods.description: The univariable Cox proportional-hazards model of Mano et al., 'CA-125 AUC as a new prognostic factor for patients with ovarian cancer', Gynecologic Oncology 97 (2005) 529-534, DOI 10.1016/j.ygyno.2005.01.040 (92 ovarian-cancer patients with primary first-line chemotherapy within 4 months of cytoreductive surgery, Coimbra University Hospital 1990-2000): per patient the one covariate is the CA-125 AUC = (sum of all trapezoid areas between C1 and C2)/(t2 - t1) (md:104-112), with C1 = the first CA-125 concentration after cytoreductive surgery, C2 = the last concentration before the end of first-line chemotherapy and t1/t2 the corresponding dates, requiring at least three CA-125 concentrations in the window (md:102-103); the model is h(t) = h0(t) exp(beta * AUC) with overall survival as the dependent variable and the patient final state (Alive or Deceased) as the censoring variable (md:250-253), fitted in four variants - no stratification and stratified by FIGO tumor stage (I, II, III, IV), residual disease (> 2 cm) and primary chemotherapy response (CR, PR, WR/DP) (md:253-255; Table 4 md:628-648, chi-squares 18.19 P<0.05 / 6.42 P<0.05 / 14.80 P<0.05 / 1.83 NS), and the survival functions for hypothetical CA-125 AUC values from the UNSTRATIFIED fit (Fig. 4, md:255-257, md:649). The wrapper reimplements the stated model in R with survival 3.7-0 (the paper names no software at all - 'a multivariant regression analysis based on the Cox proportional hazard model' (md:125-128), the fit itself univariable, md:250-252 - and publishes no code, so nothing was substituted or downloaded), refits it per survival outcome on the benchmark training fold (death from OS, the paper's endpoint; progression from PFS, the benchmark's analogous event-free endpoint - the paper has no PFS model), one fit per training fold with the four variants recorded in run.json, and predicts a new patient from the fitted unstratified model as the paper's Fig. 4 does: risk and risk_death / risk_progression = the linear predictor of the unstratified fit (the paper's direction: 'patients with a lower CA-125 AUC have a better overall survival than patients with a higher CA-125 AUC', md:373-377; a method that reports an association writes its linear predictor), p_death_H<h> / p_progression_H<h> = 1 - S(h - landmark | AUC) from the unstratified fit - P(death or progression by day h | event-free at the landmark) - the paper's survival function projected onto the benchmark horizons (the paper defines no per-patient score or probability; Fig. 4 plots hypothetical AUC values); the response outcomes no_response and progressive_disease are served with the same risk (the paper's AUC-vs-response analysis is the Mann-Whitney U / Kruskal-Wallis comparison of Table 2, md:113-118, no model), and a patient with fewer than three informative CA-125 draws, no informative pre-treatment draw (the paper's post-surgery C1) or no informative on-treatment draw by the landmark (the paper's pre-end-of-chemotherapy C2) gets no prediction with the reason in note. AUC construction on the benchmark: C1 = the first informative draw at day <= baseline_max_day and C2 = the last informative draw at day <= landmark (the harness carries no surgery date and the landmark is the decision-day cut of the benchmark, so the paper's surgery-to-end-of-chemotherapy window is mapped to the observed trajectory up to the landmark - recorded), the trapezoid rule over the consecutive informative draws (days since the first dose; only elapsed differences enter), the formula as printed (time-normalized sum, whose unit the paper prints as IU/ml*days - units discrepancy recorded, spec header), below-detection draws (value 0 with the <marker>__detected row 0) carry no concentration and never enter the trapezoid (the paper states no detection-limit rule, '?'). When the benchmark passes baseline covariates, columns whose names match the three stratification variables (params strata_*_regex, default 'figo', 'residual', 'respons', case-insensitive; a single matching column is used as its factor levels, several matching 0/1 columns are combined as dummy columns into one strata factor) are used as the STRATA of the three stratified fits only (the paper's stratification variables are strata, not regression covariates, md:253-255; the unstratified model remains the prediction model as in the paper's Fig. 4, and covariates matching nothing yield the unstratified-only fit, recorded).

methods.description: The CA-125 AUC call rule of Mano et al., 'CA-125 AUC as a new prognostic factor for patients with ovarian cancer', Gynecologic Oncology 97 (2005) 529-534, DOI 10.1016/j.ygyno.2005.01.040 (92 ovarian-cancer patients with primary first-line chemotherapy within 4 months of cytoreductive surgery, Coimbra University Hospital 1990-2000; 50 deceased / 42 alive at the evaluation date). The feature is the per-patient time-normalised trapezoid AUC of the serial serum CA-125 trajectory between cytoreductive surgery and the end of first-line chemotherapy: CA-125 AUC = (sum of all trapezoid areas between C1 and C2)/(t2 - t1) (md:104-112), with C1 = the first CA-125 concentration after cytoreductive surgery, C2 = the last concentration before the end of first-line chemotherapy and t1/t2 the corresponding dates; the paper requires 'a minimum of three CA-125 serum concentrations' in the window (md:102-103). The call dichotomises the AUC at a cut-off of the fixed ladder <= 25, 50, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 800, 1000 IU/ml*days (Table 3, md:386-387): AUC <= cut-off => favourable (the paper's direction; 'V' = '<=' per the spec OCR convention), and the per-outcome reported cut-off is the accuracy maximum over the ladder - complete response 100 (accuracy 0.82, ROC AUC 0.87), patient final state 'alive' 100 (0.74, 0.77), OS >= 1 y 1000 (0.87, 0.67), OS >= 3 y 100 (0.72, 0.75), OS >= 5 y 25 (0.66, 0.73) (md:240-249, md:378-382, Table 3 md:383-627). The wrapper (fitted true: the per-outcome cut-off IS derived in this sample, accuracy maximum over the fixed ladder, exactly the paper's derivation) computes the AUC as printed (time-normalised trapezoid sum; the printed unit IU/ml*days is kept verbatim though the printed formula divides by days - the unresolved units discrepancy of the spec header), derives the accuracy-maximising cut-off on the training fold for every outcome the training data give (the paper's per-outcome Table 3 recorded per fold in run.json, with the paper's tie convention - in every tied accuracy case, V100 over V50 and V1000 over V800, the paper reported the highest tied cut-off), and at predict writes risk = the continuous CA-125 AUC (the quantity the ladder thresholds; higher = more likely failing, the paper's direction md:373-377) and call = 1 when AUC > call_cutoff (treatment judged failing), 0 when AUC <= call_cutoff; call_cutoff is the training-derived cut-off of the paper's PRIMARY outcome, mapped to the benchmark's response-failure label: the paper's complete response to primary chemotherapy call is served on no_response (1 = SD or PD, the paper's 'without response or disease progression' class, md:144-148 - recorded: the paper's binary is stricter, CR vs PR+WR/DP, while no_response is SD/PD vs CR/PR), with the chain no_response -> progressive_disease -> death_H<first horizon> (the paper's final-state/OS-call analogue) -> progression_H<first horizon> -> the paper's headline 100 IU/ml*days (md:378-382) when no outcome label can be used; no probability is written (a rule writes the quantity it thresholds and its call; TxResBench converts the risk). On the benchmark clock the paper's surgery-to-end-of-chemotherapy window maps to the observed trajectory (the harness carries no surgery date): C1 = the first informative draw at day <= baseline_max_day (the first post-surgery value the benchmark carries, the needs_baseline anchor) and C2 = the last informative draw at day <= the landmark (the paper's pre-end-of-chemotherapy value), with >= 3 informative draws in the window; an informative draw is a finite value whose <marker>__detected companion row (when present) says detected (1) - a below-detection draw (value 0, __detected 0) carries no concentration and never enters the trapezoid, the paper states no detection-limit rule ('?'); several draws of the same day are one sample (the last row; the corpus per-day convention), and a patient with no informative pre-anchor draw, no informative on-treatment draw or fewer than three informative draws gets no prediction, with the reason in note. The paper publishes no analysis code (job.code = [], the md ends at the reference list, md:676-733) and names no software, so nothing was substituted or downloaded; the same paper's Cox model is the separate spec ca125-auc-cox.

methods.description: The GCIG (Gynaecological Cancer Intergroup) simplified CA125 response criteria of Rustin (2003) as applied to second-line chemotherapy of recurrent/refractory epithelial ovarian carcinoma by Gronlund et al. (Br J Cancer 2004;90(2):377-382; 124 consecutive patients, topotecan n=64 or paclitaxel-carboplatin n=60; 87 GCIG-evaluable, 23 nonevaluable, 14 CA125 normal; among the 72 patients assessable by both WHO and CA125 criteria the CA125 response rate was 57% (41/72) vs 39% (28/72) by WHO, P=0.045, with sensitivity 96% (27/28), specificity 68% (30/44), PPV 66% (27/41), NPV 97% (30/31) and accuracy 79% (57/72)). Evaluable patients have two pretreatment serum CA125 samples at least twice (>=70 U/ml) the >35 U/ml upper cut-off of normal and at least two on-treatment samples; a CA125 response is at least a 50% decrease from the pretreatment level confirmed by the fourth sample, evaluated on the variable day of the WHO response allocation. The wrapper takes the serum CA125 series (one marker, U/ml), computes the paper's three-class evaluability classification (CA125 normal / nonevaluable / evaluable: extra column ca125_class, and the paper's own category counts in run.json), and writes risk = the percent change of the CA125 level at the assessment moment (the last on-treatment draw by the benchmark's landmark, standing in for the WHO-allocation day) from the pretreatment reference (the mean of the quantitative pretreatment draws; the paper does not state which of its two pretreatment samples is the reference, and 'first'/'last' are exposed) - the quantity the rule thresholds; call = 0 for a GCIG CA125 response (the >=50% decrease is confirmed by the fourth drawn sample of the series, itself at most 0.5 x the reference; the paper does not state the confirmation's numeric meaning, and this reading is declared), 1 otherwise; no probability is written. Differences from the paper, all declared: the benchmark's landmark replaces the variable allocation day; the paper's 50% boundary is inclusive; below-detection values (value 0 with the <marker>__detected row 0) enter as the paper's '<35 U/ml' floor (they satisfy the decrease condition and count as a full drop in the risk); and the paper reports its call only in GCIG-evaluable, WHO-measurable patients (the 72 both-assessable), while the wrapper applies the rule's numeric criteria to every patient with a quantitative reference and an on-treatment draw and records the evaluability class per patient so the evaluable-population evaluation stays reproducible. The paper publishes no analysis code (job.code empty), so the rule is implemented from the Methods/Results text; nothing is fitted (the cutoff is the GCIG constant, borrowed from Rustin 2003, not a training estimate).

methods.description: The CA125 kinetics rate-threshold rule of Ueda et al. (Cancers 2024;16(5):871, DOI 10.3390/cancers16050871; 73 patients with advanced gastric cancer on second- or third-line taxane-plus-ramucirumab [TAX/RAM] at four facilities, June 2015-July 2019): per patient, CA125 kinetics is the daily percentage change of serum CA125 between the measurement just before starting TAX/RAM and the FIRST measurement after treatment initiation - (CA125_post - CA125_pre) / CA125_pre x 100 / days between the two measurements (md:32), where the pre-treatment measurement is one used for eligibility ('assessable serum CA125 concentrations just before starting TAX/RAM treatment', md:25) and the first on-treatment measurement was at a median of 28 days (range 7-60) after initiation (md:61). The call is CA125-increased when the kinetics is 0.0067%/day or greater - the optimal cutoff from the paper's same-sample ROC curve analysis predicting ascites progression (specificity 74%, sensitivity 100%, AUC 0.89, Figure S3; md:61) - the group the paper reports as predicting the progression of peritoneal metastases (in the 45-patient kinetics-evaluable peritoneal-metastasis cohort, 21 increased vs 24 nonincreased; PFS median 2.5 [1.6-3.6] vs 6.1 [3.8-9.7] months, HR 2.97 [1.53-5.78], p = 0.0013; OS HR 1.03 [0.55-1.95], p = 0.92; md:61). The wrapper takes the serum CA125 series (one marker, U/mL): x_pre is the last quantitative draw at day <= baseline_max_day (the paper's value just before starting TAX/RAM; day 0 or earlier, never a landmark-relative draw), x_first_on is the first draw in (baseline_max_day, landmark] (the paper's first measurement after treatment initiation; later draws are not part of the rule), the denominator is the actual days between those two draws (patient-specific, 7-60 in the paper - never a fixed 28), and it writes risk = the kinetics (%/day; more positive = faster increase = more likely failing; the quantity the 0.0067%/day cutoff thresholds) and call = 1 for CA125-increased (kinetics >= 0.0067%/day, the boundary inclusive as printed in the operational definition, md:61; the abstract's 'exceeding' is recorded), plus the pre-treatment value, the first on-treatment value and the draw interval. It writes no probability: TxResBench converts the risk. The paper publishes no analysis code (only the proprietary JMP 16, md:41) and its cutoff is derived in this sample (md:61) with the cutoff-selection criterion not stated, so the wrapper applies the published 0.0067%/day as the fixed constant (nothing is fitted; a benchmark wanting a train-fold derivation must set cutoff itself - the wrapper does not re-derive because the ROC label is ascites progression, not a benchmark outcome, and the selection criterion is unpublished '?'). The wrapper reproduces only the rate-threshold call: the paper's baseline CA125-elevated (>35 U/mL) grouping, the baseline-CA125/ascites-burden association, the KM/log-rank and logistic-regression survival analyses, and the CEA/CA19-9 kinetics comparators are association/diagnostic analyses of the same paper, not this rule. The paper restricts the kinetics evaluation to patients with peritoneal metastasis present before TAX/RAM (md:49, md:61, md:76) and its ROC to the 36 ascites-response patients (md:61); those cohort selections are not benchmark channels, so the wrapper applies the numeric rule to every patient with a quantitative pre-treatment CA125 and a first on-treatment draw by the landmark (declared deviation; the paper's reported statistics are recorded in run.json).

methods.description: The CA125 ratio response criteria of Davelaar et al (1996), as applied to second-line chemotherapy of recurrent/refractory epithelial ovarian carcinoma by Gronlund et al. (Br J Cancer 2004;90(2):377-382; 124 consecutive patients, topotecan n=64 or paclitaxel-carboplatin n=60; 102 evaluable by the ratio criteria (pretreatment CA125 >=70 U/ml, one pretreatment sample), 8 nonevaluable (35-70 U/ml), 14 CA125 normal (<35 U/ml); sequential CA125 response (CR+PR) rates 32/58/63/64% and accuracy vs the WHO response (CR+PR) 70/71/75/66% after 1-4 cycles among the 84/76/73/73 patients assessable by both criteria, best after three cycles, 75% (64-85)). The call: a CA125 ratio is calculated after every series of second-line chemotherapy by dividing the actual CA125 level following treatment by the pretreatment CA125 value directly prior to the start of treatment (md:188-195); three response categories as proposed by Davelaar et al (1996) - Response (CR+PR): ratio <= 0.5; SD: ratio > 0.5 and < 2.0; PD: ratio >= 2.0 (md:195-199) - evaluated at a fixed moment after M cycles (M = 1-4; Table 1 'Fixed(b)'), with no confirmatory sample (Table 1 '-'; md:234-236). The wrapper takes the serum CA125 series (one marker, U/ml): the reference is the pretreatment value directly prior to the start (the last quantitative draw on or before baseline_max_day, the paper's words; 'first'/'mean' exposed), the assessment moment is the benchmark's landmark (the paper's fixed after-M-cycle grid is a cycle grid, whose day-level values the paper does not print, so the wrapper uses the corpus fixed-pair convention: the last on-treatment draw at or before the landmark), and it writes risk = the CA125 ratio (the quantity the 0.5/2.0 cutoffs apply to; higher = more likely failing) and call = 1 when the ratio call is SD or PD (not a CA125 ratio response: the paper's Table 4 binary evaluation 'CA125 reduction... in predicting tumour response (CR+PR)' collapses the native three-class call exactly this way), 0 for Response. Extra columns: ca125_ratio_call (the native three-class call, 0 = Response (CR+PR), 1 = SD, 2 = PD) and ca125_class (the paper's evaluability classification of the reference, 0 = CA125 normal, 1 = nonevaluable 35-70 U/ml, 2 = evaluable >= 70 U/ml), plus per-class counts and the paper's reported results in the fit report. Differences from the paper, all declared: the benchmark's landmark replaces the after-M-cycle grid (the wrapper does not invent a day value for a cycle); below-detection draws (value 0 with the <marker>__detected row 0, the paper's '<35 U/ml' reporting floor) enter the assessment as 0 (a full drop: the Response class is guaranteed for an evaluable >=70 U/ml reference because the ratio is then < 0.5 under any reading, and the risk is the ratio of the recorded 0); the paper reports the call only in evaluable patients (>= 70 U/ml) and the paper's concordance evaluation only in patients assessable by both CA125 and WHO criteria (WHO-measurable lesions - a property the benchmark's channels do not carry), while the wrapper applies the rule's numeric criteria to every patient with a quantitative pretreatment level and an on-treatment draw and records the evaluability class per patient so the evaluable-population evaluation stays reproducible. The paper publishes no analysis code (job.code empty), so the rule is implemented from the Methods/Results text; nothing is fitted (the cutoffs are the Davelaar constants, borrowed, not training estimates).

methods.description: The 70-um CAML-size crossing risk grouping of Ali et al. (Sci Rep 2023;13:10544, DOI 10.1038/s41598-023-37671-3; preprint Research Square 2022, DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-2394390/v1; 40 metastatic-RCC patients on a new line of systemic therapy, 24-month primary endpoint): per patient the largest cancer-associated macrophage-like cell (CAML) size (um per 7.5 mL whole blood) is taken at the baseline draw (prior to induction of the new line) and at timepoint 2 (~30 days after induction), and the crossing class ('increase') = baseline < 70 um AND timepoint-2 >= 70 um - the authors' published boundary (VOR '(< 70 um) to larger (>= 70 um)'; the preprint's '> 70 um' is recorded verbatim as a paper-internal inconsistency) - with the reference class = every other patient; the class was associated with PFS and OS by univariate Cox proportional hazards regression (MATLAB R2020b, function not named), Kaplan-Meier curves and the log-rank test (published: PFS HR = 5.8 [1.56-21.5], p = 0.022; OS HR = 1.3 [0.321-5.502], p = 0.975). The wrapper writes risk = the timepoint-2 largest CAML size in um - the quantity the rule's >= 70 um side thresholds, in the paper's direction (larger CAML size = the worse side: the Fig. 2 >= 70 um baseline group HR 2.84 PFS / 3.95 OS, and the crossing 'increase' group HR 5.8 PFS) - and call = 1 for the crossing class (treatment judged failing), 0 for the reference; no probability of its own (the paper defines none; TxResBench converts the risk). Nothing is learned from the training outcomes (fitted false: the rule and the 70 um threshold are the paper's published constants, never re-derived); the paper's association layer (per-group counts, univariate Cox HR/95% CI/p per survival outcome, per-group KM medians, log-rank) is recomputed on the training fold and reported in run.json. Differences from the paper: the harness landmark approximates timepoint 2, so the wrapper takes the marker's last on-treatment draw at or before the landmark (the paper's ~30-day protocol draw carries no day label and the harness has no cycle labels); at exactly 70.0 um the crossing boundary is >= (the VOR wording) while the preprint reads '>' - both recorded; the reference class is the extraction's 'vs otherwise' (the Supplementary Figure 2 group definitions are image-only); the reported p-values are the Cox HR p-values - no log-rank p is printed for the change analysis; the per-patient risk (the timepoint-2 size) is the wrapper's contract projection of a class-only method (the paper reports no per-patient risk score or probability).

methods.description: The tumour-informed CAPP-Seq ctDNA MRD detection rule of Moding et al., Nature Cancer 2020 (unresectable stage IIB-IIIB NSCLC treated with definitive concurrent chemoradiation, with or without consolidation immune checkpoint inhibition): at each plasma draw the presence of ctDNA is queried by a previously-described Monte Carlo-based ctDNA detection index monitoring the somatic single nucleotide variants identified pretreatment (median 8 variants from tumour tissue / 4 from pretreatment plasma), and the draw is called detected when the index is less than a per-patient detection-index threshold set to achieve >=90% specificity in 54 held-out control cfDNA samples analysed using the same selector - note the direction: a LOWER index means detected. The detection engine is the CAPP-Seq custom bioinformatics pipeline, whose code is not obtainable and whose index formula and per-patient threshold values are not published, so the benchmark receives its per-draw output - the draw's detection call as the marker's detectability state (the benchmark's <marker>__detected convention) and the ctDNA concentration (mean allele fraction x plasma cfDNA concentration, 1 hGE = 3.3 pg) as the marker value. The wrapper applies the per-draw rule to the last on-treatment draw on or before the landmark (the paper's serial monitoring, re-applied at each benchmark landmark): it writes call = 1 (ctDNA detected, treatment judged failing) and, as risk, the ctDNA concentration at that draw - higher = more ctDNA = failing. It writes no probability: TxResBench converts the risk.

methods.description: The per-patient probability of being an ICI non-responder learned by caret::train(method = 'glmnet') - an elastic-net penalised binomial logistic regression - on a wide vector of derived blood-transcriptomic features from ONE sample-collection condition (Rubio-Alvaro M, Oh S, Roelandt S, et al., Sci Rep 2024;14, DOI 10.1038/s41598-024-76982-x; 33 ICI-treated metastatic NSCLC patients, 16 responders / 17 non-responders, whole blood and PBMC collected before ICI treatment and at the first image-based response evaluation after 3 +/- 1 cycles). The paper trains one classifier per sample-collection condition (PBMC/WB x before/after) on three feature sets (A: TMM/voom-normalised expression of the 5000 most variable genes via ComBat_seq; B: ssGSEA NES of immune-related MSigDB C8 gene sets; C: DWLS deconvolved proportions of 9 cell types) with 5-fold cross-validation, each model run 10 times and reported as the mean ROC AUC per fold (md:54, md:90, md:92); no classification threshold exists - the product is P(responder) and the fold AUCs. The wrapper re-implements that classifier for the benchmark as the FIRST-RESPONSE-EVALUATION condition: features are the values of every marker the dataset passes at the patient's latest on-treatment draw on or before the landmark (the three feature pipelines A/B/C are upstream of the classifier and run in the dataset's own marker preparation - the wrapper consumes the derived matrix and records which markers it got); the label is the paper's non-responder class mapped onto the benchmark's no_response (best RECIST response SD or PD - the paper's non-responder definition, md:29), the responder definition's additional 6-month no-progression rule is not expressible in the benchmark response label (recorded deviation); the model is fitted with caret::train(method = 'glmnet', metric = 'ROC', tuneLength = 3) under trainControl(method = 'repeatedcv', number = 5, repeats = 10, classProbs = TRUE, summaryFunction = twoClassSummary) - the paper's published '5-fold cross validation' and 'run 10 times' with the caret 6.0-94 package defaults where the paper is silent (tuneLength, grid alpha = seq(0.1, 1, length = 3) x lambda from a 5-lambda path at alpha = 0.5, model selection by the resampled ROC), and risk = p_no_response = P(non-responder) from the glmnet probabilities at the selected lambda (caret's prob: P(levels[2]) = P(responder), columns named by the factor levels); the sex/age-covariate secondary variant of the paper (Supplementary Fig. 14) is supported as the benchmark's optional covariate track (every cov_* column is appended to the feature matrix, encoding as supplied). Differences from the paper, all because it publishes no analysis code: the wrapper fits one model at the benchmark's landmark query (the paper's four per-condition models compete on the sample-type and timepoint axes, which the tidy marker space does not carry - the harness needs an on-treatment draw for a prediction, so the before-treatment models are not benchmark queries); the paper's per-rule tuning settings (trainControl call, tuneLength, seeds) are not published and are taken as the caret defaults with the paper-stated 5-fold CV and 10 runs; the benchmark's own train/test folds carry the evaluation (the paper's 5-fold CV is its internal evaluation, recorded per fold in run.json); a degenerate training sample falls back to the no-information base rate, recorded in run.json and declared in constant_ok.

methods.description: The acquired-resistance emergence call of Tsuji et al. (Cancer Science 2016;107(7):936-943, DOI 10.1111/cas.12959; 24 metastatic colorectal cancer patients with KRAS wild-type primary tumours treated with EGFR-blockade chemotherapy, of whom 8 acquired resistance): a KRAS point mutation newly detected in plasma circulating cell-free DNA (ccfDNA) during EGFR-blockade chemotherapy - the baseline ccfDNA was KRAS wild-type - predicts acquired resistance, with the paper's reported lead time of 2-3 months before CT-detectable disease progression (5 of the 8 acquired-resistance patients, md:194). The seven monitored mutations are G12V, G12A, G12D, G12S, G12C, G12R and G13D (Inv-Clamp assay, positive threshold ratio 0.1% mutant / 99.9% wild-type plasmid DNA, md:42; dPCR on the QuantStudio 3D platform, md:47); the call is detection-based ('mutant versus wild-type', md:80-83), the numeric dPCR mutation rate (%) is the measurement the detection threshold is applied to. The wrapper takes the per-draw ccfDNA KRAS mutation detection state (the dataset's per-variant rows or the panel-level KRAS call, any number of markers; a non-KRAS-named marker is ignored - CEA and CA19-9, which the paper measured monthly, are explicitly not part of this call, md:57, md:210): per patient, the ccfDNA KRAS state at the baseline draw (day <= baseline_max_day, the paper's first-visit draw) must be wild-type, and a KRAS mutation detected in ANY on-treatment draw up to the landmark makes the call 1 (acquired resistance predicted; the detection state updates with each new draw and once a new mutation is detected the call stays - the 'new... during chemotherapy' semantics, md:9, md:194). The per-draw detection call is the dataset's <marker>__detected rows when present (the assay's own call, not recomputed), else the value against detection_threshold (default: a documented stand-in derived from the training marker levels: 0.5 for 0/1 values, 0 where 0 encodes below-detection, else the training median, because the benchmark frame does not carry the assay's 0.1% positive-ratio limit). risk is the pre-threshold score the rule thresholds - the KRAS level (mutation rate % / VAF) of the most recent on-treatment draw by the landmark (0/1 detection state when the dataset carries no level) - with call = 1 for emergence, 0 otherwise; higher risk = the level closer to or above detection = the treatment more likely failing. No probability of its own: TxResBench converts the risk. A patient with a baseline ccfDNA KRAS mutation gets no prediction with a note: the paper reports those patients separately (the 3 with a wild-type primary tumour but a baseline ccfDNA KRAS mutation showed no treatment response, cases 47/56/63, md:216) and that baseline finding is not this call; the paper defines no handling for a patient with no baseline ccfDNA draw or an unassayable baseline, so those get no prediction too.

methods.description: Two-group survival stratification by the CD4+ T-cell polyfunctional strength index (PSI) change under immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy in advanced/recurrent NSCLC (Lim Z-F, Wu X, Zhu L, et al., Transl Lung Cancer Res 2024;13(12):3323-3343, DOI 10.21037/tlcr-24-260; 10 NSCLC patients on ICI-based regimens and 10 healthy donors, IsoLight/IsoSpeak live single-cell 32-plex cytokine profiling of magnetic-bead-enriched CD4+ T-cells from PBMC; PSI = rate of polyfunctional cells x average signal intensity of significantly secreted cytokines, empty-chamber background subtracted and <2%-of-samples cytokines excluded, md:117, md:71): per patient delta_psi = PSI (post-2 cycles) - PSI (baseline), and the rule splits high = delta_psi > 5 vs low = delta_psi <= 5 (md:180, the boundary at exactly 5 IS resolved into the low group); the paper compared the two groups by Kaplan-Meier PFS and OS - median PFS 10.8 vs 2.8 months (3.9-fold, P=0.07) and median OS 34.5 vs 11.5 months (3.0-fold, P=0.09) - a 'strong trend' only (P>0.05; no hazard ratio, no group N, no P-value test name, no PFS/OS definition, no cutoff derivation and no per-patient probability published). The wrapper takes the one marker the benchmark passes (the per-draw CD4+ T-cell PSI index value), pairs the last baseline draw (day <= baseline_max_day) with the first on-treatment draw up to the benchmark landmark (the paper's post-2-cycle draw; the protocol drew at baseline and every two cycles, no day numbers printed), forms the two groups at the published cutoff (5.0), writes the delta as risk (the quantity the rule thresholds; in the paper's own direction - higher delta = the favourable group - so the failure orientation of the benchmark is carried by call and by the package's learned risk-to-failure probability conversion) and call (1 = delta <= 5, the paper's poorer-prognosis group, treatment judged failing; 0 = delta > 5), writes no probability of its own (the paper defines none; TxResBench converts the risk per outcome), and records the training-fold per-group Kaplan-Meier median PFS/OS as fit diagnostics in run.json (the paper's reported cohort-level results are recorded verbatim as reported). A patient without a baseline PSI draw or without an on-treatment PSI draw by the landmark gets no prediction, with the reason in note. Nothing is learned from the training outcomes (fitted false; the cutoff is the paper's published constant).

methods.description: The per-patient early change (Delta = post-2-cycles minus baseline) of the CD8+ T-cell single-cell polyfunctionality indices overall polyfunctionality (PolyFx, % single cells secreting >= 2 cytokines) and polyfunctional strength index (PSI, polyfunctional-cell rate x average intensity) from the IsoLight/IsoSpeak 32-plex cytokine profiling of PBMC-derived T-cells, as a predictive biomarker of early ICI treatment response in advanced/recurrent NSCLC (Lim et al., Translational Lung Cancer Research 2024;13(12):3323-3343, DOI 10.21037/tlcr-24-260): responders (RECIST CR/PR at the 2-cycle assessment) had significantly higher CD8+ Delta-PolyFx (P=0.02 Wilcoxon / P=0.01 mixed model) and Delta-PSI (P=0.02 / P=0.006) than non-responders (SD/PD), while CD4+ Delta values and baseline values did not differ, and PD-L1 TPS alone did not correlate (P=0.08, 80% accuracy). The wrapper takes exactly two markers - the per-draw PolyFx index (markers[0]) and the per-draw PSI index (markers[1]), roles by sorted order, the corpus convention of the fixed-list wrappers (the benchmark's features polyfx_cd8 / psi_cd8 sort to that order) - computes the per-patient Delta pair (T1 = the marker's last draw on or before baseline_max_day; T2 = its last draw after that and at or before the landmark; draws after the landmark never enter; non-detects and zero values participate as 0, the raw difference of the paper), and writes as risk the Delta of the PolyFx index, signed so that higher = more likely failing: the sign is oriented at fit from the training patients' failure label (the paper's R-vs-NR comparison on the training fold - the paper's own analysis is a labeled group comparison; the paper's published direction is the fallback, so a dataset whose marker rises in responders reads the opposite sign), with the paper's direction (Delta up = responder-like) recorded in run.json. The paper defines no cutoff, no per-patient call and no probability, so the wrapper writes risk only and the roster group response-call is recorded as a deviation: the contract classification is static-risk, one score at the landmark (the method is a group-comparison/risk attribution, not a yes/no rule). The fit also reproduces the paper's Wilcoxon group comparison (R vs NR on the two Delta values) as a cohort-level record in run.json and reports the paper's published statistics as printed; the paper's linear mixed model is NOT reproduced (its response and formula are unpublished - 'different model-parameters', md:76 - and one Delta per patient makes the subject random effect degenerate; recorded in run.json). A patient without a scorable baseline + on-treatment pair of the risk marker gets no prediction with the reason in note (the paper's inclusion requirement, 'each NSCLC patient has at least two time point samples', md:191).

methods.description: The cumulative serum-CEA burden rule of Li et al. 2024, British Journal of Cancer (DOI 10.1038/s41416-024-02678-8; 1416 stage I-III NSCLC patients after curative resection with serial CEA during the first 3 years of follow-up). Stage 0: a latent-class growth mixed model (the paper's final model: cubic polynomial in time with four latent classes of log-transformed CEA; the paper's named software, R package lcmm 1.9.2) groups the patients into trajectory classes; the wrapper re-derives the class number with the paper's own rule (BIC among the models with mean posterior probability > 0.7) by a deterministic ladder 4-3-2 classes and maps the fitted classes to the paper's names (low-stable, decreasing, early-rising + later-rising = rising) by the shape of the fitted curves. Stage 1: per patient, the cumulative CEA burden = the integral (time average) of the patient's estimated CEA trajectory curve over their observed follow-up window up to the decision day, divided by the window length (md:113-117) - the patient's subject-specific curve (class curve plus the empirical-Bayes random intercept), back-transformed to ng/mL. Stage 2: among the patients NOT in the low-stable class, the burden is split into quartiles (the paper's Quantile 1-4, Table 2) and the split is jointly crossed with the trajectory class into the paper's five CEA joint groups (low-stable, decreasing & low/high, rising & low/high; Table 3) at the median burden. Cox proportional-hazards models of OS and RFS on the residual clock with the joint group as the predictor, fully adjusted for the benchmark's cov_* columns (the paper's Model 3; Models 1-2 also fitted and reported) yield the group HRs. Risk = the patient's cumulative CEA burden (the time-averaged estimated CEA curve, the quantity the quartile rule thresholds and the one the paper reports as positively associated with the risk of death), higher = more failing; probabilities = 1 - S_group(horizon - landmark) from the training-fold per-group Kaplan-Meier curves of the fitted joint group; the paper's Table 2/3 HRs, KM rates and the class/burden/quartile/joint tables are reported per training fold in run.json. Differences from the paper (no published code, exact lcmm call not published ('?'), the integration scale/window unstated ('?'), the joint low/high threshold unstated ('?'), the benchmark's landmark truncation, the min_draws 3 eligibility vs the paper's four measurements, the 266-vs-213 discrepancy) are recorded in README.md, run.json and the deviations list.

methods.description: Early ('explosive') disease-progression / EGFR-TKI-resistance call from serial serum CEA (Gao Y, Song P, Li H, et al., 'Elevated serum CEA levels are associated with the explosive progression of lung adenocarcinoma harboring EGFR mutations', BMC Cancer 2017;17:484, DOI 10.1186/s12885-017-3474-3; 155 EGFR-mutant primary lung adenocarcinoma patients, 2011-2015, Shandong Provincial Tumor Hospital, on gefitinib 250 mg/d or erlotinib 150 mg/d as 1st/2nd/3rd line; serum CEA normal range 0-3.4 ng/ml, Elecsys200 electrochemiluminescence, measured before TKI treatment and prior to each treatment cycle, every 2 months simultaneously with the CT scan): 'CEA levels 16.2 times higher than normal at any point during the 2 months prior to the determination of progress represented an early response to disease progression (HR, 5.77; 95% CI:2.36 ~ 14.11; p < 0.001; Table 4)' - a per-draw numeric predicate (any draw with CEA >= fold_uln (16.2) times the assay's upper limit of normal uln (3.4 ng/ml), i.e. >= approx. 55.08 ng/ml, the spec's arithmetic) combined by an any-timepoint OR into a per-patient binary group: elevated = the paper's early/explosive-progression call = treatment judged failing, non-elevated = not. The wrapper takes one marker (the per-draw serum CEA value, ng/ml), applies the OR to the patient's on-treatment draws after baseline_max_day up to the benchmark's landmark (a wrapper adaptation, recorded under the deviations: the paper's 2-month elevation window is anchored on the CT progression determination - outcome-side information a prediction at the landmark does not have), writes risk = the patient's maximum CEA in multiples of the upper limit of normal, exactly the quantity the rule thresholds (the paper publishes no per-patient score; the wrapper's choice, recorded in the spec's deviations - the cohort HR 5.77 and the chi-square/KM statistics are cohort-level), and call = 1 when that maximum reaches >= fold_uln, 0 when it stays below; no probability is written (the paper defines none per patient, so the package converts the risk). Fitted false: nothing is learned from the training outcomes - the 16.2 multiple was derived in the authors' own sample ('the average value (CEA levels 16.2 times higher than normal) in elevated group', md:115; a circular in-sample statistic with no implementable train-only derivation) and is treated here as the published constant (params fold_uln/uln; recorded under the deviations). A patient with no on-treatment draw by the landmark gets no prediction, with the reason in note; the paper's cohort-level numbers (multivariate Cox HR 5.769, 95% CI 2.359-14.108, Table 4 step 3 with Age Exp(B) 2.257 and Stage Exp(B) 2.351; chi-square p < 0.005; median time to the threshold 8.3 months vs median PFS 12.8 months; 4.5-month CEA lead over CT) are recorded in the fit report as reported, not fitted or predicted.

methods.description: The per-patient high/low risk-group call of Ko JMY et al., 'Liquid Biopsy Serial Monitoring of Treatment Responses and Relapse in Advanced Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma' (Cancers 2020;12(6):1352, DOI 10.3390/cancers12061352; 57 analysed of 60 recruited advanced stage III/IV ESCC patients on palliative (mostly platinum-based) chemotherapy, Queen Mary Hospital 2016-2019): from the plasma cell-free DNA concentration (copies of haploid genome (hG)/mL plasma, Qubit 2.0 dsDNA HS quantification after AVENIO cfDNA isolation) at baseline (cfDNA1) and pre-cycle III (cfDNA2, after two cycles, ~6 weeks after baseline), log10-transformed ('The cfDNA levels were log10-transformed and included as continuous variables.', md:223) and dichotomized at the ROC-derived cutoffs for overall survival: high = log10 cfDNA1 >= 3.360 (~2291 copies hG/mL plasma, AUROC 0.627, sensitivity 0.667, specificity 0.533, n = 48; Table S2), high = log10 cfDNA2 >= 3.2817 (~1913 copies, AUROC 0.595, sensitivity 0.714, specificity 0.462, n = 41; Table S2) ('the thresholds of baseline and pre-cycle III log cfDNA levels were chosen at 3.360... and 3.2817... for OS, after considering sensitivity and specificity', md:171), giving per-timepoint high vs low groups; and the change rule: 'Patients with unfavorable changes of both high cfDNA1 (>=3.360) and cfDNA2 (>=3.2817) are categorized into the high-risk group, while others including those with both low cfDNA1 and cfDNA2, or from high cfDNA1 to low cfDNA2, or with low cfDNA1 and high cfDNA2 are categorized into the low-risk group.' (md:171; 2 groups, favorable n = 21 / unfavorable n = 19, Table 2C). Published results: high vs low cfDNA1 median OS 172 vs 302 days (p = 0.007), cfDNA2 172 vs 479 days (p = 0.009), favorable vs unfavorable change 363 vs 160 days (p = 3.7e-4) (Figure 2Biv-vi, md:171); univariate continuous log10 Cox OS HR 8.338 (2.42-28.7, p = 0.001, n = 48) / 5.451 (1.74-17.1, p = 0.004, n = 41) (Table 2C), change-rule HR 4.444 (1.85-10.68, p = 0.001) univariate and 24.494 (5.076-118.198, p = 6.8e-5) multivariable (Table S5, with age, stage and the CTC1/2 change groups). The wrapper takes exactly one marker (the plasma cfDNA concentration), pairs the patient's draws (cfDNA1 = last draw on or before baseline_max_day; cfDNA2 = last draw after it and at or before the benchmark landmark - the corpus fixed-pair convention, the paper's pre-cycle III visit being at ~6 weeks after baseline, md:194), applies the log10 transform and the two thresholds, and writes risk = the log10 cfDNA2 level - exactly the quantity the on-treatment threshold applies to (the paper defines no per-patient score; higher cfDNA2 = shorter OS) - and call = 0/1 of the paper's change rule (1 = unfavorable both-high = the high-risk group = treatment judged failing, 0 = the favorable low-risk group of all other combinations); the per-timepoint calls are the change call's components and are recorded in the fit report. It writes no probability (the paper defines none per patient, so TxResBench converts the risk). Nothing is learned from the training outcomes (fitted false): the ROC thresholds were derived in the authors' own sample by ROC analysis for OS and the optimality criterion is not published, so both are treated as the published constants (params log10_threshold_cfdna1/log10_threshold_cfdna2, per the corpus's published-constant convention). A patient without both usable draws (paper's complete-case: cfDNA1 n = 48, cfDNA2 n = 41, change n = 40 of 57; no imputation stated) gets no prediction, with the reason in note; a below-detection-limit value (the benchmark's 0 with a <marker>__detected row of 0) is not log10-transformable and the paper publishes no non-detect convention (all 57 specimens quantified; Table S1 minima 1067.0 / 315.2 copies hG/mL at cfDNA1/cfDNA2), so such a patient also gets no prediction, with the reason in note.

methods.description: The two-stage cfEBV DNA response-phenotype rule of Lv J et al. (Nature Communications 2019;10:4221; 673 LA-NPC patients on induction chemotherapy plus concurrent chemo-radiotherapy, all with detectable pretreatment cfEBV DNA): stage 1 is one of eight response patterns defined by the timing of complete biological response (cBR = undetectable cfEBV DNA) over the treatment phases plus the bounce event - G1 cBR post-IC1 without bounce, G2 post-IC2, G3 post-IC3-4, G4 cBR post-CCRT with 2 IC cycles, G5 cBR post-CCRT with 3-4 IC cycles, G6 temporary bounce with cBR post-CCRT, G7 persistent bounce with non-cBR post-CCRT, G8 persistent DNA; stage 2 collapses the patterns into four prognostic phenotypes by the paper's supervised intergroup-HR clustering (G1 = Cluster 1 early responders, G2/G3/G4/G6 = Cluster 2 intermediate responders, G5 = Cluster 3 late responders, G7/G8 = Cluster 4 treatment-resistant, AHR_DFS 3.46/7.50/17.33 vs the reference, 3-year DFS 94.3/78.0/60.5/25.1%). The wrapper reads one marker, maps the paper's phase-coded readout sequence onto the benchmark clock positionally (the last draw on or before the landmark is the call-time readout = the post-CCRT window at the call; the earlier on-treatment draws are the post-IC readouts in order), classifies on the per-draw detectability call (<marker>__detected rows when present, else 0/1 values, else value compared with detection_threshold, default the training median as a documented stand-in for the assay's undetectable call), and writes the phenotype as risk (0 Cluster 1 early, 1 Cluster 2 intermediate, 2 Cluster 3 late, 3 Cluster 4 treatment-resistant; higher = worse, the paper's AHR_DFS ordering) and call 1 for Cluster 4 (treatment-resistant: the paper's failure class, AHR_DFS 17.33) and 0 otherwise. It writes no probability (the paper defines none; TxResBench converts the risk). A patient with undetectable pretreatment cfEBV DNA gets no prediction with the reason in note (inclusion criterion 3: 'pretreatment EBV DNA >0 copies/ml'), as does a patient whose number of IC cycles is unknown when the first cBR is only at the call-time readout - the G4-vs-G5 (and G2-vs-G3) labels encode the cycle count, which the marker draws alone cannot supply; the wrapper reads the per-patient cycle count from the covariates table when the dataset carries it (ic_cycles_covariates, first present column) and otherwise abstains with the paper's no-fallback reason rather than inventing a count.

methods.description: The three-category ctDNA clearance call from serial cfMeDIP-seq percent-ctDNA trajectories of Burgener et al. (Clin Cancer Res 2021;27(14):3955-3964, DOI 10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-21-0110; 30 locoregionally confined HPV-negative HNSCC patients treated curatively by surgery +/- adjuvant (chemo)radiotherapy, blood at diagnosis and 3 months post-surgery plus pre-RT/mid-RT/12-month draws in some patients): the per-draw marker is the percent ctDNA (mean RPKM across the 941 plasma-derived hyper-DMRs, fragments limited to 100-150 bp, converted by RPKMtoCtDNA(x) = 3.2394x - 0.1233, the linear regression of baseline cfMeDIP mean RPKM on matched baseline CAPP-seq mean MAF; the wrapper takes the marker already as percent ctDNA, or as the mean RPKM with value_scale 'rpk'), and the paper's definitions (verbatim, md:231) are: complete clearance = a decrease below the 0.2% detection threshold (the maximum of mean RPKM values across all healthy controls converted to percent ctDNA) at the first available mid-/post-treatment timepoint; partial clearance = an observed >=90% decrease in ctDNA abundance from diagnosis compared with last follow-up; no clearance = an observed <90% decrease or >=0% increase from diagnosis to last follow-up. The wrapper reads the baseline as the last draw on or before baseline_max_day, the first post-treatment draw as the first draw after it and at or before the landmark (the paper's first-available-draw check for complete clearance) and the last follow-up draw as the last draw after it and at or before the landmark (the paper's last-follow-up comparison for partial/no), and writes risk = the native three-group code (0 complete clearance, 1 partial clearance, 2 no clearance; higher = more likely failing - the paper's ordering: the 5/18 no-clearance patients were more likely to recur, HR 8.73, 95% CI 1.5-50.92, log-rank P = 0.0046, vs the 13 with undetectable post-treatment ctDNA, 9/13 disease-free at 44.4-month median follow-up) and call = 1 for no clearance, 0 for complete/partial clearance (the paper's own A/B contrast for the group association, and its flagged finding 'lack of ctDNA clearance post-treatment strongly correlating with recurrence'). It writes no probability (the paper defines none; TxResBench converts the risk). A patient with no baseline value, a baseline not above the detection threshold (not evaluable: the paper's analysis is 'on the basis of the criteria of having detectable ctDNA in baseline samples by CAPP-seq', n = 18/30; the CAPP-seq marker is not carried by the benchmark, so the wrapper applies the same set's in-marker half, baseline percent above the threshold, as the code does), or no draw between baseline and the landmark gets no prediction with the reason in note. At fit the paper's group association is recomputed on the training patients and reported in run.json: KM and log-rank test and the univariable Cox (no clearance vs complete/partial clearance) of recurrence-free survival, from the harness progression outcome (pfs_time/pfs_event) as the stand-in for the paper's recurrence-free survival (the paper's clock starts at the diagnosis visit, the harness's at the first dose). Wrapper differences from the paper (detailed in README.md): the named protocol visits have no benchmark channel (the benchmark clock's landmark replaces the paper's last-follow-up date; a run decides at the landmark), the paper's sample-derived 0.2% detection threshold is used as the published fixed value (the benchmark carries no healthy controls to recompute the max mean RPKM), the paper's CAPP-seq baseline detectability has no marker channel (the code's in-marker condition baseline meanRPKM > Norm_maxRPKM is applied instead; the two select the same 18 patients in the paper's cohort), the marker conversion/kinetics are the paper's published regression constants (fitted on the 30 baseline samples, applied to post-treatment as the paper does), and the strict '<' below-threshold comparison is the code's (a value exactly at 0.2% is not complete clearance).

methods.description: The per-patient ctDNA clearance call from the joint cfMeDIP-seq score of Stutheit-Zhao et al. (Cancer Discov 2024;14(3):454-469, DOI 10.1158/2159-8290.CD-23-1060; 87 patients with various metastatic cancers on pembrolizumab in INSPIRE, cfMeDIP-seq on 204 plasma samples plus 100 normal controls): the score is the predicted log-odds of cancer from the paper's fitted logistic regression glm(cancer ~ log10(CSM + 0.01) + FLS, family = 'binomial') - CSM = cancer-specific methylation score (the arithmetic sum of methylation probabilities over the 200-DMC immune-depleted cancer signature) and FLS = fragment-length score (the mean log2 cancer-to-normal fragment-length ratio over CSM-signature fragments) - fitted on the 85 baseline (SB) INSPIRE cancer samples vs 100 normal controls (99 used after the FLS join), and a sample is 'clearance' when its score is below the CMC-calibrated threshold -1.754 (the value derived by max-F1 on the CMC-detectability ROC of the 128 samples with CMC, reproduced -1.754328; AUROC 0.902; 11 of the 87 patients cleared, 9 concordant with CMC clearance). The wrapper takes exactly two markers (markers[0] = the per-draw CSM score, markers[1] = the per-draw FLS; roles are also recognised by name, declared in required_markers with the positional fallback documented in the README), computes the score per draw, and per patient with a baseline draw (day <= baseline_max_day) and at least one on-treatment draw (day > baseline_max_day and <= landmark) writes risk = the minimum on-treatment score (the quantity the paper's 'any on-treatment sample below the threshold' call thresholds: called cleared exactly when the minimum is below it) and call = 1 when no on-treatment sample clears (the paper's not-cleared side: Increase/Decrease groups), 0 when cleared. The classifier and threshold are the paper's published fitted values - the benchmark's contract carries no normal-control stream, no per-sample cancer-vs-control labels and no CMC (tumour-informed Signatera MTM/mL) values, so the wrapper applies the published model as the fixed rule (readiness: new-patient prediction is just the coefficients applied to a new sample's log10(CSM + 0.01) and FLS); the four constants are method_params with defaults from the reproduced fit (intercept 1.532508, log10(CSM+0.01) 1.877978, FLS 1.049207, offset 0.01, threshold -1.754328), so a benchmark's own train-fold-only derivation can replace them. The score is a log-odds of cancer (higher = more cancer-like = treatment more likely failing), not a probability; no per-horizon probability is part of the method, so TxResBench converts the risk per outcome. A patient without a baseline draw, without an on-treatment draw, or whose on-treatment draws lack both markers gets no prediction, with the reason in note.
methods.licence: the wrapper applies the paper's published fitted values (three logistic coefficients, the log10 + 0.01 offset and the -1.754 clearance threshold) in base R; the authors' reference code repository github.com/pughlab/paper-inspire-cfmedip commit 30c5af528e7b0a0577b6844bbd5533f52ca8aee9 carries no licence file (checked in the store clone) and no code from it is copied; the container contract helper TxrMethod of the base image is MIT

methods.description: The combined tiered ctDNA molecular response rule of Sivapalan et al. (Clinical Cancer Research 2023;29(9):1646-1654, DOI 10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-22-2242; 33 metastatic SCLC patients on platinum-based or immunotherapy-containing therapy, 171 serial plasmas): per timepoint the cell-free tumor load (cfTL) is read from two modalities - markers[0], the MAF (%) of the most abundant tumor-derived mutation (0% MAF = complete elimination, the mutation-based cfTL of the n = 27 mutation-arm patients), and markers[1], the per-sample plasma aneuploidy (PA) score (above 4.90 = tumor aneuploidy, at or below 4.90 = normal ploidy), which is the readout for the n = 6 patients without detectable tumor-derived sequence alterations and the second operand for the n = 20 patients with both evaluable. The paper's combined tiered approach ('based on combined mutation and aneuploidy dynamics, or PA for patients without detectable mutations') and its cfTL definition ('the contribution of the most abundant tumor-derived sequence and/or PA score > 4.9') are read by the wrapper as per-timepoint presence P(t) = sequence detectable OR PA > 4.90 (a modality with no row at t contributes no evidence), and the per-patient 3-category call is made on the on-treatment trajectory from the baseline to the final timepoint: molecular response (call 0) when P is absent at the final timepoint (the paper's 'sustained complete elimination' plus its AND requirement - both mutation and PA elimination - for the molecular response category), molecular progression (call 1, the paper's inferior class and the reference category of its Cox analyses) when P is present at every on-treatment timepoint ('persistence of cfTL across all sampled plasma time points'), and molecular response followed by recrudescence (call 0) when cfTL returns at the final timepoint after an intermediate elimination. The wrapper writes risk = the combined cfTL readout at the final timepoint (the sequence max-MAF when detectable there, else the PA score when above 4.90, else 0; higher = more cfTL at the final timepoint = the paper's worse classes) and no probability (the paper defines none - its AUCs, log-rank and Cox HRs are group-level validation); TxResBench converts the risk. The paper publishes no analysis code, so the rule is implemented from the Methods/Results text; the paper's three documented special cases (PT 2 / PT 24 final-timepoint-only sequence detection, PA-driven PT 6, partial-discordance PT 25) all fall out of the general rule, and the wrapper's own readings (benchmark-clock draws, baseline value not gating a category, risk scalar choice, mPD-only call=1, 3-draw minimum, upstream WBC-informed variant filtering and the <3 ng cfDNA exclusion being the dataset's marker contract) are listed in the method's README.

methods.description: The per-patient molecular response classification rule of Murray et al. (Clinical Cancer Research 2024; DOI 10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-23-1469; 30 patients with advanced or metastatic NSCLC treated with single-agent immunotherapy or chemoimmunotherapy, 162 serial plasma samples, TEC-Seq): the cell-free tumor load (cfTL) of each plasma sample is the maximum MAF (%) of the most abundant tumor-derived mutation, and the patient is called on the serial cfTL trajectory from the baseline (pre-treatment; median 0 weeks, or the pre-cycle-2 sample for 4 patients) to the final timepoint analyzed - molecular response (mR) when cfTL is cleared to 0% at the final timepoint (below the assay's level of detection, supermutant count >= 3), molecular response followed by recrudescence or emergence when clearance is followed by a subsequent increase, and molecular progression (mPD) when cfTL persists across all time points analyzed; patients with no detectable tumor-derived ctDNA (4 of 30) are undetectable and not evaluable. The rule is fixed (no fitting, no tuning; the only cutoff is the assay detection limit) and no analysis code is published, so the wrapper implements it from the Methods/Results text. It writes risk = the cfTL (%) at the final timepoint (0 = the clearance state; higher = more tumor load at the final draw = the paper's worse class mPD) and call = 1 for molecular progression (the paper's inferior-outcome group: median PFS 2.70 vs 18.51/17.82 months, OS 5.75 vs 23.01/18.51 months, log-rank P = 0.001/0.04) and 0 for molecular response and for molecular response followed by recrudescence or emergence; no per-patient probability is defined by the paper (its Kaplan-Meier/log-rank and univariate/multivariate Cox associations are group-level validation), so TxResBench converts the risk.

methods.description: The CIRI-LCRT dynamic risk model of Moding EJ et al., 'Integrating circulating tumor DNA analysis and radiomics for dynamic risk assessment in localized lung cancer', Cancer Discovery 2025, DOI 10.1158/2159-8290.CD-24-1704: a Bayesian Cox proportional-hazards model (the Continuous Individualized Risk Index framework, 'as described previously (66)' - identified by web evidence and recorded in the spec as Kurtz DM et al., Cell 2019, DOI 10.1016/j.cell.2019.06.011) that produces per-patient personalized survival functions as treatment features become available. The published model's final features are tumor histology (non-squamous vs squamous), the pre-CRT radiomic score (1.75 x margin blurriness + 1.67 x vessel scattering) and the log-transformed mid-CRT ctDNA concentration (hGE/ml), with the risk updated when the mid-CRT ctDNA measurement arrives (pre-CRT: histology + radiomics; mid-CRT: + ctDNA). The wrapper implements the paper's stated structure on the benchmark's single training fold: (1) a baseline survival function defined across the full training cohort before considering individual risk factors (the paper pools n=357 from RTOG 0235 + the historical + ctDNA training cohorts; the benchmark gives one fold, recorded); (2) per-covariate coefficient hyper-parameters (normal mean mu and variance sigma^2) inferred from the uncertainty around the prior survival curves via Greenwood's formula weighted by the number of patients at risk (the paper infers them per covariate from different subset cohorts; the benchmark gives one fold, recorded); (3) Cox partial likelihood as the likelihood (Efron tie handling, R's default - the paper states no tie method); (4) Markov Chain Monte Carlo (random-walk Metropolis, seed from the run) to compute the individual posterior survival curves from the data available at the landmark. The final model has the fewest features, histology + radiomics + mid-CRT ctDNA (the model among the top 10 in the ctDNA training cohort by C-statistic; the wrapper also supports the pre-CRT (no-ctDNA) variant as the Bayesian missing-covariate property when the marker or a covariate is unavailable: 'patient-level risk can be calculated even if all prognostic factors are not available'). Undetectable ctDNA is assigned an allele fraction one log below the limit of detection (Poisson LOD in the paper; the benchmark's <marker>__lod row, else the training fold's smallest positive detected value, recorded) before the log transform; concentrations are log10-transformed and all covariates standardized (the paper's stated conventions). The wrapper writes as risk the PFS model's first-horizon probability of progression or death conditioned on being event-free at the landmark (P(progression or death by day h | event-free at L) via the survival curve), the same per-outcome for death, and the 0/1 call of the paper's mid-CRT two-way risk-group split (<=50% vs >50% predicted risk of progression or death by 36 months, md:78); the three-way cutoffs (<33%, 33-66%, >66%) are recorded per patient in run.json. The paper publishes no CIRI code (no repository, no package; the availability statement names only the CAPP-Seq pipeline, the Lung-CLiP SNV score and the lung-radiomics feature extractor) and the fitted hyper-parameters are not printed, so nothing was substituted or downloaded: the wrapper reimplements the model from the paper text, and every deviation is recorded in the README and run.json.

methods.description: Week-4 landmark two-group risk classification on the serum cumulative methylation index (CMI) of the six-gene cMethDNA panel, with multivariable Cox models of PFS and OS and a logistic regression of PD at first restaging on the change in log CMI (Visvanathan et al., J Clin Oncol 2017, TBCRC 005). The wrapper's marker is the one marker passed, treated as the CMI and transformed to the paper's analysis scale (natural log after adding 0.1, a transform setting). The benchmark's week-4 value is the last marker draw after the baseline day and at or before the landmark day; the cut point is re-derived in each training fold by the maximal log-rank statistic (maxstat LogRank, the paper's selection procedure; its sample values 9 (PFS) / 21 (OS) are not hard-coded) separately for progression and death, high CMI means the value is at or above the cut point, and a Cox model on the landmark cohort (patients event-free at the landmark, clock from treatment initiation) records the group association with every cov_* column when covariates are passed (the paper's five adjustment covariates have no default harness channel, so the group-only model is the benchmark's default). It writes the log week-4 CMI as the risk and the two-group call (1 = high CMI at the PFS cut point, or the OS cut point when the training data have no progression outcome); TxResBench converts the risk into probabilities. A patient without a baseline value or without a marker draw during treatment by the landmark gets no prediction.

methods.description: Favorable vs unfavorable chromosomal-instability (CNA) change of plasma ctDNA, the per-patient rule of Cheng et al. (Cancer Innovation 2025;4:e70014, DOI 10.1002/cai2.70014) at the before-third-cycle draw of pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (PLD, 40 mg/m2 Q4w, 6 cycles) or PLD + apatinib (250 mg po qd) in platinum-resistant recurrent ovarian cancer (PROC): the marker is the per-draw chromosome-instability I score (the sum of the absolute Wisecondor X Z scores of the usable bins/segments with Z > 2 or Z < -2, from shallow whole-genome sequencing, unitless); a favorable CNA change is (1) CNA negative during treatment (I score < 14), or (2) the I score declined by more than 27.8 from baseline (or (3), CNA positivity at baseline that became negative, covered by (1)); everything else is unfavorable (CNA negativity at baseline turning positive, or positivity that increased, or a decline of 27.8 or less). In 49 patients (35 cohort A + 14 cohort B; 30 no clinical benefit / 19 clinical benefit), a favorable CNA change before the third cycle predicted the best overall response (RECIST) with 70.0% sensitivity (21/30) and 78.9% specificity (15/19) and was associated with longer PFS (HR 2.19, 95% CI 1.15-4.17, log-rank p = 0.007; multivariate Cox p = 0.009). The wrapper takes the per-draw I score as its single marker (the I-score computation from Wisecondor X is upstream of the rule), writes the signed change of the I score from the baseline draw to the on-treatment draw as risk and the 0/1 call (1 = unfavorable = the treatment judged failing); the thresholds are the paper's fixed values, nothing is fitted.

methods.description: The combined ctDNA criteria for resistance to HER1/HER2 blockade of F2016 et al., Oncotarget 2016;7(33):53804-16 (DOI 10.18632/oncotarget.11791): 18 HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer patients on pyrotinib (oral anti-HER1/HER2 TKI, 28 d/cycle), blood sampled before treatment and after every two cycles until progression (md:178), 368-gene target-capture NGS of plasma matched with blood cells, HER2 (ERBB2) amplification by CONTRA and per-gene mutation allele fractions (md:188, md:193). The rule ('Drug resistance should be indicated during treatment if any of the following situations applies: 1) recurrence or persistence of HER2 amplification in the blood; 2) emergence or >=20% increase in the fraction of mutations in any of these resistance-related genes including TP53/PIK3CA/MTOR/PTEN.', md:124; the 20% is a relative-increase factor >= 1.2 after the assay error margin, md:124, md:170) is applied per patient at the last on-treatment draw by the benchmark landmark against the pre-treatment draw: call = 1 when criterion 1 (HER2 amplification detected at the evaluation draw - under the two-point reading 'recurrence or persistence' reduces to 'detected at the evaluation draw') or criterion 2 (in any of the four genes: the fraction undetectable at baseline and detected at the evaluation draw, the paper's 'emergence' branch, or a >=20% relative increase with the boundary included) fires; an unevaluable arm counts as not firing. The wrapper's risk - the quantity the call's 20% rule thresholds, averaged over the genes - is the geometric mean of the per-gene relative change factors x1/x0 over the genes detected at the evaluation draw (an emergence factor is measured against the patient's smallest positive value of the gene's fraction, else the training minimum positive, because the magnitude of a rise from an undetectable fraction is undefined in the paper, '?'; the paper defines no per-patient scalar at all - its two arms live on different scales - so the wrapper writes the strongest single quantitative criterion's scale, and the paper's Table 2 sensitivity/specificity/concordance and Figure 4 PFS split are cohort-level validation statistics, not per-patient output). It writes no probability: TxResBench converts the risk. The genes' multiple variants per gene are not defined in the paper (Table 1, md:101-105 has e.g. two TP53 and two PIK3CA variants in patient No. 17, '?'), so the method takes one or more per-draw allele-fraction series of the resistance genes plus the per-draw HER2 amplification state (declared as required_markers): series are identified by marker name (gene symbol / erbb2-her2 with amplification-cnv-copy number), several fraction series of one gene are aggregated per draw by the maximum (the strongest variant's fraction), a set of names identifying no role uses the positional convention markers[0..n-2] = the fraction series, markers[n-1] = the amplification state, a partially identified set is refused, and a patient without a baseline/on-treatment pair of a resistance-gene fraction abstains with the reason in note. The HER2 amplification state is read from the dataset's <marker>__detected rows (the assay's amplification call; the paper's CONTRA absolute copy-number threshold is in the missing Supplementary Figure S1, '?'), else from a 0/1 amplification-status marker, else from the amp_detection_threshold setting; without any of these the amplification arm is unevaluable and the call rests on criterion 2 (the paper's cohort always carries the call, md:135-136).
