methods.description: The five-factor on-treatment biomarker index of Soerensen et al. (Acta Oncol 2016;55(4):464-470, DOI 10.3109/0284186X.2015.1091499, DARENCA research 2; 735 Danish first-line mRCC patients on TKI (sunitinib, sorafenib) or IL2-based immunotherapy 2006-2010; overall survival from start of first-line treatment): five binary on-treatment features - sodium >= LLN, LDH <= 1.5 x ULN, platelets < LLN, neutrophils < LLN and systolic BP >= 140 mmHg (Table IV) - each standardized to the treating hospital's upper/lower limit of normal, derived by univariate (p <= 0.1) then multivariable time-dependent Cox with p < 0.05 retention on baseline IMDC risk groups, stratified for TKI vs IL2-based therapy (Table III, N = 588; the haemoglobin interaction excluded it, md:154) and internally validated with 300 bootstrap samples (md:29); the published per-patient tool is the fixed rule: one point per feature MET at ANY day-1-of-cycle draw in the paper's window (after baseline, within 12 weeks of treatment, 'the patient would remain in the category despite subsequent reversal of values', md:20), summed to the 0-5 index (Table IV), then split into a good (3-5 features, median OS 23.5 months) vs poor (0-2 features, 9.6 months, p < 0.0001) biomarker profile (md:186). The wrapper takes exactly the five markers (serum sodium, serum LDH, platelet count, absolute neutrophil count, systolic BP; the fixed list is recorded in required_markers), evaluates the 'ever met, stays 1' indicators over the on-treatment draws after baseline_max_day within the paper's 12-week (day 84) window capped at the benchmark's landmark, and writes risk = 5 - index (the paper's index is oriented favourably - higher = better prognosis; the wrapper inverts monotonically to the harness convention higher = worse; the inversion is recorded in README, the spec's deviation) and call = 1 for the paper's poor profile (0-2 features, treatment judged failing) and 0 for the good profile (3-5 features); no per-patient probability is written (the paper publishes none - the C-index 0.625 (IMDC alone) vs 0.683 (with the five covariates, md:174), bootstrap C-index 0.685 (md:181), per-feature HRs (Table III) and per-profile median OS (md:186, Table V md:217-224) are cohort-level and are recorded in the fit report as reported, not fitted). The paper's per-hospital LLN/ULN reference values are NOT published ('BS were standardised to upper (ULN) and lower level of normal (LLN) for the treating hospital', md:20; the spec records the reference ranges as a per-patient input not published), so the wrapper applies standard clinical reference limits as documented defaults (sodium LLN 135 mmol/L, LDH ULN 250 U/L, platelets LLN 150 x 10^9/L, neutrophils LLN 2.0 x 10^9/L; the SBP 140 mmHg threshold IS the paper's), each overridable per dataset through method_params, and records that substitution in run.json and README under the differences; a patient missing any of the five features in the window gets no prediction with the reason in note (the paper's complete-case rule: 467/596 had complete data for the index, md:186, and no imputation or fallback is defined, new_patient_prediction.fallback in the spec). The five markers are identified by name (serum sodium, LDH, lactate dehydrogenase, platelets/PLT, neutrophils/ANC, SBP/systolic); on markers whose identity cannot be recognized (the benchmark gate's synthetic M1-M5) the wrapper assigns the paper's criteria in the paper's own index-component order of md:186 ('LDH <=1.5 times ULN, SBP >=140 mmHg, sodium >= LLN, neutrophils or platelets < LLN'), keeps the SBP criterion at the published 140 mmHg and the direction-only criteria at the standard reference limits, and derives a reference value only for the one criterion the paper defines with a multiple of the reference - LDH's 1.5 x ULN - applying the published 1.5 to the marker's training-fold within-window median (all recorded in run.json; documented, not a paper claim, mirroring the cutoff_fallback precedent of cox-baseline-threshold-relchange-indicators).

methods.description: The univariate workflow of Ding, Yuan, Yang & Xu (medRxiv 2023.10.24.23297462), the per-marker analysis of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) dynamics in IMpower150 patients treated with atezolizumab and chemotherapy. One marker at a time: the marker's trajectory up to the landmark day (the paper's C3D1, Week 6, or C4D1, Week 9) is reduced by functional principal component analysis (the Karhunen-Loeve decomposition; the PACE estimator of Yao, Mueller & Wang 2005 with a penalized-spline smoothed covariance), the first two FPC scores are the features, and a Cox proportional-hazards regression of the outcome on those two scores is fitted with survival::coxph; one model per marker per survival outcome (overall survival, progression-free survival) per landmark. The paper names no FPCA implementation and publishes no code, so the estimator and its defaults (nbasis 10, pve 0.99) are recorded wrapper choices; patient FPC scores are the conditional-expectation scores under the training-fit basis. The Cox linear predictor is written as the per-outcome risk (higher = more likely failing) and as the plain risk for the response outcomes, which the paper's univariate analysis does not model and which TxResBench converts. The paper's univariate analysis reports per-marker time-dependent c-indices only - no absolute risk, no horizon, no cutoff - so the wrapper writes no own probability and no call. A marker whose FPCA basis cannot be estimated (too few patients or measurement days, a constant marker, a degenerate or failed fit) falls back to a Cox model on the last observed value at or before the landmark - the paper's handcrafted on-treatment ctDNA level - and records the reason in run.json; if even that feature is constant, every patient gets the same risk (declared in constant_ok).

methods.description: FPCRF (Ding, Yuan, Yang & Xu, medRxiv 2023.10.24.23297462): a five-step machine-learning pipeline over the trajectories of the ctDNA summary markers up to the landmark. Step 1: per-marker functional principal component analysis (FPCA; Karhunen-Loeve expansion) of each marker's trajectory, the first two FPCs per marker (the paper's fixed choice). Step 2: the FPC features of all markers are combined. Step 3: the combined features are screened with a random forest of conditional inference trees built by cforest with a survival response, and ranked by varimp (the paper's named functions, R party), keeping the top important features. Step 4: standard PCA retains the final feature matrix capturing 99% of the variability of the feature data (the paper's stated value). Step 5: the reduced feature matrix enters Cox proportional-hazards regression (survival::coxph, the paper's named function), giving a per-patient predictive risk; the paper then stratifies patients into low/intermediate/high risk by tertiles (the benchmark takes the risk itself, the stratification cutoffs being derived in the test cohort in the paper). The wrapper fits one such pipeline per survival outcome the training data give (progression and death; the paper reports separate models for OS and PFS at each landmark) with the outcome clock measured from the landmark among the patients still at risk there, writes the Cox linear predictor as the outcome's risk and 1 - S(horizon - landmark) from the fitted Breslow baseline as the outcome's own probability by each horizon day, maps the paper's two landmarks (C3D1 week 6, C4D1 week 9) onto the benchmark's landmark day, and abstains with a note for a patient it cannot score. Differences from the paper, all recorded in README.md: the paper publishes no code, so the univariate FPCA is implemented with refund::fpca.sc (PACE, nbasis 10, pve 0.99, var = FALSE; the paper names no FPCA package), the cforest ensemble settings are the party defaults (the paper states none), the response of the screening forest is the survival outcome (the paper's Surv response is not stated - party's varimp for Surv is the experimental Brier-score varimpsurv), the number of top features is not published (Figure S5 is unreachable) so the wrapper keeps the features with positive OOB permutation importance (all of them if none is positive), PCA is prcomp center-only (the paper states no scaling), the event probability projection at the harness horizons is the fitted Cox's (the paper reports only the risk score and tertiles), the survival clock is measured from the landmark (the paper's Cox clock is not stated and its KM comparisons are post-landmark), and per-marker FPCA that cannot be estimated (too few subjects or distinct measurement days, a constant marker, degenerate eigenvalues) falls back to the marker's last value by the landmark and its least-squares slope, recorded in run.json - the paper excludes such patients.

methods.description: The FULL Bayesian multivariate joint model (Mauff et al. 2020, Sections 2-3: 'Joint models with multiple longitudinal outcomes and a time-to-event outcome: a corrected two-stage approach', the reference estimator the paper compares its proposed two-stage approach against). Each framework marker is one longitudinal outcome of a linear mixed model (intercept and slope, baseline covariates when given), the random effects of the K outcomes are linked as b_i ~ MVN(0, D) with an LKJ(1.5) prior on the correlation and half-Student-t(3) priors on the scales, and the hazard of treatment failure is h_i(t) = h0(t) exp{gamma' w_i + sum_k alpha_k eta_ki(t)}: the current underlying value of each marker (the paper's Model 1 / Scenario I form), with a penalised cubic B-spline baseline hazard (Q = 15, Lang & Brezger 2004 penalty with the Jullion & Lambert hyper-prior) and the paper's priors (normal(0, 1000) for gamma; the global-local ridge shrinkage prior for alpha). The paper publishes no code and names no software for the full model (its only software statement covers the proposed two-stage estimator, JMbayes::mvJointModelBayes, which is NOT this model); the wrapper therefore estimates the full joint model from the paper by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (NumPyro's NUTS) over the marginal posterior, where the random effects are integrated numerically per patient by a deterministic quasi-Monte Carlo rule in the space of a Laplace-tilted Gaussian conditional (the numerical integration over the random effects the paper calls for). It is fitted for progression (the training patients need pfs_time/pfs_event, as for the paper's single time-to-event outcome); each patient's risk is the posterior-mean patient-specific current-value log-hazard contribution of the markers at the landmark, and p_progression_H<h> is the posterior conditional probability of progression by each horizon given the draws up to the landmark and being event-free at it (the joint model's dynamic prediction, as the paper's simulation summaries for the full model). Time in the model is years since the first dose; values are log1p-transformed (the paper's analyses log-transform the markers; a non-detect records 0).

methods.description: The Gaussian copula joint model with random effects of Zhang et al., Computational Statistics & Data Analysis 2023 (DOI 10.1016/j.csda.2022.107685): a linear mixed-effects model of the transformed marker (random intercept and slope on time; squared-root CD4 in the paper's AIDS application) is linked to the time to progression by a relative-risk hazard exp(alpha (b0 + b1 t)) with a piecewise-constant baseline hazard, and the conditional joint law of the event time and the marker given the random effects is tied together by a Gaussian copula whose correlations increase towards the later measurements (the paper's AIDS scenario 3: rho_ty^(16,8,4,2,1) at five visits, generalised by visit position; AR1 within the marker). The likelihood of the paper's equation (2) is rearranged with the adaptive kernel f(b|y) (equation 3) and integrated with the authors' rotated adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature; the wrapper writes the copula-adjusted dynamic conditional survival probability pi(u|t) = P(T > u | T > L, Y(L), w) of the paper's equation (4), first-order approximation at the posterior mode b_hat, as p_progression_H<h> (event probability by each horizon) and the first-horizon probability as risk; death and the response outcomes are converted by TxResBench from the same risk. Fitted for progression (the benchmark's primary survival outcome) on every training draw before each patient's own outcome time. The wrapper re-implements the fit driver because the authors' published code contains the log-likelihoods and prediction functions but no runnable driver (and its leave-one-out function has published bugs); the copula structures are generalised to an arbitrary sorted measurement history, the marker transform is a setting (log1p default) and, when the joint model cannot be estimated, the wrapper falls back to a Cox model on the covariates alone (recorded in run.json; the published method defines no such fallback).

methods.description: The genotype-specific end-of-induction (EOI, day 29) MRD risk stratification of O'Connor et al. (J Clin Oncol 2018;36(1):34-43, UKALL2003, 3,113 patients with ALL; MRD by Ig/TCR real-time quantitative PCR, quantitative range 0.01%, detection limit 1 x 10^-5; this analysis is the whole cohort): the EOI MRD category (Undetectable / 0 to <0.01% / 0.01 to <0.1% / 0.1 to <1.0% / 1 to <5% / >=5%) combined with one of four mutually exclusive genetic subtypes (CYTO-GR, CYTO-IR, CYTO-HR, T-ALL) assigns each patient a fixed risk group by the Table 2 rule - SR = {CYTO-GR and MRD < 0.1%} or {CYTO-IR and MRD < 0.01%} or {T-ALL and MRD undetectable}; IR = {CYTO-GR and 0.1% <= MRD < 5%} or {CYTO-IR and 0.01% <= MRD < 1%} or {T-ALL and 0 < MRD < 5%}; HR = {MRD >= 5%, any subtype} or {CYTO-HR, any MRD} or {CYTO-IR and MRD >= 1%}. Group outcomes: SR 5-year EFS 94% / RR 4% / OS 98%, IR 83% / 13% / 90%, HR 58% / 33% / 70%; the supporting continuous model is a univariable Cox regression per endpoint on tau(MRD) = |ln(transformed MRD)| (undetectable = one log below the 1 x 10^-5 detection limit, maximum assumed 0.99999): HR per log reduction EFS 0.81, RR 0.80, OS 0.77. The wrapper takes one marker - the per-draw EOI MRD level in percent or fraction as reported (value_scale 'auto' distinguishes the two at fit), the EOI value being the last draw on or before the landmark after the baseline window (the benchmark's stand-in for the paper's day-29 draw; an undetectable draw arrives as value 0 with a <marker>__detected 0 row) - and writes risk = the EOI MRD level (the quantity the categories threshold; higher = more MRD = more likely failing, HR 33% vs SR 4% relapse) and call = 1 iff the group is HR, or 1 iff the trial's MRD-only class is MRD high (EOI >= 0.01%, md:26 / the Table 2 row labels) when the patient's subtype is not known; the paper defines no per-patient probability, so TxResBench converts the risk. The genetic subtype enters as the covariates column named by genotype_covariate (labels CYTO-GR/CYTO-IR/CYTO-HR/T-ALL or integer codes 0-3 (0-based) / 1-4 (1-based) in that order; genotype_codes 'auto' picks the encoding); without that column the wrapper runs the paper's MRD-only class for every patient and warns in run.json (the same fallback the other MRD wrappers use). At fit the paper's Table 2 cell counts and the univariable Cox analyses (EFS -> the benchmark's progression, OS -> death; RR has no benchmark endpoint; the genetic-subtype strata are recomputed when the subtype column is present) are reproduced on the training patients and reported in run.json.

methods.description: The two-class dynamic GIN pattern rule of Attademo et al. (Cancers 2021;13(6):1331; 25 metastatic breast cancer patients starting a new systemic treatment line, GIN = Genomic Instability Number from low-pass WGS of plasma cfDNA, GIN > 170 = detectable): from the three draws T0 (baseline before the new line), T1 (within 10 days of treatment start, median 7) and T2 (days 11-22, median 14), the per-patient % change of GIN between the consecutive pairs (T1 vs T0, then T2 vs T1; nondetectable on-treatment values imputed to the detection boundary 170, both-T1-and-T2-ND excluded, detectable baseline required) is classified by direction only: pattern 1 = a decrease at T1 followed by a decrease or no change at T2 (continuous decrease; the paper's favourable pattern, 7/8 three-month responders, predictive value 88% at 3 months), pattern 2 = a decrease at T1 followed by an increase at T2 (V-shaped; the nonresponse pattern, 3/5 and 4/5 progressive disease at 3 and 6 months; NPV for nonresponse 60%/80%). The wrapper writes risk = 0 (pattern 1) / 1 (not pattern 1) and call 1 for the not-pattern-1 side (treatment judged failing); a patient with no detectable baseline GIN, a missing T0/T1/T2 slot, or both T1 and T2 nondetectable gets no prediction with the reason in note (the paper's analysis set was 'the 13 patients with detectable GIN at the baseline and GIN measured at T1 and T2', md:130). The wrapper maps the paper's T1/T2 day windows onto the benchmark clock as the first two on-treatment draws after the baseline (the corpus fixed-pair convention; the wrapper records the adapted call and the paper's open points in run.json and README.md - the paper's per-pair %-change group comparisons and the 170 threshold are the paper's, and neither the GIN computation (reference [16], not in the paper text) nor the MEDCALC/GraphPad analyses are reproduced).

methods.description: Per-observation binomial generalized linear mixed-effects classifier (logit link, per-patient random intercept, lme4::glmer) of the disease status at a sampling point - progressive disease accompanied by therapy change (PDTC) vs stable disease (SD) - on the change (Delta) of liquid-biopsy parameters between two consecutive draws: serum IL-8, ctDNA VAFmean and ctDNA t-MAD, one, two or all three entering as fixed effects (the paper's 'different combinations', md:306-310 - Angeles AK, et al., Br J Cancer 2023;129:112-121, DOI 10.1038/s41416-023-02284-0: 38 ALK+ NSCLC patients, 296 longitudinal serum samples during ALK-TKI therapy; the trivariate DeltaIL-8 + DeltaVAFmean + Delta t-MAD model was the optimum, in-sample ROC AUC 0.8936 [0.8325-0.9546]; reported are only in-sample AUCs, no per-observation probability, coefficient, cutoff or call, and no analysis code - the named software is lme4 1.1-23 and pROC 1.16.2 on R 4.0.2, md:310-317). The method is DEFINED for the fixed three-parameter list (required_markers, all-three match), which the runner passes on such units; on a call with a different marker count the wrapper fits the same model structure on the markers passed (the paper's univariate and bivariate instances). The paper labels each consecutive-draw sample pair with the CONCURRENT RECIST status of the sampling point; the benchmark's per-patient outcomes replace that, so the wrapper refits the published structure against the harness failure labels directly: one GLMM per response outcome the training data carry, no_response (best RECIST response SD or PD - the paper's 'stable disease' failure side together with PD itself, the nearest harness equivalent of the SD/PDTC dichotomy) and progressive_disease (best response PD), every complete consecutive-draw Delta observation of a training patient carrying that patient's label (the per-observation statuses the paper annotated are not in the benchmark input). The illustrated inputs use the paper's own change formula for every marker, Delta = 100 x (value(t2) - value(t1)) / value(t1) (md:296-305; the ref 16/17 ctDNA change definitions - absolute DeltaVAFmean and percent Delta t-MAD - cannot be told apart from the marker names, recorded as a deviation); a pair with a zero or missing earlier value has no Delta and is unused. The paper never predicts new patients and does not state which prediction variant its ROC curves used; the wrapper predicts at the population level (fixed effects only, re.form = NA - a new patient has no fitted random effect) and writes, per response outcome, the model's fitted probability of the failure status for the patient's most recent complete consecutive-draw Delta observation before the landmark (the paper's per-observation output applied to the most recent sample; a patient with no such observation gets no prediction with the reason in note). Risk is the no_response model's probability (the progressive_disease model's when the training data give no no_response outcome); p_no_response and p_progressive_disease are the two GLMMs' own probabilities. The paper's evaluation (in-sample ROC/AUC, pROC, 2000-stratified-bootstrap 95% CI, DeLong comparison) is the benchmark's scoring step and is not run by the wrapper; the in-sample AUC of each refit (population-level and conditional variants) is recorded in run.json. Survival outcomes are not modelled by this method (the paper's classifiers are status classifiers, not survival models); TxResBench converts the risk for them.

(Frontiers in Immunology 2022;13:906352) trained an elastic net Cox regression with the glmnet R package on the changes (FU sample - BL sample) of the MAE-specific CD8+ T cell populations detected in their dextramer screen (117 of 167 tested), outcome OS from the first administration of ICB; the model reported at alpha = 0.7 (their grid search in [0.1, 1], best prediction accuracy on their 80/20 test split, the value at which the model had 'the highest prediction accuracy as well as a smaller set of features', Supplementary Table 6) selected the regularization lambda by 10-fold cross-validation on the training set, and its stated output is the identification of the most informative populations (9, then 3 in the follow-up uni-/multivariate survival::coxph and the combinatorial disappearance rule - the exploratory stage, not re-implemented: the wrapper re-fits the elastic net per dataset, since the paper's per-population identities and coefficients are publication-specific). The wrapper derives one delta feature per marker the benchmark passes (baseline = the marker's last draw on or before baseline_max_day; follow-up = its last draw after that and at or before the landmark, the paper's one follow-up sample at a median of 42 days; a population not present at an endpoint is 0 there, the paper's appeared/disappeared rule), fits glmnet family='cox' with the paper's alpha = 0.7 and a lambda from 10-fold cross-validation on the training patients (event-stratified folds drawn from the seed, so a fit is reproducible), refits on the whole training sample at that lambda, and writes as risk the Cox linear predictor (glmnet type='link', higher = more likely failing, no probability and no cutoff since the paper defines none; TxResBench converts the risk). methods.description: The elastic-net landmark survival model of Assaf et al. (Nature Medicine 2023;29:859-868, the 'C3D1 OS ctDNA model' of IMpower150). From every marker's serial draws up to the landmark the wrapper derives per on-treatment visit features of the paper's metric families: the level, the change from baseline (difference and percent change) and the trapezoid area under the level curve from baseline to the visit (the paper's 'area under the curve for ctDNA level from BL to C2D1'), plus the baseline level and landmark-anchored level/change/AUC at the patient's last draw at or before the landmark (the paper's 'at C3D1'). Features are IQR-scaled on the outcome's at-risk training patients (missing = training median, the paper's imputation rule), and a glmnet Cox elastic net (alpha = 0.5, the paper's equal lasso/ridge weight) is fitted on the survival times rebaselined at the landmark; the lambda is the average over 10 repeated nested cross-validations of the lambda that minimizes the prediction error (the paper's per-LOOCV rule), the final features are those retained in at least 50% of the cross-validation folds and with a positive gain, and the final model is refit on the whole at-risk training set with them. The wrapper writes the linear predictor as the risk (higher = more likely failing) and the paper's three-call classification as the call (molecular progressive disease = the high-risk group), with the paper's training-data thresholds re-derived from the wrapper's own training scores by the paper's rules (mPD = the mean of the 75th percentile of SD and the 70th percentile of PR patients; mResp = the median score of the patients with landmark OS of at least 30 months; documented fallbacks when those subgroups are absent). It writes no probability (the paper reports only rank concordance; TxResBench converts the risk). The paper's R code is not public (controlled-access EGA EGAS00001006703), so the wrapper reimplements the stated recipe and documents every unstated choice (Supplementary Tables 3 and 6 are not in the article, the inner CV scheme and the exact next-door gain statistic are not given; the paper's leave-one-out cross-validation is replaced with 10-fold for tractability).

methods.description: The per-patient probability (score) of pathological complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant anti-HER2 chemotherapy, from the elastic-net (EN) binomial regression of Yoshida, Wei et al. (Breast Cancer Research 2026;28:99, DOI 10.1186/s13058-026-02259-y; HER2-positive breast cancer, JBCRG-16/Neo-Lath trial, 102-112 serum samples) on the IgG titers to 63 non-overlapping 20-mer HER2-derived peptides (H1-H63): 'elastic net (EN) regression was performed, considering pCR (a binary outcome) as the target variable and the IgG titers or fold changes in 63 HER2-derived peptides as the input features' (md:295-299), fitted with glmnet::cv.glmnet 'where alpha = 0.5 was fixed to balance L1 and L2 regularization, and lambda was optimized to minimize classification error' (md:304-306) - lambda.min from 10-fold CV (md:307-308, Fig. 5A md:704-707) - on a training matrix that the authors z-standardized externally, recording the center and SD and applying them to the validation set (md:299-312). The paper fits ONE model per dataset - pre-NAC titers, post-NAC titers and log2(post/pre) fold changes (md:279-285) - each reported by training/validation AUC alone (pre 0.74/0.64 with 8 peptides, post 0.76/0.69 with 9, fold 0.78/0.79 with 6; md:623-668) with bootstrap (n=1,000) 95% CIs via an unnamed 'roc function' (md:314-318); no probability cutoff exists (extraction cutoff null). The wrapper implements all three datasets as method.json setting dataset (default fold, the paper's dynamic branch; pre/post are the two snapshot branches, selectable): one feature per marker the benchmark passes (for the T2026 dataset the marker preparation passes the 63 peptide titers; the EN is a generic penalized binomial - the corpus records marker_origin 'application' - so the method runs on any unit's marker vector, and the wrapper records the feature count), with x0 = the marker's last draw at day <= baseline_max_day (the paper's pre-NAC baseline, md:281-283) and x1 = the marker's last draw after it and at or before the landmark (the paper's post-NAC draw, md:283-284; the corpus fixed-two-draw convention substitutes for the paper's labeled draws, and the fold feature is log2(x1/x0), md:284-285); the training samples are z-standardized with the recorded center/SD (population SD, zero-variance columns kept centered at 0) and applied to the prediction matrix; the label is read as the harness's no_response (best response SD/PD or responder 0 - the failure reading of pCR-vs-non-pCR, md:296-298), so the wrapper fits P(no pCR) directly and risk = p_no_response is failure-oriented by construction (the paper's P(pCR) = 1 - risk). Differences, all because the paper publishes no code (job.code = []; data-only availability, md:987-988; every argument-level choice - family, type.measure, standardize, foldid, seed, predict type - is '?' in the spec): the wrapper fixes family = 'binomial' (the monotone logistic of the stated binary outcome; the misclassification loss exists only for lognet/multnet, cvtype.R), type.measure = 'class' (the paper's stated criterion 'minimize classification error', md:305-306 - the cv.glmnet DEFAULT for binomial is deviance, and the paper's Fig. 5A plots misclassification error, md:704-707), standardize = FALSE (the paper's recorded z-standardization IS the standardization; glmnet's standardize = TRUE default would standardize the already-standardized matrix a second time - the alternative reading is recorded), a final glmnet refit at the CV-selected lambda (the paper does not say whether the final model is a refit or another cv.glmnet call, '?'), deterministic stratified 10-fold assignment drawn from the benchmark seed (the cv.glmnet default fold assignment is an unstratified random sample, md '?', cv.glmnet.R:257-258), the benchmark's own train/test folds carry the evaluation (the paper's 80/20 stratified split, md:289-291, md:619-622, is not re-run; the wrapper reports the training-fold AUC and its 1000-resample stratified bootstrap 95% CI computed with base R - the paper's 'roc function' package is unnamed '?' and pROC is not substituted), and the paper's assay preprocessing (background subtraction with Z-score normalization and the 1.96 threshold, md:273-278) is upstream: the wrapper consumes the titer values the dataset's marker preparation passes and records that assumption. It writes risk and p_no_response (no call - no cutoff is published), abstains a patient whose feature vector is incomplete (a missing draw at an endpoint, or a zero/negative titer in the fold dataset, which makes log2 undefined - the paper defines no epsilon rule, spec traps.log_of_zero) with the reason in note, and falls back to the training failure base rate only for the declared degenerate fits (constant_ok).

methods.description: The GRU variant of the SHERLOC framework of Mamann et al. (bioRxiv 2026.06.04.730097) for overall survival from the landmark: the patient's longitudinal ctDNA profile is read as a sequence of per-visit feature vectors (in the paper, 17 gene-level ctDNA VAFs + 4 panel-level aggregated features = 21 channels at each of the T clinical timepoints baseline to C4D1), batch-normalized along the timestep axis, processed by a single gated recurrent unit (input size = hidden size = number of channels, one layer, batch_first, GRU.py:32-37), and the terminal hidden state is fused with per-timestep representations of a frozen genomic-interaction encoder (MLP pretrained with the Cox partial-likelihood on solid-biopsy VAF data, frozen after pretraining, 2 dimensions per timestep; the paper uses the external MSK-CHORD cohort, 22,068 patients) and with baseline clinical covariates; the concatenation is dropped out at 0.4 and passed to a single linear layer with sigmoid output whose value is the Cox log-risk fed to pycox's CoxPH, trained by the negative log-partial likelihood (lr 0.005, batch 50, up to 256 epochs, early stopping patience 20, 20% validation split). The wrapper refits it per survival outcome of the training data (death first - the paper's OS, then progression), rebases the outcome times to the benchmark's landmark (the paper's OS from the final on-treatment ctDNA collection), resolves the sequence to the patient's visits up to the landmark (baseline slot = last baseline visit, then the most recent on-treatment visits, at most n_timepoints = 4 slots; the paper's evaluability rule requires all configured timepoints, md:1404-1408) and writes the paper's native outputs: the sigmoid log-risk (risk, monotone in the Cox log-risk) and per-horizon failure probabilities from the Breslow baseline-hazard survival curve. The frozen genomic-interaction encoder cannot be reproduced as published (MSK-CHORD is not redistributed, scripts/data/msk_chord/README.md:1-17), so the wrapper pretrains the same MLP architecture on the training cohort itself - the paper's transfer-learning step is replaced by an in-cohort pretraining (recorded deviation); the marker set is data-driven (the paper derives its channel count from the data, d_input = train_ds[0][0].shape[0], train_DL.py:287-289), so the wrapper take whatever markers a unit carries as the channels.

methods.description: The two-question predictive algorithm of Peng et al., Scientific Reports 2017;7:42879 (DOI 10.1038/srep42879; 529 NA-naive genotype B/C chronic hepatitis B patients on entecavir 0.5 mg/d, 195 HBeAg-positive / 334 HBeAg-negative): question 1 = baseline serum HBsAg <3,000 IU/mL (yes/no), question 2 = HBsAg decline >=75% from baseline at Month 3 of treatment (HBeAg-positive) or Month 12 (HBeAg-negative) (yes/no); the four cross-classification cells of Figure 5b are annotated with the paper's predictive values for achieving HBsAg loss during 5 years of treatment - both characteristics: PPV 70% (n=10); baseline <3,000 & decline <75%: NPV 98% (n=128); baseline >=3,000 & decline >=75%: NPV 88% (n=25); neither: NPV 100% (n=52) - so the paper's positive prediction is BOTH characteristics and the negative prediction is every other cell (Figure 5a records the same boundary for the HBeAg-negative <100 IU/mL endpoint: PPV 100% / 27% / 41%, NPV 100%; the paper publishes no analysis code - SAS 9.4 named only, no procedure or syntax, nothing downloaded - so the wrapper implements the rule from the Results text and the published figure). The wrapper takes exactly one marker (the serum HBsAg level, IU/mL), maps the paper's scheduled assessment month onto the benchmark's landmark day (the decline = 100 x (baseline - assessment)/baseline with the baseline = the last draw on or before baseline_max_day and the assessment = the last on-treatment draw on or before the landmark day; the paper's HBeAg-status timepoints Month 3 / Month 12 and its HBeAg-negative <100 IU/mL panel are not representable on the single-landmark harness clock, recorded as the README's deviation), writes risk = the cell's failure propensity from the paper's own Fig. 5b annotation (0.30 both / 0.98 / 0.88 / 1.00 neither; higher = worse - the call-only rule's ordered class, per the capability record O1) and call = 1 = predicted not to achieve HBsAg loss (the paper's negative cells), 0 = the both-characteristics positive cell; the wrapper writes no probability (the paper defines none per patient; TxResBench converts the risk), nothing is learned from the training outcomes (fitted false - the cutoffs and the cell values are the paper's published constants), and a patient without both a quantitative baseline draw and an on-treatment draw by the landmark (or with a baseline of 0, which makes the per-cent change undefined) gets no prediction with the reason in note.

methods.description: The two-indicator HBsAg-kinetics rule of Han C, Jin L, Zhu M, et al., 'Efficacy and predictors of pegylated-interferon in hepatitis B surface antigen seroclearance in immune active and inactive chronic hepatitis B patients' (Journal of Virus Eradication 2025;12:100616, DOI 10.1016/j.jve.2025.100616; 211 HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B patients on pegylated-interferon alpha-2b, FAS): (1) the on-treatment criterion 'HBsAg decline ≥1 log10 IU/mL at any 12-week interval, Yes vs No' (Table 3, md:169; met n = 98 with 52.0% vs 5.2% week-48 HBsAg seroclearance, P < 0.001, AUC 0.785 (95% CI 0.718-0.852), multivariate HR 11.205 (95% CI 4.379-28.674), md:178/md:184) and (2) baseline 'HBsAg (IU/mL), <100 vs ≥ 100' (Table 3, md:168; multivariate HR 2.999 (95% CI 1.625-5.536), AUC 0.67, md:173/md:184; the sample's ROC optimum 2.135 log10 IU/mL ~= 136 IU/mL is reported alongside, md:173). The paper publishes no analysis code (SPSS 27.0 named only, md:50; nothing downloaded), so the wrapper implements the rule from the Methods/Results text: the patient's day-ordered visit sequence (baseline draw = the last on or before baseline_max_day, then on-treatment draws up to the landmark) is paired consecutively - the paper's 12-week nominal schedule (weeks 12/24/36/48 with a ±6-week window per visit, md:26/md:30) applied to the benchmark's own visit sequence (recorded in run.json) - and indicator 1 is met when some pair has log10(prev) - log10(next) >= 1.0 log10 IU/mL (a >=10-fold drop, md:136). The wrapper writes risk = the smallest interval ratio value_next/value_prev (the quantity indicator 1 thresholds; higher = less decline = worse), call = 1 = indicator 1 not met (treatment judged failing; the paper's 5.2% group), 0 = met (the 52.0% group), and indicator 2 as its own column baseline_hbsag_lt100 - the paper defines no per-patient score, no probability and no combination of the two indicators ('we did not attempt to establish a prediction model', md:199; TxResBench converts the risk). A draw at or below the assay's lower detection limit (0.05 IU/mL = HBsAg-negative, md:41) enters the interval ratio as the assay floor - a lower bound on the decline: the criterion is guaranteed when the bound clears the 1 log10 cutoff, undetermined otherwise (abstain with the reason in note, never an invented call; the paper states no handling, '?'); a seronegative baseline draw is outside the paper's cohort (HBsAg positivity >6 months, md:30) and gets no prediction; a patient without a baseline draw, without an on-treatment draw by the landmark (no complete 12-week interval; patients treated for fewer than 12 weeks are unlikely to benefit, md:180/md:195), or with an interval whose decline cannot be decided gets an empty risk and call with the reason in note. Nothing is learned from the training outcomes (fitted false): both cutoffs are the paper's published constants (1 log10 author-chosen for clinical practicality, md:178; 100 IU/mL the applied Cox cutoff, md:168).

methods.description: The ANRS HC02 RIBAVIC early-response treatment algorithm (fig 3) of Payan C, Pivert A, Morand P, et al., 'Rapid and early virological response to chronic hepatitis C treatment with IFN a2b or PEG-IFN a2b plus ribavirin in HIV/HCV co-infected patients', Gut 2007;56:1111-1116, DOI 10.1136/gut.2006.106690 (323 HIV/HCV co-infected patients on 48-week IFN a2b 3 MU 3x/week or PEG-IFN a2b 1.5 mg/kg/week + ribavirin 800 mg/day; the paper published no analysis code - the analyses ran on proprietary SPSS V.10.1, no procedure or syntax published): a staged sequential decision rule on serial serum HCV RNA at fixed on-treatment weeks - W4 (day 28): qualitative undetectable (Cobas Amplicor HCV v2.0, 50 IU/mL) = RVR -> continue the full-dose 48-week course (PPV 97.5%, Table 3); if detectable, quantify (Versant HCV RNA 3.0 bDNA): above 460,000 IU/mL (5.6 log10) = predicted non-SVR -> discontinue (NPV 100%, 32% of the non-SVR detected; fig 3 caption 33%); otherwise continue to W12 (day 84): above 39,000 IU/mL (4.6 log10) = predicted non-SVR -> discontinue (NPV 100%, 61% of the non-SVR; fig 3 caption 32% incremental); otherwise assess at W24 (day 168, as proposed by Davis): qualitative detectable = predicted non-SVR -> discontinue (NPV 99%, 93% of the non-SVR detected, 28% incremental per the fig 3 caption); undetectable = continue to completion (all 88 SVR in the cohort would have continued; 17.6% of continuing responders may relapse after treatment). At a benchmark run the wrapper applies the latest stage whose week is on or before the landmark (the landmark-to-stage rule; a patient stopped at an earlier stage never reaches a later one), taking for each stage the patient's serum HCV RNA draw closest to that stage's week within a +-14-day tolerance (the paper defines no tolerance), with risk = log10 of the stage draw's viral load in IU/mL (qualitative undetectable / below-detection value 0 = the paper's below-quantification-cut-off substitution, 2.49 log10 IU/mL, md:194-197) - the quantity the stage's cut-off thresholds - and call = 1 for the paper's predicted-non-SVR (discontinue) branches, 0 for every continue branch (RVR, below the W4/W12 cut-offs, undetectable at W24 where the paper's semantic is continued treatment = treatment judged working); no probability is written (the paper defines none per patient, so TxResBench converts the risk); the paper's reported operating points (branch PPV/NPV and detection shares, per-arm odds ratios, Fig. 3 caption counts, the assay details and the below-quantification substitution) are recorded in the fit report as reported, not fitted.

methods.description: The response-guided-treatment (RGT) DAA-duration rule (Fig. 3) of Goyal A, Cotler SJ, Matthews GV, et al., 'Modeling predicts shortening of DAA treatment duration to 5 weeks in individuals with recent or chronic infection with HCV RNA negativity at day 7 on treatment', J Infect Dis 2026;234(4):547-555, DOI 10.1093/infdis/jiag260 (the paper published no analysis code or software statement - the rule is described only in prose and the Fig. 3 flowchart; the derivation is an in silico multiscale viral-kinetics model over 100,000 parameter combinations per infection stage, md:34-53): a per-patient, deterministic, modeling-independent decision tree on the QUALITATIVE on-treatment HCV RNA detectability call at day 7 and day 14 of DAA therapy, identical for recent and chronic infection ('a simplified algorithm to reduce duration of DAA treatment for HCV that does not require modeling or knowledge of infection stage i.e., recent or chronic', md:101): (1) undetectable at day 7 -> recommend 5 weeks of DAA (5 weeks achieves >95% SVR in this stratum, md:65/md:78/md:93 - the ordered rule is 'first undetectable on day 7 or day 14', so the day-14 result is not read); (2) detectable at day 7 but undetectable at day 14 -> recommend 7 weeks (7 weeks achieves >95% SVR; 6 weeks reaches 90% only, md:63/md:80/md:93); (3) detectable at day 7 AND day 14 -> recommend the standard-of-care duration (8 weeks for glecaprevir+pibrentasvir [G/P], 12 weeks for every other DAA regimen; md:67/md:80/md:99, Fig. 3 caption: 'Standard of care duration is 12 weeks for all DAAs that were used to treat chronic infection in the training set except G/P treatment for which 8 weeks is recommended.'). The call is 1 for branch 3 (treatment judged failing: a standard-duration recommendation - detectable at both rule timepoints), 0 for branches 1 and 2 (de-escalation possible: 5- or 7-week recommendations = treatment judged working); risk = log10 of the day-14 draw's viral load in IU/mL (the quantity the rule's terminal detectability criterion thresholds; the undetectable state is placed at nondetect_substitution_iu_ml = detection limit / 2, the wrapper's convention - the paper never states the numeric encoding of 'undetectable'); no probability is written (the paper defines none per patient, so TxResBench converts the risk). The wrapper takes exactly one marker (per-draw HCV RNA; required_markers LOINC 29609-5), takes the draws closest to day 7 and day 14 among the draws after baseline_max_day and on or before the landmark within timepoint_tolerance_days (default 14; ties to the later draw - the paper defines no tolerance and no fallback), derives the detectability call from the benchmark's __detected rows when present, else by thresholding the quantitative value at detection_limit_iu_ml (default 15 IU/mL, the paper's primary chronic-analysis value; 10 IU/mL recent and the 1 IU/mL sensitivity case with its 4-week branch-1 recommendation are reached by overriding the params), and abstains - empty risk and call with the reason in note - any patient without an in-window day-7 draw, or whose day-7 draw is detectable but has no in-window day-14 draw (the paper's flowchart presumes both measurements; the clinical trials it cites excluded cases with missing viral load measurements, md:29). Nothing is learned from the training outcomes (fitted false: all branch durations and the detection limit are the paper's fixed values), and the fit report records the paper's in silico derivation statistics, target SVR rates and reported prediction-vs-observed comparisons as reported, not fitted.

methods.description: The month-1 ultrasensitive-detectability SVR rule of Garbuglia et al., PLoS ONE 2016;11(8):e0158989, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0158989 (23 HCV genotype 1 patients on telaprevir/PEG-IFN/RBV triple therapy; the paper published no analysis code - the ROC/cutoff step ran in the authors' own unpublished proprietary MATLAB routine ROCout, md:87): a fixed single-draw threshold rule - plasma HCV RNA measured by the authors' ultrasensitive (US) protocol (modified Abbott RealTime HCV 1, LOD 1.2 IU/ml, md:10) at month 1 (T1m = day 28 of the day-0/1/2/3/4/5/14/28/weeks-8/12/24 schedule, md:38, md:64) is 'not detected' (below the LOD = the ROC Max Efficiency cut-off 1.2 IU/ml derived in-sample on the 20 patients with a month-1 US measurement, md:199) -> predicted SVR; 'detected' -> predicted no-SVR. Reported operating point at T1m: area under the ROC 0.70 (md:199), PPV 100%, NPV 46.7%, sensitivity 38.4%, specificity 100% (all 5 'not detected' patients achieved SVR), two-tailed Fisher's exact p = 0.07 (md:201); the negative call is explicitly not actionable ('being positive at US HCV RNA at T1m cannot be used as a stopping rule, because of its low NPV (46.7%)', md:223). The wrapper takes exactly one marker (the per-draw plasma HCV RNA; required_markers: LOINC 20416-4, the US-protocol quantity, consumed as the qualitative state with the benchmark's below-detection encoding - value 0 with a <marker>__detected row), selects the draw closest to t1m_day (default 28) among the draws after baseline_max_day and on or before the landmark within t1m_tolerance_days (default 14; ties to the later draw; the paper defines no tolerance), and writes risk = log10 of that draw's IU/mL on the paper's log scale (the quantity the cutoff thresholds; the 'not detected' state is placed below every detectable value at LOD/2 = 0.6 IU/ml because the paper never states the numeric code of 'not detected' in the ROC, md:199 - the wrapper's documented reading) and call = 0 for 'not detected' (predicted SVR = treatment judged working), 1 for 'detected' (predicted no-SVR = treatment judged failing); no probability is written (the paper defines none per patient, so TxResBench converts the risk). A patient with no T1m draw in the window gets no prediction with the reason in note (the paper's month-1 cohort is 20/23, no fallback is defined, and a T1m result from the standard ART assay alone is outside the rule's evidence because US retesting covered only the 47 low-viremia samples, md:135). Nothing is learned from the training outcomes (fitted false - the cutoff is treated as the published constant; in-sample derivation by the unpublished ROCout is not reproduced) and the fit report records the paper's reported operating points and cohort arithmetic as reported, not fitted. The paper's other analyses (LDA at days 1/4, PCA on slopes, IL28B genotyping, the ART-only ROC) are separate methods and are not this rule.

methods.description: The three-class HD-CTC kinetics profile rule of Shishido et al. (J Transl Med 2019;17:294, DOI 10.1186/s12967-019-2035-8; 81 stage IV NSCLC patients entering a new line of systemic therapy, kinetics subset n = 25 with a baseline and at least one follow-up sample within 3 months, 117 samples): HD-CTCs/mL (CK+ CD45- cells with an intact DAPI nucleus, morphologically distinct from WBCs, counted per mL by the non-enrichment HD-SCA workflow on 7.5 mL blood; 0 is a measured count - 'Sample positivity was defined as > 0 CTC/mL') measured at the baseline draw (time 0, at initiation of the new line, before chemotherapy) and at the follow-up draw(s) within the first 3 months; the paper (verbatim, md:84): 'HD-CTC Kinetics in patients undergoing chemotherapy were shown to follow 3 distinct patterns as determined by the first 3 months: an increase in HD-CTCs numbers, unchanged HD-CTCs numbers (stable), and a decline in HD-CTCs numbers with therapy... HD-CTC stability was defined as less than a 5.0 HD-CTCs/mL change from baseline.' The wrapper reads the baseline as the last draw on or before baseline_max_day, the follow-up draw as the draw after it and at or before the landmark inside the 3-month window (three_month_days, default 91.25 days) closest to the 3-month point (the paper's 'data from the specific timepoint of 3 months post start of treatment was analyzed', md:105), ties going to the later draw, and writes risk = the change in HD-CTCs/mL itself (follow-up minus baseline - the quantity the 5.0 deadband thresholds; a rule writes the quantity it thresholds, and the paper's direction is counterintuitive: the INCREASING profile is the favourable one, median PFS 17.41 vs 4.57 stable / 6.92 decrease months, median OS 32.46 vs 7.23 / 12.65 months, p = 0.0040 / 0.0080 PFS and 0.00003 / 0.0089 OS, stable vs decrease p = 0.0397 - so the wrapper does not flip the sign or invent a failure score, and TxResBench learns the risk -> failure direction per outcome) and call = 1 for the stable or decreasing profile, 0 for the increasing one (the paper's two-group contrast of Fig. 4b/d: stable + decreasing combined vs increasing, the group with the worse PFS and OS). It writes no probability (the paper defines none, only per-profile KM estimates and log-rank p-values), so TxResBench converts the risk. A patient without a baseline value, without a draw after the baseline within the 3-month window by the landmark, or whose window draw has no value gets no prediction with the reason in note; a baseline of 0 HD-CTCs/mL is a valid count (4 of the 25 kinetics patients were CTC-negative at baseline) and enters the rule as 0. The paper's group-level evaluation of the call - Kaplan-Meier and log-rank on PFS and OS across the three profiles and across the two-group contrast (md:43, md:88, md:90) - is reproduced at fit on the training patients and reported in run.json, not in the predictions; the paper's own baseline-to-last-draw delta rules (md:71) are different analyses (recorded as delta-threshold variants) and never enter this rule.

methods.description: A two-group progression-risk call from serial ichorCNA estimated tumour fraction and a recalculated threshold, after Beddowes et al. (Mol Oncol 2025): per patient the draws up to the landmark form a counting-process dataset (each draw opens an interval carried forward to the next draw or the outcome), a time-dependent Cox model with a restricted cubic spline (rms::cph + rcs) is fitted 50 times on 70-patient subsamples, and the first breakpoint of a segmented linear regression on the spline's fitted values is a changepoint; its sample mean is the low/high threshold (the paper: 6.70% - rounded to 7% because ichorCNA has no decimals - and a high-risk call for ichorCNA >= 7%). The wrapper writes the current ichorCNA value as the risk and the threshold call, re-derives the threshold in each training fold (the derivation procedure, as published), and lets TxResBench convert the risk into the benchmark's probabilities; the per-subtype models and the overall-survival subtype covariate of the paper's code are not reproduced (the benchmark has no subtype column) and the cohort diagnostics (hazard ratio, c-index) go to run.json.

methods.description: The 7% ichorCNA stopping rule with previous-timepoint direction of Beddowes et al., Molecular Oncology 2025;19:3518-3534 (DOI 10.1002/1878-0261.70015; 149 metastatic breast cancer patients of the DETECT research, 1013 serial plasma samples, 0.1x shallow whole-genome sequencing; the analysis of 244 possible interventions over 164 treatment regimens on 91 patients): at each plasma sample time point during a treatment line, predict the result of the next CT scan - predict treatment response (action Continue) when the current ichorCNA estimated tumour fraction is below 7%, or is at least 7% but has decreased from the previous plasma sample of the same treatment line; predict progression (action Stop) when it is at least 7% and increased or unchanged from the previous sample. The paper's case selection limits the sample and its paired scan to (21, 180] days after the treatment line started (first 3 weeks to first 6 months) with the sample at most 90 days before the scan; the previous time point must be on the same treatment line, and a value at or above 7% without one gets no call ('when available' - the reference code drops the row). The published implementation (github.com/Rueda-Lab/BAY-ML, Code/PredictionTreatmentResponseModels.R, commit 0745dee) reproduced the reported sensitivity 43% and specificity 86% (0.43/0.86, 285 sample-scan pairs, 91 patients). The wrapper uses one marker (the per-draw ichorCNA tumour fraction, integer per cent, 0 a measured value), takes the baseline as the draws at day <= baseline_max_day and the on-treatment draws as those after it, makes the call at the benchmark's decision day (the landmark) with the latest on-treatment draw in the rule's (21, 180] window at or before it, and uses the previous on-treatment draw of the same run (one treatment line per patient x run, the harness frame) as the direction reference (the pre-treatment baseline is never the reference). It writes risk = the current ichorCNA value - the quantity the rule thresholds; the rule's own analyses orient higher toward failure (progression-free survival HR 5.02 [3.16, 7.99] for >= 7%, OS HR 11.15, md:210-215) - and call = 1 for Stop, 0 for Continue, no call (empty risk) with a reason when the current value is at or above 7% and there is no previous on-treatment draw, when there is no on-treatment draw in the window by the landmark, or when the patient has no draw after the baseline. It writes no probability: the rule defines none (the paper reports the confusion matrix only) and TxResBench recalibrates the risk. Wrapper differences from the paper (detailed in README.md): the harness has one treatment line per patient x run and no scan dates, so the paper's Cartesian (sample, next scan) pairing and the 90-day sample-before-scan rule cannot be applied and the benchmark's horizon outcomes stand in for the next CT scan; the paper's ended-treatment-line filter and its non-NA subtype (Group) row filter have no harness channel; the paper's case-selection window is applied to the current sample as published.

methods.description: A per-patient binary risk-group call from TWO draws of plasma IGF2BP3 (pg/mL, ELISA): at diagnosis before any treatment and after induction (preoperative) chemotherapy before surgery (Mancarella C et al., Scientific Reports 2026; DOI 10.1038/s41598-026-55275-5; 60 Ewing sarcoma patients of IRCCS Rizzoli, 25 with paired samples, 16 localized + 9 metastatic). Favorable group 'L + H/R (reduction/low)' = circulating IGF2BP3 < 1326 pg/mL at diagnosis (the paper's ROC-derived cut-off vs 27 healthy donors, sensitivity 43.1%, specificity 77.8%) OR >= 1326 pg/mL at diagnosis AND a reduction of MORE THAN 31% after induction chemotherapy (the observed median reduction of the 13 high-expressors); unfavorable group 'H/P (persistent elevation)' = >= 1326 pg/mL at diagnosis AND reduction <= 31% ('persistently elevated levels after chemotherapy'). The H/P group had significantly worse 5-year RFS and DSS (28.6% vs 60.6%, p = 0.045; 28.6% vs 68.9%, p = 0.01; n = 25, Fig. 4A) and a stepwise-Cox DSS HR of 6.36 (95% CI 1.33-30, p = 0.02); in the localized subgroup (n = 16) 5-year RFS/DSS 16.7% vs 100% (p = 0.001 / p < 0.0001). The wrapper takes the marker's last draw on or before baseline_max_day as the diagnosis draw and its last on-treatment draw up to the landmark as the post-induction draw, writes the per cent change from the diagnosis value as risk (higher = more likely failing; it is the quantity the change branch thresholds; the paper's level branch is expressed in the call) and the paper's call (1 = H/P = treatment judged failing, 0 = L + H/R); the percent-reduction formula is assumed (baseline - post)/baseline x 100 (the paper prints only the words 'reduction of > 31%'), the cutoffs are the paper's fixed values, neither is re-derived on the benchmark folds, no probability is written per patient (the paper's KM/log-rank/Cox results are cohort-level, not per-patient risks), and a patient without both draws gets no prediction. The paper publishes no analysis code (SPSS 22.0 + GraphPad Prism only; no procedure/function named), so the wrapper implements the rule from the paper's text.

methods.description: The two-stage information-cumulating dynamic-prediction model of Huang et al. 2016 (Statistics in Medicine 35:2167-2182): stage I fits a Cox proportional-hazards model on the baseline covariate information only (the marker's baseline value and any cov_* columns), giving the baseline cumulative hazard by the Breslow estimator; stage II uses the marker value measured during treatment (the last value at or before the landmark) as a time-dependent covariate whose effect beta(t) is a smooth fractional-polynomial function of time, estimated from every marker measurement of every training patient by a working-independence estimating equation (each patient's event or censoring outcome is used once per measurement time). Prediction is the conditional probability of progression-free survival from the landmark to each horizon, {S0(H)/S0(L)}^exp(alpha'Y + beta(L)'Z(L)), and the wrapper writes the complement 1 - S (the paper's own risk-of-progression quantity, eq. 24) as the model's probability per horizon and the two-stage linear predictor as its risk score (higher = more likely failing). The wrapper differs from the paper in that the benchmark restricts the training data to patients event-free at the landmark (the baseline hazard is then estimated over the landmark-to-horizon window), the marker value at the landmark is the last observed value (not necessarily measured exactly at t), and one two-stage model is fitted per survival endpoint.

methods.description: The joint latent class model (JLCM) of repeated sqrt(CD4) counts and time to death of Tiruneh F, Chewaka L & Abdissa D, 'Statistical Joint Modeling for Predicting the Association of CD4 Measurement and Time to Death of People Living with HIV Who Enrolled in ART, Southwest Ethiopia', HIV/AIDS (Auckland, N.Z.) 2021;13:283-293, DOI 10.2147/HIV.S283059 (358 adults on ART in southwest Ethiopia, 2009-2014, 68 deaths (18.99%): a three-class joint latent class model linking (1) a class-specific linear mixed model of the square-root CD4 count (cells/mm3, measured at baseline and then every six months from ART initiation; class-specific intercept and linear time effect, random intercept and random slope with an unstructured same-over-classes covariance, common effects of sex/age/nutrition), (2) a class-specific Weibull proportional-hazards model of time to death (months from ART initiation; common effects of sex/age/nutrition) and (3) a multinomial-logistic class-membership model (class-specific effects of the same covariates, last class the reference; md:92 note a), linked 'using a shared latent structure' with conditional independence given the class (md:55, md:99); the number of latent classes is chosen by the paper's rule 'We consecutively estimated the models with 1, 2 and 3 latent classes. The ideal number of classes was determined by the model with the lowest BIC.' (md:75; the paper's comparison of G=1/2/3 - loglik, BIC, condition-independence score test, class proportions - is in its Table 3, md:90), and each patient is 'assigned to the class on the basis of higher posterior probability of membership' (md:59), the classes interpreted as high/moderate/low risk of death (class 1 = 'intense hazard of death' high risk; class 3 = 'little hazard' low risk; md:94, md:107; cohort proportions 9.39/37.51/53.05% and average maximal posterior probabilities 0.84/0.80/0.84, md:90/md:94). The paper publishes no code and names no software (job.code = []; the spec records its observation that the structure matches the lcmm R package family as an observation, not an attribution), so the wrapper reimplements the specified model in R with lcmm::Jointlcmm 2.1.0 (Proust-Lima, Philipps & Liquet, JSS 78(2) 2017): the class-specific linear mixed model (fixed = y ~ t + covariates, mixture = ~ t, random = ~ t, idiag FALSE, nwg FALSE), the multinomial-logistic membership (classmb = ~ covariates), the class-specific Weibull baseline hazard (hazard 'Weibull', hazardtype 'Specific', common covariate effects), maximum likelihood via the robust Marquardt algorithm (the paper's stated estimator, md:55; the paper's contradictory 'Bayesian approach' with DIC statement, md:73, is recorded and not implemented - no Bayesian details are published), and the paper's BIC rule for the class count. The marker is sqrt-transformed by the wrapper (the paper's submodel, md:57), the clock is months since the first dose (day / 30.4375; the paper's clock for the CD4 schedule and the time to death, md:45/md:85), and the training fit uses every repeated draw up to each patient's outcome time with the survival outcome (the paper's whole-follow-up fit) while the benchmark's decision day truncates the marker history used at prediction (recorded deviation). The paper's endpoint is death: the JLCM is fitted on overall survival when the training data carry it, else on progression-free survival (the same model; the benchmark convention that a method does not require overall survival). Outputs per patient: risk = the fitted model's own P(event by the first horizon | event-free at the landmark, marker history to it) (lcmm::dynpred from the class posterior and the class-specific Weibull submodel - the model the paper defines; the paper prints no per-patient probability), call = 1 for the patient's most probable class being the class with the strongest fitted cumulative baseline risk at the first horizon (the paper's high-risk class 1, md:94/md:107), p_death_H<h> (or p_progression_H<h> when the training data carry no overall survival) = the same model's own conditional event probabilities by each horizon; the per-patient class and posterior, the class order, and the cohort-level class proportions and average maximal posterior probabilities (the paper's md:90/md:94 outputs) are reported per training fold in run.json. The benchmark converts the risk for the outcomes the model is not fitted on. The paper's fixed covariates (sex, age, nutrition; 'addiction' appears in the equations only, is in no table and has no benchmark channel) map to the cov_* columns of the benchmark when passed (covariates optional; without them the model is fitted on the marker alone); degenerate cases (a constant marker, an unconverged joint model, a single-class BIC choice) take recorded fallbacks declared in constant_ok. The benchmark refits on each fold: the paper's published numbers are the paper's own 358-patient cohort's.

methods.description: The five-fold cross-validated multivariate joint model WITH HORSESHOE REGULARIZATION of Suman S., et al., 'Prognostic Role of Dynamic Changes in Serological Markers in Metastatic Hormone Naive Prostate Cancer', Cancers 2023;15(17):4392, DOI 10.3390/cancers15174392 (secondary analysis of the LATITUDE trial, mHSPC, ADT + abiraterone vs ADT + placebo; 1138 patients with a baseline and at least two post-baseline measurements of every marker; landmark longitudinal information up to 12 or 24 months, follow-up up to 60 months): per marker k one linear mixed-effects longitudinal sub-model (fixed effects treatment arm, time of evaluation, the marker's baseline value, and the treatment arm x time interaction; random intercept per patient and random slope of time of assessment), one Cox proportional-hazards time-to-event sub-model on the baseline covariates (ECOG performance status; skeletal lesions 0-9 vs >=10; liver metastasis; nodal stage N0/Nx vs N1; Gleason <9 vs 9-10; baseline Hb; log(baseline PSA + 1); worst pain score; treatment arm), the two linked through a shared random effect - a current-value association structure, one association coefficient per marker - and estimated with horseshoe regularization, fitted separately for overall survival and for prostate-cancer-specific survival. The paper names no software, no function and no code (its only software statement is 'All statistical analyses were performed using R version 3.6.3 with its packages.', md line 32; the supplement contains no code), so nothing is attributed to it: the wrapper implements the model with JMbayes2 0.6-5 (the only implementation found that offers horseshoe penalties for exactly these coefficient groups, its penalty_alphas / penalty_gammas = 'horseshoe'; the package and its version are the wrapper's choice, recorded in the README and run.json) - the K per-marker lme sub-models, the Cox sub-model on the cov_* columns (the paper's W; every covariate column the benchmark passes enters as a numeric baseline main effect and, in the per-marker longitudinal fixed part, as the paper's treatment-arm term with its time interaction), one current-value association parameter per marker, and the package's default penalized B-spline baseline hazard. The wrapper fits one such model per survival outcome present in the training data (death from overall survival, the paper's OS model; progression from progression-free survival, the benchmark's analogous event-free endpoint - the paper's second endpoint is cancer-specific survival, which the benchmark does not carry), prints the model's own per-horizon conditional event probabilities P(event by day h | event-free at the landmark and the marker history up to it) (p_death_H<h> / p_progression_H<h>, from JMbayes2's event prediction, conditioned at the landmark), writes the first-horizon probability of the death model (or of the progression model when there is no OS) as risk with risk_death / risk_progression carrying each model's own first-horizon score, and gives the response outcomes (no_response, progressive_disease - the paper has no response model) to TxResBench's conversion. A patient with fewer than two marker draws by the landmark, no baseline value of a marker, or a missing baseline covariate gets no prediction with the reason in note. Wrapper choices recorded against the paper: the longitudinal sub-model's treatment arm is generalized to every covariate column the benchmark passes ('optional' covariates; without the covariate track the models have no arm/other baseline design), the marker values are log1p-transformed by default (the paper states a log transformation only for PSA, log(x + 1)), non-detects arrive as value 0 and stay at log1p(0) = 0 (the paper gives no below-detection rule), the model clock is months (time_unit_days 30.4375), MCMC sizes/priors are the implementation's (no MCMC settings are published; horseshoe prior hyperparameters are JMbayes2's defaults) and a constant marker is dropped from the multivariate model rather than failing it (recorded). The paper's 4-marker set (Hb, NLR, PLR, LMR; the 5-marker variant adds log(PSA + 1)) is its application: the K sub-model + horseshoe structure is marker-agnostic (survey record md_0142: marker_specificity any, n_markers 1+), so the method takes any number of continuous markers.

methods.description: The joint model of longitudinal and time-to-event data of Posch et al., Front Cardiovasc Med 2022;9:933428 (DOI 10.3389/fcvm.2022.933428): the marker trajectory follows a linear mixed-effects model with up to a cubic specification of follow-up time, a random intercept and a random linear-time effect; the event rate follows a Weibull model; the hazard of the event is linked to the subject-specific trajectory through the association parameter alpha under the paper's two examined specifications - the current marker value ('current parameter' specification, alpha quoted per 1% LVEF increase as HR 0.81, 95%CI 0.72-0.92) and the 1st derivative of the trajectory (rate of change per month) - fitted by maximum likelihood (pseudo-adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature over the random intercept and slope) on the training patients; a patient's prediction is the dynamic-risk quantity of the paper's Rizopoulos approach, P(event by day h | event-free at the landmark and the marker draws so far), written as the method's own p_<outcome>_H<h> and as risk at the first horizon. The wrapper takes one marker at a time, fits the paper's model with the two alphas ('both' by default), selects the polynomial degree by sequential likelihood-ratio tests ('auto', the paper's degree model-checking), and fits the survival outcome the training data give (progression from pfs, else death from os); the published fit and prediction were performed in Stata 15.0 with code available on request, so the equations of the paper's methods paragraph are implemented here directly (README states each wrapper choice).

methods.description: Joint model of a longitudinal marker and overall survival (the sensitivity analysis of Alimu et al., Br J Cancer 2023;129:233-242): a linear mixed-effects model of the log marker with a random intercept and slope, a compound-symmetry covariance of the random effects and fixed effects time since treatment plus its interaction with the treatment arm (linear mixed model, time in months), is linked by the current marker value (JM::jointModel, parameterization 'value', the JM 1.4-8 default Weibull baseline hazard 'weibull-PH-aGH') to a proportional-hazards model for overall survival whose time-fixed design is the treatment arm and, in the paper's Model 1, the baseline detection status of the marker. The paper reports only the association coefficient of this model; here its dynamic prediction is used (JM::survfitJM): the probability of death by each horizon, given that the patient is alive at the landmark and the marker draws up to it. It writes the probability at the first horizon as risk and the model's own p_death_H<h> (the same model fitted on progression-free survival when the training data have no overall survival).

methods.description: The joint model for longitudinal and time-to-event data of van 't Land et al., Ann Surg 2023 (DOI 10.1097/SLA.0000000000005865): a linear mixed-effects model of the log-transformed marker with random intercepts and slopes and time-varying effects of the two treatment phases (FOLFIRINOX, SBRT), linked to overall survival by the current value of the patient-specific fitted trajectory as a time-varying covariate in a relative-risk (proportional-hazards) model adjusted for the baseline covariates (the paper: baseline body mass index, baseline age, sex), fitted with JM::jointModel (piecewise-constant baseline hazard) and predicted with JM::survfitJM (Monte Carlo). The wrapper fits for death only (the paper's endpoint); with the covariate track on, every cov_* column enters the baseline adjustment (the paper's BMI, age, sex), without it the relative-risk model is intercept-only (the benchmark's none-by-default state); the treatment phases are mapped positionally onto the patient's draw sequence (the paper's three treatment-anchored time points); the wrapper writes the model's own probability of death by each horizon as p_death_H<h> and the probability at the first horizon as risk; a patient with fewer than two marker draws by the landmark gets no prediction. The paper names no package, formula or code (its statistical analysis is SPSS 25 and R 4.1.2); the wrapper builds the paper's described model from the JM/nlme/survival framework the paper's methods references describe, and every unspecified functional form (baseline hazard, phase coding, Monte Carlo size) is a documented wrapper choice.

Fitted for progression (the paper's graft-failure-or-death composite endpoint), else death when the training data carry only overall survival; a patient with fewer than two marker draws by the landmark gets no prediction with the reason in note.

methods.description: The corrected two-stage Bayesian multivariate joint model of Mauff et al., Statistics and Computing 2020 (DOI 10.1007/s11222-020-09927-9, estimator mvJointModelBayes in JMbayes 0.8-85, the paper's own pinned version), applied as its Bio-SHiFT Model 3: K repeated biomarkers, each with its own gaussian linear mixed submodel (JMbayes::mvglmer, JAGS engine; the paper's per-marker constructions: linear random intercept + slope for the first three markers, a natural cubic spline in both the fixed and the random part with percentile knots for the rest), a Cox submodel of progression on the baseline covariates (the paper's eight baseline variables; with the covariate track on the wrapper enters every cov_* column as a numeric main effect, without it the Cox is intercept-only), and one association parameter per marker multiplying the INTEGRATED longitudinal profile (area under the curve, the paper's Model 3), estimated with the global-local ridge-type shrinkage prior of the paper. Each patient's conditional probability of progression by every horizon comes from JMbayes::survfitJM (M = 150 posterior simulations), conditioned on being event-free at the benchmark landmark with the draws up to it; the wrapper writes the model's own probability at the first horizon as risk and the same model's p_progression_H<h> for the later horizons. It is fitted only for progression (the paper's composite event): the training patients need pfs_time and pfs_event. The paper applies a log base 2 transform by the caller and its model clock is years since baseline, so the wrapper transforms raw marker values with log2 (values at or below zero become missing, i.e. the complete-case rows mvglmer keeps) and uses time_unit_days 365.25 to convert the harness days; a patient with fewer than two complete-case draws by the landmark gets no prediction. methods.description: Dynamic prediction of treatment failure by the multivariate shared random-effect joint model of Wang, Li, Lan, Zhao, Zheng and Li (Computational Statistics & Data Analysis 2022, DOI 10.1016/j.csda.2022.107528; authors' code GitHub ShikunW/JMGPU), in the linear-trajectory version the paper compares against ('LJ, sigma_um = 0'): for every marker the longitudinal sub-model is a linear trajectory Y_m(t) = [1,X']beta_m0 + beta_m1 t + b_m0i + b_m1i t + eps, the subject-specific intercepts and slopes of all markers follow one zero-mean multivariate normal with covariance Sigma_b (2M x 2M, no spline terms, no sigma_u), and the survival sub-model is a Cox hazard h_i(t) = h0(t) exp(X'alpha_1 + sum_m alpha_2m (b_m0i + b_m1i t)) associating the current adjusted linear trajectory with the event. Estimation is the paper's two-stage procedure: stage 1 fits each subject's unpenalized [1,t] trajectory and forms the closed-form variance components; stage 2 runs an EM with Monte Carlo integration of the random effects (PyTorch, GPU-accelerated in the paper, CPU in the container) with the stage-1 variance components held fixed, alpha started from a lifelines Cox model and updated by one Newton-Raphson step per EM iteration, and the piecewise-constant baseline hazard on the sample-quantile cut points of the scaled time axis (the wrapper divides days by the largest training endpoint time, as the authors' renal driver divided by the cohort's maximum follow-up). Prediction is the dynamic prediction of the paper: for a new patient it draws the random effects from the Gaussian posterior given the baseline covariates and every biomarker draw up to the landmark, and reports the conditional event probability P(T <= landmark + Delta | T > landmark, history) for each horizon, i.e. 1 - S(s+Delta|H(s))/S(s|H(s)); the fitted model conditions on still being at risk at the landmark, and the same fitted model can be re-used on a later history. The wrapper fits one such model per survival endpoint of the training data (progression from pfs_time/pfs_event, death from os_time/os_event; a single fit serves both when the two endpoint columns coincide), writes the progression and death event probabilities for every horizon and the progression probability at the first horizon as risk, and lets the benchmark convert the risk for the response outcomes. The wrapper keeps the authors' data conventions: values clipped to [0,1e5] then z-scored with the training mean/sd, baseline covariates z-scored, at least three measurements of every marker per training subject. Where the published code cannot run as-is (semicolon comment banners, NumPy 2 ragged-array handling, a pandas 2 indexing call, a non-positive-definite Sigma_b, the control['MCmax'] ignored, the broken predict function), the wrapper applies the smallest fixes and records them in the README; everything the paper reports for the linear model is reproduced from the estimation core.
