methods.description: The combined progression-risk call of Wu et al. (Cancer Medicine 2024;12:e70316, DOI 10.1002/cam4.70316; 44 inoperable localized NSCLC patients on platinum-based CRT/RT, 97 plasma samples at TP1 (week 4 of CRT/RT, n=39), TP2 (1 month after CRT/RT completion, n=33) and TP3 (3 months after completion, n=25), each sample by targeted NGS of 474 cancer-related genes (GeneseeqPrime) and by cfDNA neomer profiling (1758 16-bp neomers recurrent in cancer genomes, absent from the reference genome, md:20, md:41, md:50)): the OR combination of the neomer-model predicted risk status with the ctDNA mutation-detection status - high risk for progression if the neomer sSVM model (scikit-survival v0.17.2, one model per time point, LOOCV, 90%-specificity training-set cutoff, md:52, md:57, md:79) calls the patient high risk OR the panel sequencing detects a ctDNA mutation (md:121, md:133); low risk only when both are negative. The paper's results: combined sensitivity/specificity 60%/78.6% (TP1), 55%/92.3% (TP2), 54.5%/85.7% (TP3), all-TP 77.8%/70.6% with HR 4.51 (1.77-11.51), and 19-patients-at-all-three-timepoints 88.9%/80% with HR 13.37 (1.63-109.4) (md:107-115, md:135, md:137). The wrapper takes exactly two markers (the neomer-model high-risk status and the ctDNA mutation-detection status, identified in required_markers; roles by marker name, positional fallback markers[0] = neomer status, markers[1] = ctDNA status), reads each draw's status as value > 0 (the benchmark's below-detection encoding; the paper's mutation-positivity threshold is NOT stated - recorded as a difference), applies the OR at the patient's most recent draw with both statuses on or before the landmark (the paper's per-time-point status pair), and writes call = 1 for combined high risk (treatment judged failing) and risk = the sum of the two status values at that draw (the quantity the OR thresholds; the paper defines no per-patient score - the count of positive arms for 0/1 statuses, with the arms' own values when the dataset carries them; TxResBench converts the risk). No probability is written (the paper defines none); a patient with no on-treatment status pair by the landmark gets no prediction, with the reason in note (the paper's per-time-point analyses are complete case, md:32, md:52, md:137).

methods.description: The three-group rule of the relative NLR change from the baseline draw to the 6 (±2)-week draw of Lalani et al. (J Immunother Cancer 2018, 142 mRCC patients on PD-1/PD-L1 ICB at Dana-Farber 2009-2017). The rule (the paper's Methods): '% change ({[NLR week 6 / NLR week 0] - 1}*100)' is grouped at ±25% into ≥25% decrease (<= -25), no change (-25 < change < +25) and ≥25% increase (>= +25), with the exact -25/+25 boundaries in the outer groups; the groups were the exposure of multivariable Cox (PFS, OS) and logistic (ORR) models from the 6-week landmark adjusted for line of therapy, number of IMDC risk factors, histology and baseline NLR - vs the no-change reference, the increase group had adjusted HR 2.60 (PFS) / 1.57 (OS) and OR 0.45 (ORR), the decrease group HR 0.55 / 0.33 and OR 1.52, so an NLR increase is the unfavourable direction. The wrapper takes one marker, the raw NLR per patient per draw; its baseline value is the last NLR draw on or before baseline_max_day (the paper's 'NLR at start of IO'), and its week-6 value is the draw after the baseline and at or before the landmark whose day lies inside week6_days ± week6_window_days (default 42 ± 14 days, the paper's '6 (±2) weeks', i.e. 4-8 weeks after the first dose) closest to week6_days, ties going to the later draw; draws outside that window or after the landmark never enter the rule. It writes risk = the % change itself (the quantity the two cutoffs apply to; negative = decline, the favourable direction, higher = worse) and call 1 for the ≥25% increase class (treatment judged failing) and 0 otherwise; it writes no probability, the paper defines none (TxResBench converts the risk). The wrapper learns nothing from the training outcomes; a patient without a baseline draw, without a draw in the 6 ± 2-week window by the landmark, with a missing value, or with a non-positive NLR in either draw (0 is the harness's below-detection encoding and an NLR, a ratio of counts, cannot be 0) gets no prediction with the reason in note - the paper reports no imputation or fallback. The group-level HRs and ORs of the paper's association models are cohort-level validation of the grouping, not part of the call.

methods.description: The four-group prognostic classification from the absolute neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) in blood at two fixed draws of Lee et al. (J Cancer Res Clin Oncol 2012;138:2009-2016, DOI 10.1007/s00432-012-1281-4; 199 never smokers with advanced lung adenocarcinoma, the First-SIGNAL first-line gefitinib vs gemcitabine+cisplatin trial, 4 patients of 203 excluded for a missing NLR value). The rule: the NLR (neutrophils/lymphocytes, md:79) is read at the pretreatment draw (leukocyte counts with differential within 14 days before the first cycle, md:75 - the baseline draw) and at the posttreatment draw (day 1 of the second treatment cycle, median 21 days after the first cycle, range 20-28 days, md:79 - the draw closest to 21 days after the first dose, ties to the later draw); the patients are split at the ROC-derived pretreatment cutoff (3.25) and each half is dichotomized at the ROC-derived posttreatment cutoff (2.90) - the best pair of sensitivity and specificity for the 1-year survival rate, md:85/md:127 - into four pre/post groups (low-low, low-high, high-low, high-high). The paper's findings: the high-high group is the worst (median OS 7.9 vs 20.7 months for high-low, P < 0.001, md:127) and the posttreatment NLR is the dominant axis (it stays the independent predictor of PFS and OS in the treatment-arm-stratified adjusted Cox: per-unit HR 1.23 [1.15-1.31] PFS and 1.13 [1.06-1.21] OS, md:116). The wrapper writes risk = the posttreatment NLR value itself (the quantity the posttreatment cutoff thresholds; a ratio, higher = more likely failing per the paper's per-unit HRs) and call = 1 for a high posttreatment NLR (> 2.90, the paper's on-treatment high/low dichotomy and its 'early evaluation of whether the current treatment should be maintained' call, md:140), 0 otherwise; it writes no probability (the paper defines none: its survival quantities are group medians, KM curves and adjusted HRs; TxResBench converts the risk) and the four-group cell and the per-timepoint high/low counts go to the fit report as per-cohort counts (the driver rejects non-numeric columns). A patient without both draws, with a missing value, or with an NLR value of 0 in either draw (0 is the harness's below-detection encoding and an NLR, a ratio of counts, cannot be 0) gets no prediction with the reason in note - the paper excludes such patients, reports no imputation and defines no fallback. The cutoffs 3.25/2.90 are published constants that the paper derived in this sample by ROC without a train/test split; the wrapper uses them as the method's settings (per-fold re-derivation would not reproduce the published rule, and the ROC cohort, AUC and operating point are not reported in the paper text). The paper's KM/log-rank and the treatment-arm-stratified multivariable Cox (HRs) are cohort-level associations of the grouping, not part of the per-patient call.

methods.description: The three-layer neural network classifier (per the bioRxiv preprint Appendix 6.2: 'a model with three layers each with 60 nodes', trained 'for 300 epochs on 70% of the data', the model receiving 'the six ctDNA samples' and 'a binary classification of whether partial response was achieved or not') that Li, Lou, Leder and Foo (JCO Clinical Cancer Informatics 2025;9:e2400160, doi:10.1200/cci-24-00160) trained in PyTorch to predict whether a patient treated with targeted therapy, chemotherapy or radiotherapy achieves partial response (maximum tumor shrinkage MTS >= 0.3, complete responders included) from the six early ctDNA samples of the paper's dense sampling protocols (48 hours around treatment start for targeted/chemotherapy; days 7, 9, 11, 14, 16, 18 for radiotherapy). The paper publishes no code, no weights and no architecture beyond those lines (the journal's Data Supplement was not retrievable), so the wrapper re-implements the stated architecture in PyTorch (three 60-node hidden layers with ReLU, a logistic output on one logit, Adam, binary cross-entropy, 300 epochs, 70/30 train/test split) and refits it on the benchmark training patients: input = the patient's ctDNA draws up to the landmark in chronological order as a fixed vector of up to six values (past six, carry-forward padding, log1p then per-position z-scoring with the training mean/sd), label = the harness no_response outcome (best RECIST SD or PD, the benchmark analogue of the paper's non-PR class, fitted as P(no response) so that risk is failure-oriented - the flip of the paper's P(PR), which the paper reports through ROC AUCs only: 0.94 targeted / 0.85 chemotherapy / 0.97 radiotherapy test AUCs); every hyperparameter the paper does not state (activation, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, input scaling, initialisation seed) is the wrapper's documented choice, recorded in run.json and the README. The wrapper writes risk = p_no_response = the network's fitted probability of no response and no call (the paper reports no operating threshold); a patient without a baseline draw or any on-treatment draw by the landmark gets no prediction with the reason in note.

methods.description: The stage-2 parametric lognormal time-to-event model for progression-free survival of Nassar et al. (Cancers 2023;15(22):5429, DOI 10.3390/cancers15225429; 257 advanced-NSCLC patients of the CEPAC-TDM biomarker substudy, first-line paclitaxel/platinum): at the landmark of the start of treatment cycle 3 (day 42 from the first dose), PFS is modelled from the landmark with the lognormal baseline hazard h0(t) = phi((ln t - mu)/sigma)/(sigma*t*(1-Phi((ln t-mu)/sigma))) (Eq. 1) modified by the two predictor terms h(t) = h0(t)*(1+E_CRPcycle3*CRPcycle3)*(CRPcycle3-2)^E_CRPcycle3-2 (Eq. 2, control stream TTE_PFS.mod of the paper's own Github repository: linear in CRP at cycle 3 day 1, power in the cycle-3-minus-cycle-2 day-1 CRP difference), estimated in NONMEM 7.4.3 with the first-order method on the 203 patients event-free at the landmark and with no interindividual variability (one event per patient, $OMEGA 0 FIX). The two per-patient predictors are model-estimated CRP values from the paper's stage-1 coupled tumour-dynamics-CRP turnover model; the benchmark gives blood biomarkers only (not the RECIST tumour size, IL-6, disease stage, smoking status or paclitaxel AUC the stage-1 model consumes), so the wrapper derives the two Table-1 metrics from the observed CRP draws at the two protocol times (cycle 2 day 1 = landmark - 21 days, cycle 3 day 1 = landmark; below-LLOQ draws excluded as in the paper) and re-implements the published TTE verbatim: landmark risk set, hours-from-landmark clock, the same linear + power covariate terms, no IIV. NONMEM is commercial and not fitted here, but the TTE has no random effects, so the first-order likelihood is the ordinary parametric-TTE likelihood; the wrapper maximizes it per training fold with scipy (multi-start bounded maximum likelihood; the paper's final estimates are not re-used), and writes each patient's own P(event by day h | event-free at the landmark) = 1 - S(h) for progression and - with the same lognormal structure (a recorded stand-in; the paper's OS model is the separate Weibull specification with tumour-size and liver-lesion predictors) - for death; the response outcomes are the TxResBench conversion of the risk, which is the model's own first-horizon probability. The paper's per-patient curve has no IIV, so patients differ only in the two CRP covariates.

methods.description: Cui et al. (npj Precision Oncology 2025;9:102, DOI 10.1038/s41698-025-00879-9; 37 advanced BTC patients on Camrelizumab + GEMOX, plasma Olink PEA NPX at T1 baseline / T2 6 weeks / T3 6 months, md:105-110) screened the 92 measured proteins with per-protein linear mixed effect models (OlinkAnalyze::olink_lmer, NPX ~ Time*Response + (1|Subject), F-test with Satterthwaite df, BH 5% FDR, Tukey-adjusted p < 0.05, md:742-759): 50 proteins were significant for the interaction effect, and the most significant three were HO-1, ANGPT2 and IL15, whose values in the SD_PD group were all higher than in the PR group at all three time points (md:268-272); the three proteins' 'combined protein biomarker' was then evaluated by a receiver operating characteristic curve against the PR vs SD_PD label (AUC = 0.74, md:273-275). The paper publishes neither the combination rule nor the ROC's input time point, and no operating cutoff, per-patient call or probability (md:567-568); the LME selection is the provenance that fixes the marker set, so the wrapper implements the published fixed three-marker biomarker: for each marker, its latest value measured on or before the landmark (a below-detection draw is represented by the draw's LOD value when the data carry one, otherwise that draw is unused), and the risk is the arithmetic mean of those three values (all in the same NPX log2 arbitrary unit and all moving the same way, higher in SD_PD, so higher risk = treatment more likely failing), requiring at least two of the three to be measured; a patient with fewer gets no prediction, with the reason in note. The wrapper writes no call and no probability of its own (the paper defines neither), so TxResBench converts the risk for the four outcomes; the ROC/AUC discrimination the paper reports (0.74, in-sample, no validation) is the benchmark analysis's, not the wrapper's. Nothing is learned from the training outcomes (fitted false: the markers, the draw choice and the combination are fixed declarations; the OlinkAnalyze LME that selected the markers is not refit, and no ROC package is substituted because none is named).

methods.description: Per-patient call of initial-treatment success vs failure in perioperative septic shock from the serum procalcitonin (PCT) trajectory at ICU admission (day 0) and days 1, 3, 5 (Jung et al., Critical Care 2013, DOI 10.1186/cc13082): success is predicted when the lowest PCT from ICU admission to day 5 (the nadir) is below 0.5 ng/ml, or when PCT dropped by at least 80% from its peak over the same window ((peak - nadir)/peak >= 0.80). Both thresholds are fixed constants borrowed from the medical-ICU PCT-guided-antibiotic literature, not derived here (the paper performed no ROC). The wrapper writes the two per-threshold calls and the combined call (the extraction's OR reading) as extra columns, the combined decision margin as risk (nadir minus the larger of 0.5 ng/ml and 20% of the peak, in ng/ml; higher = more likely failing, and call = 1 = treatment judged failing exactly when risk > 0) and the two features; it writes no probability. Patients with fewer than three PCT measurements are not analyzed (the paper's exclusion).

methods.description: Per-draw call of imaging-defined RECIST v1.1 (and dramatic) progression from serial plasma pEGFRmut detectability during first-line EGFR-TKI therapy (Zhu YJ, Zhang HB, et al., 'Estimation of cell-free circulating EGFR mutation concentration predicts outcomes in NSCLC patients treated with EGFR-TKIs', Oncotarget 2017;8(18):30071-30080, DOI 10.18632/oncotarget.14490; 57 previously untreated stage III/IV NSCLC patients with TKI-sensitive tEGFRmut, imaging every 2 months (max 3), plasma ddPCR at WuXi AppTec every 2 months at the same time as imaging, md:121): the monitoring rule is a per-draw state - pEGFRmut POSITIVE = L858R or exon 19 deletion detectable by ddPCR at the draw, NEGATIVE = the mutant concentration decreased to zero ('mutant pEGFR concentrations decreased to zero in 43 patients (89.58%)', md:77) - compared against the concurrent imaging-defined progression call; in the 48 followed-up patients Table 3 gives concordance 93.75% (86.90-100%), sensitivity 92.59% (82.71-100%), specificity 95.23% (86.12-100%), PPV 96.15% (88.76-100%), NPV 90.91% (78.90-100%) against RECIST v1.1 progression (27/21) and 87.5% (78.14-96.86%), 100%, 78.58% (63.38-93.78%), 76.92% (60.72-93.12%), 100% against the Jin-ji Yang dramatic-progression classification (20/28), and the 43 cleared-to-zero patients had significantly better PFS than the 5 who remained detectable (md:77, md:103). The wrapper reads the rule on the benchmark's landmark frame: per patient, at each on-treatment draw up to the landmark the state is positive when any of the two TKI-sensitive assays is detected (the assay's own <marker>__detected companion row when the data has one, else value > detection_threshold, default 0.0 - the benchmark's non-detect is value 0, matching 'decreased to zero'; the paper prints no per-draw LOD, the 0.02% assay detection sensitivity (md:16) is a mutant-fraction figure from the authors' prior work), and the wrapper's per-patient call (declared aggregation, see the README: Table 3's per-patient timepoint is not defined) is the state at the LAST draw at or before the landmark: call = 1 = pEGFRmut positive = imaging-defined progression predicted = treatment judged failing, call = 0 = negative ('decreased to zero'). risk is the pre-threshold quantity the rule thresholds - the larger of the two assays' copies/mL at that same draw (0 when both read zero; higher = more likely failing); no probability is written (the paper defines none per patient, so TxResBench converts the risk). Nothing is fitted - the rule learns nothing from the training outcomes (`fitted` false); the paper's baseline high/low stratification (>= 200 copies/mL L858R or >= 75 copies/mL ex19del, KM/log-rank + multivariate Cox HR 3.96) is a different method (recorded as an application variant of median-split-survival) and is not this wrapper; a patient with no readable pEGFRmut (L858R/ex19del) state in the on-treatment draws by the landmark gets no prediction with the reason in note. Markers named T790M are reported but never used (the paper's T790M finding is descriptive: 20 patients detectable during follow-up, earlier/concurrent/after pEGFRmut in 3/12/3 of the 18 progressed, md:92).

methods.description: The joint four-slope penalized logistic model of Campenni et al. (Clin Chem Lab Med 2026, aop, DOI 10.1515/cclm-2026-0757; 23 patients with advanced medullary thyroid carcinoma and confirmed structural disease, serum calcitonin, CEA, ProGRP and CA 19-9 every 3-6 months over a median 37 months; 'To explore the combined contribution of biomarkers, a penalized logistic regression model was used to mitigate the risk of overfitting.', md:160-162; published result: 'In multivariable penalized models, ProGRP slope remained the most consistently associated marker after internal validation.', md:35-36). The predictors are the four per-patient log-linear slopes - per patient and marker the ordinary least squares regression of the natural logarithm of the serum concentration on time, ln(marker) = beta0 + beta1 x time (the paper's method 1, md:147-153), evaluated on the draws on or before the benchmark's landmark day and reported in ln-units/month (Table 4's unit). The paper publishes NO penalty type or strength, NO predictor scaling, NO outcome label (its two research outcomes are structural progression, n = 13, and disease-related death, n = 3; md:199-201), NO coefficient, NO per-patient probability and NO analysis code, so the wrapper declares every unpublished choice: it fits a ridge (L2) logistic regression (scikit-learn LogisticRegression penalty='l2', solver='lbfgs', C parameter, default 1.0) of each failure label the benchmark's training data give on the four slopes standardized by the training-set mean/sd - the response outcomes' labels as given, and for progression and death one fit per horizon on the event-by-h label (patients censored before h carry no label and are left out of that fit) - and writes that model's own probability per outcome as p_no_response, p_progressive_disease and p_progression_H<h> / p_death_H<h>, with risk = the fitted linear predictor of the paper's primary reading (structural progression vs non-progressive disease, Figure 2 left panel: the benchmark's progressive_disease channel, with the no_response and then the progression fit as fallbacks when the response outcomes are absent), higher = the treatment more likely failing. The paper's per-marker ROC AUCs (Table 5: ProGRP 0.93 death / 0.91 progression), the KM/log-rank results and the PFS HR 3.8 (95% CI 1.4-10.2) are method 1's per-marker evaluation quantities of the same paper, not this model's outputs, and are not reproduced; no per-patient probability, coefficient or validation metric is published for the penalized model, and its 'internal validation' (md:36) names no scheme, so nothing is validated or calibrated here - the benchmark's own folds and evaluation provide the arena. A patient who lacks any one of the four slopes (fewer than 2 positive draws on 2 distinct days of a marker, e.g. a below-detection series) gets no prediction with the reason in note; below-detection draws (value 0) are outside the log's domain and excluded - the paper states no handling. No call is written (no probability threshold is published).

methods.description: The per-landmark PhasED-Seq ctDNA minimal residual disease (MRD) call of Alig et al. (Nature 2024, DOI 10.1038/s41586-023-06903-x; 310 serial on-treatment plasma samples from 109 adult classical Hodgkin lymphoma patients during curative-intent frontline therapy): at each on-treatment landmark (C1D15, C2D1, C3D1, after >=4 cycles) patients are called MRD-positive (ctDNA detectable) or MRD-negative (undetectable) by the ultrasensitive phased-variant (PhasED-Seq) assay monitoring the patient-specific phased variants (VAF >= 0.5%) identified in the pretreatment plasma genotype; detectable ctDNA was associated with inferior progression-free survival at each landmark (C1D15 P=0.028, C3D1 P=7.3e-5, after >=4 cycles P=2.7e-7; MRD negativity rates 38%, 85% and 90% at C1D15, C2D1 and C3D1). The PhasED-Seq detection engine and the RePhyNER germline-free filter (pseudocode only, maxIter=50, FDR=0.1) are assay software/algorithm output that this wrapper consumes, not reimplements: the benchmark marker is the per-draw ctDNA level (hGE/mL) with its per-draw detection call (the marker's __detected companion rows), and the wrapper's rule is the per-landmark application - at the benchmark landmark the call is the detection state of the last on-treatment draw (the paper's landmark draw; the KM/log-rank association is cohort-level and is recomputed at fit in run.json), call = 1 for detectable ctDNA (treatment judged failing, the paper's inferior-PFS group) and 0 for undetectable; risk = the ctDNA level at that draw on the paper's regression unit log10(hGE/mL) (scale 'linear', default: values as measured, the wrapper takes log10; 'log10': values already log10), higher = more ctDNA = worse; an undetectable draw with a marker detection limit (__lod rows) is scored at the limit and otherwise has no risk (the paper defines no numeric value for an undetectable sample; the MRD call is binary) with the reason in note. No per-patient probability is defined by the paper: TxResBench converts the risk. A patient with fewer than one on-treatment draw by the landmark gets no prediction: the paper defines no imputation and later draws must not leak into an earlier landmark.

methods.description: The phase-specific LightGBM binary classifier of kidney graft failure (Salybekov A, et al., Front Artif Intell 2025;8:1682639, DOI 10.3389/frai.2025.1682639; UNOS/OPTN deceased-donor kidney transplant recipients 2015-2021, five phase-specific post-transplant cohorts 0-3 to 39-72 months): per phase, one lightgbm 4.3.0 LGBMClassifier predicts graft failure DURING that interval from the follow-up record at one selected visit (chiefly recipient serum creatinine, plus recipient BMI; md:42, md:132) and the pre-operative donor/recipient waiting-list record (md:26), after the paper's preprocessing - features with >30% missing values removed, the rest imputed with MICE via the miceforest package, RandomUnderSampling to the minority-class count (md:40) - with stratified fivefold GridSearchCV tuning (md:47; 'The mean ROC-AUC served as the primary performance metric'). The paper publishes no analysis code (md:154, md:200) and no hyperparameter grid, seed, feature-selection rule or classification cutoff ('?' per the spec), so the wrapper makes documented choices, every one recorded in run.json and the README: the benchmark's graft-failure endpoint is the progression outcome (the sibling cox-phr-kidney-graft reading), whose paper binary interval label stands in as the horizon label progression_H<h> (label_horizon 'first' = the first horizon as the phase end, 'last' available); because TxResBench scores all four outcomes, the same classifier is also fitted on the training data's other outcomes (death by death_H<h>, no_response directly - the rf-immune-params-recurrence convention, the progressive-disease rows being scored by the no_response classifier since PD is a subset of non-response and the paper defines no PD-specific model), the primary classifier (risk and call) being progression, else death, else no_response, else progressive_disease; the selected visit is the wrapper's last marker draw in (baseline_max_day, landmark_day] (same reading as the cox-phr-kidney-graft sibling; min_draws 1, the paper's single-visit row); the waiting-list record enters as the cov_* columns when the dataset provides them (covariates 'optional': the mindraws census reads the record as required, and the benchmark's covariate-free mode fits the marker at the visit alone - the statistica-svm-pcr fallback convention); the LightGBM defaults apply with min_child_samples 5 (the package default 20 cannot split the smallest benchmark folds at all) and a small search grid (params.grid; scikit-learn 1.5.2 GridSearchCV, StratifiedKFold 5, roc_auc scoring - the paper's primary metric). It writes risk = the primary classifier's class-1 probability of graft failure within the interval and risk_<outcome> = each outcome's own probability (higher = more likely failing; predict_proba per lightgbm 4.3.0, the paper's own model output), and call = 1 when the primary's risk reaches call_threshold (the wrapper's default 0.5, the LightGBM/sklearn default decision boundary: the paper reports no cutoff but evaluates F1 and G-mean, which require a threshold). No p_* probabilities: a response-call decision writes the quantities it thresholds as its risks and its call, and TxResBench converts each risk per outcome. MICE imputation uses the paper's named miceforest package (no version published: the wrapper pins 6.0.5, the reference sdist) and falls back to training-median imputation with a recorded warning; a patient with no marker draw in the visit window gets no prediction with the reason in note (the paper's cohort eligibility rule is not published, '?'). Differences from the paper (each recorded): the five phase-specific cohorts collapse into the benchmark's single landmark call; the paper's feature selection on the combined train+validation set by RF/XGB/LGBM importance is not reproduced (its rule and feature count are '?'); the paper's 'iteration rate = 100 repetitions' (md:40) is not interpreted ('?'); the per-outcome fitting extends the paper's one classifier per phase to the benchmark's four scored outcomes; the paper's months-since-transplantation clock is the benchmark's days-since-first-dose clock.

methods.description: The per-patient early change score Delta = week 1 value - baseline value of a plasma immune marker, evaluated by ROC/AUC against the binary RECIST v1.1 treatment response, of Kim et al. (Cancers 2025;17(19):3131, DOI 10.3390/cancers17193131; 50 advanced gastric cancer patients on nivolumab + XELOX/FOLFOX, 28 objective responders): 'For dynamic changes, Delta (delta) values were calculated as week 1 minus baseline levels.' (md:50); 'ROC curve analysis was performed with Granzyme B as the primary variable (Figure 3). Both DeltaGranzyme B alone and the combination of DeltaGranzyme B with DeltaKi-67 showed effective prediction of response (AUC = 0.794 and 0.810, respectively).' (md:77). The analysis is the primary DeltaGranzyme B score (the paper's defined marker: plasma Granzyme B by ELISA; required_markers HGNC GZMB with the paper's published direction responders rise, md:72 - so higher Delta = response-favorable and the failure-oriented risk is -Delta). The wrapper takes exactly one marker, computes the per-patient Delta between the baseline draw (day <= baseline_max_day, the paper's pre-treatment draw within 1 day before or on the day of treatment initiation) and the draw closest to the paper's week 1 (day 7, within week1_tolerance_days 14, ties to the later draw; abstain otherwise - the week 6 draw is never substituted) and writes it as risk in the failure direction. The paper defines no operating cutoff, no per-patient call and no probability (AUCs only, md:77), so the wrapper writes risk only and the survey/roster group response-call is recorded as a deviation: the contract classification is static-risk, one score at the landmark (the c3-two-spot-delta-roc resolution). The risk's sign is oriented at fit by the paper's own group comparison (the Mann-Whitney U test of Fig. 1, the paper's Delta responder-vs-non-responder analysis) on the training fold's failure label (no_response, else progressive_disease, else the first event-by-horizon label), with the paper's published direction (Delta up = responder-like -> risk = -Delta) as the recorded fallback when the training data cannot orient it - the wrapper then reproduces the paper's group comparison on the fold as a cohort record in run.json. The published additive ladder DeltaGranzymeB + DeltaKi67 (+ DeltaCXCL10 + DeltaIFNgamma, Fig. 3a) is NOT reproduced: the '+' combination equation and the ELISA units are not published ('?'), and no combination formula is invented (recorded deviation). A patient without a scorable baseline + in-tolerance week-1 pair gets no prediction with the reason in note (the paper defines no imputation for a missing draw).

methods.description: The per-sample binary-presence monitoring call of Keup et al. (Cells 2021;10(2):212, DOI 10.3390/cells10020212; 27 HR+ HER2- metastatic breast cancer patients, 81 samples at the three 3-monthly staging time points TP0/TP1/TP2): at a staging time point, the presence of a liquid-biopsy parameter - one of the 51 binary parameters (17 CTC mRNA overexpression signals, 17 EV mRNA overexpression signals, 17 cfDNA gene variants) or a disjunction (logical OR) of 2-3 of them (the paper's tested 20 combinations) - is a progressive-disease (PD) call at that same time point, and absence is a stable-disease (SD) call; the paper's paper-level result was that no single parameter correlated with progression (Fisher's exact), while two disjunctions were significant unadjusted (CTC_ERBB3 OR CTC_ERBB2, p = 0.023, sens 36% / spec 86% / acc 59%; cfDNA_ERBB3 OR CTC_ERBB3 OR EV_ERBB3, p = 0.032, sens 32% / spec 89% / acc 58%), neither surviving Holm-Bonferroni. The wrapper takes one or more markers (the parameters; with several it evaluates the paper's disjunction - the combination is present iff any member parameter is present, and the paper's fixed tested sets are listed in the README), reads each parameter's binary state (the marker's __detected companion row when the data has it, else the value above 0 - the paper's binary state, no numeric threshold, the assay thresholds of the upstream pipelines [21]/[22] are not in the paper) at the patient's most recent on-treatment staging draw on or before the landmark, and writes the call (1 = combination present = PD call, 0 = absent = SD call - the paper's polarity, PD is the failure class) plus as risk the sum of the members' measured values at that draw (the quantity the presence state is thresholded from; the paper defines no per-patient score, and the benchmark converts the risk; higher = more signal = the progression side). It writes no probability (the paper defines none) and saves a model (fixed rule; the marker list). A patient with no on-treatment draw by the landmark, or no member value at the call draw, gets no prediction with the reason in note - the paper excludes such samples (all parameters characterized per sample) and defines no fallback.

methods.description: The five-category PSA-decline stratification of Armstrong et al. (Cancer 2017;123(12):2303-2311, DOI 10.1002/cncr.30587; post hoc analysis of the AFFIRM phase 3 trial, NCT00974311: 1199 men with post-docetaxel metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, 2:1 to enzalutamide 160 mg/day or placebo): per patient, the percentage PSA decline = (baseline PSA - minimum serum PSA during the first 90 days of treatment)/baseline PSA, and the maximal (deepest) decline is evaluated against five NON-EXCLUSIVE categories, each compared with the reference 'increase/no decline' - any decline (>0%), >=30%, >=50%, >=90% decline, and achievement of a posttreatment PSA <= 0.2 ng/mL (an absolute level, not a per cent change); each category is duplicated unconfirmed and confirmed (confirmatory value measured at least 4 weeks after day 90 and no higher than the maximal 90-day decline). The stratum association was evaluated by Kaplan-Meier estimates (median OS, 12- and 16-month OS, median PSA PFS, median rPFS, pain response; Table 1), Cox models and surrogacy statistics (Prentice criteria 1-4, PTE, PVE R2; Supporting Tables 1-2); the paper finds PSA declines of any, >=30% and >=50% strongly associated with longer OS, PSA PFS, rPFS and pain response (P <.001 / P <.026) and a lack of PSA decline by 90 days a poor-prognosis indicator. The wrapper is a fixed rule: it computes the feature exactly as defined (the last draw on or before baseline_max_day as baseline, the minimum over the draws after it up to min(landmark_day, decline_window_days)) and writes as risk the quantity the relative-decline categories are thresholds on - the per cent change at the deepest on-treatment value, 100*(minimum in window - baseline)/baseline (negative = decline, the favourable direction; higher = more likely failing: the paper's 'increase/no decline' reference category gives risk >= 0). It writes no per-patient probability (the paper defines none - only group-level KM estimates, hazard ratios and surrogacy statistics, which are cohort quantities and are not per-patient predictions) and no call (the five categories are nested and non-exclusive, and no single decision rule is defined; Figure 4's <30% versus >=30% split is an evaluation view of the same strata); TxResBench converts the risk. It learns nothing from the training outcomes (the categories and the 90-day window are fixed published constants).

methods.description: The combined deep/shallow PSA response rule of Wong et al. (Prostate 2025;85:30-39, DOI 10.1002/pros.24797): 131 consecutive patients with de novo metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (Hong Kong Prostate Cancer Research Group Database, 2016-2022) treated with upfront intensification (ADT plus docetaxel or an androgen receptor signalling inhibitor), landmark analysis at 6 months post-ADT. Per patient the lowest serum PSA recorded after treatment initiation (the nadir) is compared with the PSA level before treatment, and the time to that nadir (TTPN) is documented in months: the patient is a deep responder (call 0) when the PSA decline at the nadir is >=95% AND the TTPN is >=6 months, and a shallow responder (call 1, the paper's worse-outcome class) otherwise - 'the deep response group... versus the rest... which included those with non-PSA95 or TTPN < 6 months' (md:101; 119 landmark-eligible: 64 deep (53.8%) vs 55 shallow, and deep responders had longer PFS (median 42.7 vs 20.3 months, HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.34-0.91, p=0.019), OS (72.1 vs 67.8 months, HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.26-0.97, p=0.036) and CSS (NR vs 67.8 months, HR 0.43, 95% CI 0.19-0.99, p=0.042; the KM/log-rank/Cox association is not part of the rule). The wrapper is a fixed rule (learns nothing from the training outcomes): baseline = the last PSA draw on or before baseline_max_day (the paper's pretreatment level); nadir = the minimum PSA among the draws after it up to the landmark (the first draw achieving the minimum; the paper's design allows an any-time nadir, md:140, but the benchmark call uses the draws up to the landmark only); the decline fraction at the nadir and the TTPN in months (month_days = 365.25/12 = 30.4375, the package's month conversion) give the call, with the '>=95%' and '>=6 months' boundaries inclusive as printed. It writes as risk the AND-rule shortfall in threshold units - max(0, 1 - decline/0.95, 1 - TTPN/6), 0 exactly for a deep responder, higher = further from the deep-response criteria (the paper defines no per-patient score; a rule writes the quantity it thresholds, and the two thresholded quantities are combined in their own threshold units) - and no probability (TxResBench converts the risk). A patient with no baseline PSA, a below-detection baseline (value 0 or <marker>__detected 0, so the per-cent reduction is undefined; the paper excludes patients lacking comprehensive baseline data, md:26), or no on-treatment PSA by the landmark gets no prediction, with the reason in note. The paper publishes no analysis code (data-on-request only), so the rule is implemented from the Methods/Results text.

methods.description: The PSA.KELIM prognostic classification of Carrot, Oudard, Colomban, Maillet, Sartor, Fizazi, Freyer, You et al. (JCO Clin Cancer Inform 2024;8:e2300208, DOI 10.1200/CCI.23.00208; post hoc analysis of the phase III FIRSTANA trial NCT01308567, cabazitaxel 20 mg/m2 or 25 mg/m2 q3w v docetaxel 75 mg/m2 q3w, all plus prednisone, in 1,168 chemo-naive mCRPC patients, 1,050 K-PD-assessable): the 'previously described' (ref 11) 3-compartment K-PD semimechanistic population nonlinear mixed-effects model of log-transformed serum PSA during the first 100 treatment days - treatment central compartment C1 with AMT fixed to 1 (no PK data), transit compartment C2, PSA compartment; zero-order PSA production KPROD (ng.mL-1.day-1) regulated by an indirect effect EFFECT(EC50) = 1 - C2/(EC50 + C2), first-order elimination KELIM (day-1), initial condition PSA(0) = PSA0E; the per-patient individual PSA elimination rate constant PSA.KELIM (day-1) is estimated, standardized by the sample median (Std PSA.KELIM = PSA.KELIM/median, md:69) and dichotomized into the PSA.KELIM score (unfavorable if Std PSA.KELIM < 1.0, favorable if >= 1.0, md:69), whose prognostic value for composite PFS (PSA-PFS + tumor PFS + pain PFS) and OS is assessed at the 100-day landmark by Kaplan-Meier/log-rank and multivariate Cox (univariate: median PFS 3.58 v 4.70 months, HR 0.77 [0.66-0.91] P =.0016; median OS 17.41 v 28.45 months, HR 0.54 [0.46-0.63] P <.001; multivariate PFS HR 0.79 [0.67-0.93] P =.005, OS 0.66 [0.54-0.80] P <.001 with PSA-DT, baseline radiological tumor progression, PSA response; the abstract's OS HR 0.51 [0.44-0.60] is a verbatim inconsistency, md:9 v md:134). The fit ran in COMMERCIAL Monolix 2020R1 (SAEM, SEs by Monte-Carlo importance sampling, md:78) and no code, dataset or model project was published; the paper's Data Supplement Table S2 (the Monolix refit parameter estimates) is not retrievable this session, so the wrapper follows the kpd-psa-nonmem convention for this model family: the published final population estimates of the SAME model from the origin paper it points to (Cancers 2022;14:815, Supplementary Table S2: K 2.130 day-1, KPROD 0.002 ng.mL-1.day-1, EC50 0.357 AU, PSA0E 4.220 ng.mL-1, KELIM 0.081 day-1, log-normal diagonal IIV) as a fixed population (fitted: false - the Monolix fit is not reproducible and nothing is learned from the training outcomes), per-patient maximum a posteriori individual parameters with that log-normal diagonal prior (the wrapper's analytic solution of the ODEs; base R stats::optim), the training-fold individual-PSA.KELIM median for the paper's standardization, and the benchmark risk = -log(Std PSA.KELIM) oriented to failure - the paper's favorable group (Std >= 1.0) has the longer PFS and OS - with call = 1 (treatment judged failing) when Std PSA.KELIM < 1.0, the paper's 'unfavorable PSA.KELIM'; the per-patient PSA.KPROD (the paper's second kinetic axis, results in the Data Supplement) is computed and recorded for the analysis but is not the benchmark risk (weakly identified from the benchmark's sparse draws, and A2024 reports no favorable/unfavorable direction for it). Documented deviations: population fixed from the A2022 Table-S2 estimates instead of the A2024 Monolix refit (the refit's Table S2 is unreachable; the spec's fitted_model input records the same substitution); per-patient MAP instead of the Monolix empirical-Bayes EBEs; residual sigma_log = 0.25 on the log scale (the paper publishes no residual error); below-LLOQ PSA (0.1 ng/mL; value 0 with __detected rows) excluded from the likelihood instead of the origin implementation's NONMEM M3 (A2024 states no handling); >= 3 detectable draws from the paper's >= 3-assays rule; dosing AMT 1 every 21 days x 5 (all three arms are q3w; the exact dosing-event times are not published); window = [0, min(100, landmark)]; 100-day-landmark event exclusion is the benchmark's own survival-cohort rule (patients at risk at the landmark), as in the paper (md:73); the score cutoff is the training-fold sample median, re-derived per fold as the paper derives it in its sample.

methods.description: The four-band PSA-nadir risk stratification of Kapar et al. (Ther Adv Med Oncol 2025;17:17588359251369037, DOI 10.1177/17588359251369037; PMID 40895017; retrospective single-centre research of 203 patients with metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer [mCSPC] who initiated first-line systemic treatment between January 2019 and January 2025): per patient, the PSA nadir = the lowest serum PSA achieved within the first 6 months of treatment (PSA measured at 1, 3 and 6 months per the institutional follow-up protocol; 'the lowest PSA level achieved within 6 months after treatment', Figure 1), and the nadir is binned into four FIXED published bands - ⩽0.02, 0.02-0.2, 0.2-4, >4 ng/mL (Table 1). The bands are compared by Kaplan-Meier rPFS curves (log-rank p < 0.001 overall; pairwise ⩽0.02 vs 0.02-0.2 p = 0.049; per-band median rPFS 59.2 / 31.4 / 23.5 / 17.0 months and 2-year rPFS rates 81% / 60.7% / 39.7% / 11.4%), and the headline association is a multivariable Cox regression of rPFS on the binary indicator 'PSA ⩽ 0.02 ng/mL vs higher' (HR 2.02, 95% CI 1.51-2.72). The wrapper is a fixed rule (learns nothing from the training outcomes): it computes the nadir as the minimum of the measured on-treatment PSA values in (baseline_max_day, min(landmark_day, 6 months)] and writes risk = the nadir value in ng/mL (higher = more likely failing - the paper's own direction, since the ⩽0.02 ng/mL group has the longest rPFS and the Cox HR 2.02 is for higher nadirs vs ⩽0.02) and call = 1 when the nadir > 0.02 ng/mL (the higher-nadir arm of the paper's binary Cox contrast), 0 when the nadir ⩽ 0.02; it writes no per-patient probability (the paper defines none - the KM medians, 2-year rates, log-rank p-values and Cox HRs are cohort-level association statistics; TxResBench converts the risk), and no per-patient score beyond the nadir and its band. At fit it reports the training-fold per-band Kaplan-Meier estimates (median rPFS, 2-year rPFS rate), the multi-group log-rank test and the paper's published results verbatim (the paper's multivariable adjustment set - disease volume, metastatic timing, hemoglobin, LDH, ALP, therapy type - is not an input of this method, so the adjusted HR is recorded as the paper's result, not recomputed). The four-band class itself is carried exactly by the nadir value plus the published cutoffs (0.02 / 0.2 / 4 ng/mL, boundary encoding from Table 1: ⩽0.02, 0.02-⩽0.2, 0.2-⩽4, >4) and is recorded per patient in the fit record.

methods.description: The poor-prognostic-factor count rule of Tsai C-S, et al. (BMC Cancer 2023;23:491, DOI 10.1186/s12885-023-10885-4; 202 patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer on first-line androgen receptor axis-targeted therapy - abiraterone acetate or enzalutamide): from the on-treatment serial serum PSA trajectory two per-patient response features are derived - the PSA nadir (the lowest PSA since the start of the initial ARAT, confirmed per the paper by two consecutive increases) and the time to PSA nadir (TTN, months from ARAT onset to the nadir) - and each is compared with the paper's in-sample ROC-derived cutoffs ('Higher PSA nadir after ARAT treatment was associated with higher mortality as shown with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.769 (P < 0.001) indicating a cutoff PSA of 2 ng/mL. Shorter TTN after ARAT indicated faster treatment failure and was associated with lower OS, as shown with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.640 (p = 0.001) indicating a cutoff TTN of 7 months.', md:113). Each patient accumulates 0, 1 or 2 poor prognostic factors (TTN < 7 months; PSA nadir > 2 ng/mL, md:145) and is stratified as 0-1 factors vs 2 factors (the 'high risk for all-cause mortality' group, md:158, md:172): IPTW-adjusted multivariate Cox HR 9.21 (95% CI 5.14-16.49, p < 0.001) for 2 vs 0-1 factors, 1 vs 0 factors HR 2.85 (1.21-6.71, p = 0.017) and 2 vs 0 factors HR 13.55 (5.96-30.82, p < 0.001) (Table 3, md:145, md:151-156); 2-year OS estimates 91% (0-1 factors) vs 46% (2 factors) (md:158). The wrapper is a fixed rule (nothing is fitted; the two cutoffs are the published constants and the optimality criterion of the paper's ROC step is not stated, so it is not re-derived): it computes the nadir and TTN from the PSA draws up to the benchmark landmark (the paper defines no landmark and no PSA schedule - the wrapper evaluates the rule at the harness's decision day with the draws up to it, and records the paper's two-increases confirmation as a status flag: at a prospective landmark the confirmation is not yet observable for most patients, so the wrapper scores the current response features and records the flag rather than excluding them - deviation 1), writes as risk the PSA nadir value in ng/mL (the quantity the paper's first poor-factor threshold is set on and the paper's strongest failure-oriented discriminator, AUC 0.769; the discrete count that the paper's factor stratification sums is carried by the call, which is 1 for the high-risk 2-factor group and 0 for 0-1 factors - a single risk number cannot carry both threshold quantities without inventing weights the paper never defines), writes no per-patient probability (the paper defines none; the 2-year group survival estimates and the KM/HR association results are cohort-level quantities), and lets TxResBench convert the risk. A patient without an on-treatment PSA value by the landmark gets no prediction, with the reason in note (the paper's complete-case rule, md:28).

methods.description: The four-level PSA nadir / time-to-nadir (TTN) risk-group rule of Mastroleo F, Villa R, Zaffaroni M, et al. (Eur Urol Oncol 2025; DOI 10.1016/j.euo.2025.12.001; PMID 41402161; retrospective multicentre research of 1189 patients with biochemical recurrence after radical prostatectomy treated with salvage radiotherapy [SRT] without androgen deprivation therapy, 15 European centres): per patient, the PSA nadir = the lowest serum PSA achieved after SRT over the follow-up draws, and the time to that nadir (TTN) is recorded in months; the two features are dichotomised at fixed published cutoffs (nadir <0.1 vs ≥0.1 ng/mL; TTN <6 vs ≥6 months, borrowed from prior literature, refs [9,13] = Scharl 2024 and Jackson 2014) and crossed into four exhaustive risk classes - favorable (nadir <0.1 ng/mL, TTN ≥6 months), low (nadir <0.1 ng/mL, TTN <6 months), intermediate (nadir ≥0.1 ng/mL, TTN ≥6 months), high (nadir ≥0.1 ng/mL, TTN <6 months) - 670/224/120/175 of the cohort respectively; the classes are compared by Kaplan-Meier curves and log-rank tests (BRFS and DMFS p < 0.0001; the extremes at 5 years: favorable 5-yr DMFS 96% vs high 63%), and the paper's Cox models confirm both features as independent adverse factors (nadir ≥0.1: HR 10.12 BRFS / 7.05 DMFS; TTN <6 months: HR 3.02 BRFS / 1.75 DMFS). The wrapper is a fixed rule (learns nothing from the training outcomes): the nadir = the minimum measured PSA over the on-treatment draws (after the first dose) up to the benchmark landmark, TTN months = the nadir day / month_days (365.25/12 = 30.4375; the harness clock is days since the first dose, the paper's TTN clock is not stated verbatim), the four-level class per the paper's definitions (nadir exactly 0.1 ng/mL and TTN exactly 6 months belong to the ≥ sides as in the Abstract and Methods; the Table 1 '>' glyphs are the export's '≥' eaten by the rendering), risk = the PSA nadir value in ng/mL (higher = more likely failing - the paper's direction: nadir ≥0.1 ng/mL HR 10.12 for BCR-free survival and 7.05 for DMFS, and the high-risk class has the worst quoted outcomes), call = 1 when the class is high-risk (nadir ≥0.1 ng/mL and TTN <6 months; the paper's explicitly worst class, 5-yr DMFS 63% vs 96% favorable) and 0 otherwise, and no per-patient probability (the KM/log-rank quantities are cohort-level association statistics; TxResBench converts the risk). A patient with no measured on-treatment PSA by the landmark gets no prediction, with the reason in note. The paper publishes no analysis code (R 4.4.2 environment only), so the rule is implemented from the article text, and the KM/log-rank association layer of the paper is recomputed on the training fold into run.json with the paper's published figures recorded verbatim.

methods.description: The three-layer neural network classifier that Li, Lou, Leder and Foo trained in PyTorch as a reference comparator in their early-ctDNA biomarker research (bioRxiv 2024.07.01.601508, doi:10.1101/2024.07.01.601508): 'we defined a model with three layers each with 60 nodes', trained 'for 300 epochs on 70% of the data', the model receiving 'the six ctDNA samples' and 'a binary classification of whether partial response was achieved or not' (Appendix, Model validation), and producing 'a binary prediction of whether the patient would exhibit partial response (PR) or not' - PR meaning at least a 20% decrease in tumor burden during treatment (MTS >= 0.2) - from the six early ctDNA samples of the paper's dense sampling protocols (targeted therapy/chemotherapy: three samples in the 24 h before plus three in the 24 h after treatment start; radiotherapy: days 7, 9, 11, 14, 16, 18). The paper publishes no code, no weights and no architecture beyond those sentences (no activation, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, scaling or operating threshold; the preprint reports no classifier AUCs - only that in all three treatments the biomarker AUC 'matches that of the classifier extremely closely', with biomarker AUCs 0.92 targeted / 0.84 chemotherapy / 0.96 radiotherapy), so the wrapper re-implements the stated architecture in PyTorch (three 60-node hidden layers with ReLU, one linear output logit, Adam, binary cross-entropy, 300 epochs, shuffled mini-batches) and refits it on the benchmark training patients: input = the patient's ctDNA draws up to the landmark in chronological order as a fixed vector of up to six values (carry-forward padding; log1p then per-position z-scoring with the training mean/sd), label = the harness no_response outcome (best RECIST SD or PD; responder = 0), the benchmark analogue of the paper's non-PR class, fitted as P(no response) so that the risk is failure-oriented - the flip of the paper's P(PR). The wrapper writes risk = that fitted probability and call = 1 when it is at least 0.5 (the natural boundary of the paper's binary prediction; no threshold is published), together with a note and no score for a patient it cannot score; every hyperparameter the paper does not state is the wrapper's documented choice (README and run.json).

methods.description: The per-patient residual-disease kinetics category rule of Puig N et al. (Haematologica 2024, DOI 10.3324/haematol.2024.285742; 62 high-risk smoldering multiple myeloma patients with serum samples from the 90-patient GEM-CESAR trial, NCT02415413, treated with 6 cycles of KRd, high-dose melphalan + ASCT, 2 cycles of consolidation KRd and up to two years of maintenance, landmark = end of treatment after the 24 maintenance cycles): from the serial per-draw binary residual-disease detection status between post-induction and treatment completion (peripheral residual disease = the M-protein by quantitative immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry in serum; minimal residual disease = clonal plasma cells by next-generation flow cytometry in bone marrow at 10^-5; one marker per run - the paper's Fig 4A and Fig 4B are the same rule with a different marker) each patient is one of four kinetics categories - sustained negativity, sustained positivity, conversion positive-to-negative, conversion negative-to-positive (md:94: PRD 12 [34%] / 6 [17%] / 16 [46%] / 1 [3%] of the 35 patients with paired samples at >= 2 of the 5 protocol time points; md:99: MRD 8 [23%] / 11 [31%] / 15 [43%] / 1 [3%]) - and the categories map to an outcome group: favorable = sustained negativity or conversion positive-to-negative (mPFS not reached, median follow-up 65 months), unfavorable = sustained positivity or conversion negative-to-positive (mPFS 1.66 years PRD, P<0.0001, / 2.1 years MRD; the single negative-to-positive converter mPFS 3.8 months), compared by Kaplan-Meier and a two-sided log-rank test in the landmark analysis from treatment completion (md:94, md:99, md:114). The wrapper takes one marker (the per-draw detection status: the marker's <marker>__detected rows when present, else 0/1 values, else the value-0 below-detection encoding, else the value against detection_threshold, default the training median as a documented stand-in for the assay's detection call - the paper publishes no numeric threshold, the call being the EXENT-iQ software's for MS and the EuroFlow 10^-5 definition for NGF), orders the on-treatment draws by day (the paper's five named visits in order; the exact visit day offsets are not published) and classifies the status series: all negative -> sustained negativity, all positive -> sustained positivity, one negative-to-positive transition -> conversion negative-to-positive, one positive-to-negative transition -> conversion positive-to-negative; a non-monotone series of >= 3 draws (e.g. +,-,+) has no category in the paper (spec '?') and gets no prediction with the reason in note. Writes risk = the category ordinal 0 sustained negativity / 1 conversion positive-to-negative / 2 sustained positivity / 3 conversion negative-to-positive (the paper's own favorable/unfavorable split in the call; within the unfavorable pair the paper publishes no ordering - the wrapper places conversion negative-to-positive above sustained positivity, by the reported medians 3.8 months vs 1.66/2.1 years and md:114 'imminent risk') and call = 1 for the unfavorable group (treatment judged failing: the defined failure class, mPFS 1.66 years PRD / 2.1 years MRD vs not reached), 0 for the favorable group; no per-patient probability is defined by the paper (TxResBench converts the risk). At fit the paper's landmark two-group KM and two-sided log-rank comparison for PFS is recomputed on the training patients and reported in run.json along with per-category counts and the published values as the reference. Differences from the paper, all recorded in the README: the benchmark clock's days replace the paper's named visits and cycle/months counts (no day offsets published); the paper's >= 2 paired-BM-and-PB time points become >= 2 on-treatment draws of the marker (the harness has no paired-sample concept); the detection call needs a stand-in threshold for a level-valued marker (training median, warned); non-monotone series abstain (paper undefined); the four-level ordinal's within-unfavorable ordering is the wrapper's mapping; the landmark KM at fit uses the benchmark's fit data (patients still open at the landmark) and reports the paper's published results separately.

methods.description: Four-group risk stratification at cycle 3 from the ctDNA change and the radiographic response (Bratman, Yang et al., Nature Cancer 2020, INSPIRE, pembrolizumab): Delta ctDNAC3 - the percentage change of the absolute ctDNA level from baseline to the cycle-3 draw - is dichotomized a priori at zero (decrease vs increase) and crossed with the cycle-3 RECIST v1.1 call (PD vs CR/PR/SD) into the paper's groups (1) increased ctDNA + PD, (2) increased ctDNA + CR/PR/SD, (3) decreased ctDNA + PD, (4) decreased ctDNA + CR/PR/SD; group 1 is the paper's very-poor-survival 0%-ORR group. It writes the percentage change as risk (the quantity the rule dichotomizes; an increase is positive, so higher = more likely failing), the 0/1 call (1 = group 1) and no probability of its own. Baseline and cycle-3 draws are the last draw on or before baseline_max_day and the last one after it up to the landmark. The benchmark has no native slot for the cycle-3 RECIST call, so the wrapper takes it from a numeric cov_* column named by the setting recist_covariate (1 = PD, 0 = CR/PR/SD); without it, the wrapper runs the paper's Delta-ctDNAC3-alone arm (call 1 for an increase). A patient with no baseline/C3 pair or a baseline of 0 (the percentage change is undefined) gets no prediction, with the reason in note; the four groups of the training patients are reported at fit.

methods.description: Assignment of each patient to a risk group with a homogeneous nomogram-predicted probability - six groups for TW8 response (splits on the log10 reduction in HCV RNA from baseline to treatment week 4 and on platelets) and eight groups for SVR (splits on the TW4 decline, HCV-RNA genotype 1 subtype and BMI) - from recursive-partitioning decision trees fitted to the nomogram-PREDICTED probabilities (not the actual outcomes): 'The outcome variable being examined by the recursive partitioning trees was the predicted probability of the outcomes from the nomograms, not the actual outcome... The response variable was formed using the leave-one-out method... Continuous variable cut points were determined to optimize categorization.' (paper md:51; tree outputs and C-statistics 0.853 TW8 / 0.784 SVR at md:148 - Thompson, Devine, Kattan, Muir, PLoS ONE 2014;9(8):e103370, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0103370; boceprevir + peginterferon alfa/ribavirin triple therapy, genotype 1 chronic hepatitis C, SPRINT-2/RESPOND-2/PROVIDE, TW8 tree n = 856, SVR tree n = 522). The paper names no tree software and publishes no split criterion, no complexity controls and (except the two extreme leaves and the group counts) no tree structure, so the wrapper implements the described algorithm in base R (rpart, party and friends are NOT stated in the paper and are not used): per benchmark fold (1) the two published nomogram structures of the same paper (the step-down-selected final models of md:133 - TW8 response: TW4 decline + race + baseline platelets + ALT/ULN; SVR: TW4 decline + HCV G1 subtype + gender + BMI + ribavirin starting dose + baseline platelets - each continuous predictor a 3-knot restricted cubic spline with the PUBLISHED knot values of Appendix S1 S1a/S1b) are refit by binary logistic regression on the harness failure label no_response (best RECIST SD/PD vs CR/PR, or responder = 0 - the failure reading of the paper's TW8 response and SVR, both mapped to the benchmark's response outcome like the sibling nomogram wrappers), the paper's baseline covariates matched to the cov_* channels by name (a channel a dataset omits is recorded and the remaining published structure is fitted - never invented); (2) the response of each tree is the leave-one-out nomogram probability (each training patient's probability from the same structure refit on the other training patients, the realized reading of the paper's leave-one-out construction); (3) each tree is grown by best-first recursive partitioning on the paper's own split variables (TW8 tree: TW4 log10 reduction + platelets; SVR tree: TW4 decline + genotype 1 subtype + BMI), continuous cut points at the midpoints of the training values and chosen to maximize the between-group sum of squares of the response (minimize within-group heterogeneity - the 'optimize categorization' criterion realized as the squared-error CART criterion), stopping at the published group counts (params leaves_tw8 6 / leaves_svr 8) with a minimum leaf size (params min_leaf 10); risk = p_no_response = the assigned group's mean leave-one-out nomogram probability (failure-oriented by construction), the group-level quantity the paper's box-and-whisker plots summarize (only the group mean is written per patient; the group ranges, sizes and the fitted splits are recorded in run.json), and the second tree's grouping is fitted and recorded per fold too (its own endpoint SVR at 24 weeks post-completion is not a harness outcome; params primary_tree 'tw8' (or 'svr') selects which tree's group value the wrapper writes as risk, recorded in run.json). No call is written (the paper publishes no probability cutoff and the trees are multi-group assignments, not dichotomous rules) and TxResBench converts risk for the survival outcomes and progressive disease. Differences from the paper (each in README.md and run.json): the nomograms and trees are refit per benchmark fold (no analysis code or data is published - the Appendix S1 formulas and the prose tree summaries are the only artifacts; the published tree structure is not reproducible, only the group counts and the two extreme leaves are printed, and the two published extreme cut points are recorded, never hard-coded), the algorithm's unstated details are realized as recorded defaults (best-first squared-error criterion, midpoint cut points, target group counts as the stopping rule, min_leaf 10, the leave-one-out realized as a leave-one-PATIENT-out refit of the published structure), the marker pair is the benchmark's baseline + last-draw-by-landmark convention (the paper's fixed TW4 draw after the 4-week PR lead-in; draws after the landmark never enter), the paper's MICE imputation and modified-ITT / RGT-ineligibility exclusions are not reproduced (no imputation specification published; a patient with a missing value gets no prediction with the reason in note), the non-detect policy is declared (default 'abstain' - the paper defines undetectable as the LOD 9.3 IU/mL but never states the numeric coding of an undetectable value in the log10 change; 'lod' substitutes the draw's own <marker>__lod value), and the method is marker-specific (plasma HCV RNA, LOINC 20416-4 - required_markers; the runner runs it only on units carrying that marker).
methods.licence: n/a for the model (the paper - Thompson AJ, Devine SJ, Kattan MW, Muir AJ, PLoS ONE 2014;9(8):e103370 - is open access under the Creative Commons Attribution License, but it publishes no analysis code and no data: its only published artifacts are the two Appendix S1 linear predictors (S1a, S1b) and the prose tree summaries; no tree software is named (rpart/party/ctree are NOT stated) and no licence is stated for any code). The wrapper is a reimplementation in base R (stats::glm plus the base image's TxrMethod helper): the two published nomogram structures are refit per benchmark fold and the recursive partitioning is a base-R best-first binary partitioning with the published split variables and group counts - no package is installed and nothing of the authors' is redistributed

methods.description: The two-phase regression-growth equation of Stein, Figg, Dahut et al. (The Oncologist 2008;13(10):1046-1054, DOI 10.1634/theoncologist.2008-0075): each patient's serial marker trajectory, normalized to its first value, is fitted per patient by nonlinear least squares with the paper's equation (1) f(t) = exp(-d*t) + exp(g*t) - 1 - an exponential regression process with rate constant d (days-1) and an independent exponential regrowth with rate constant g (days-1), f normalized to 1 at the start of treatment - with the reduced forms f = exp(-d*t) (eq. 2, continuous decrease) and f = exp(g*t) (eq. 3, continuous increase) for monotone series; among the converged models whose growth or regression constant is significant at p < 0.05 (the paper's inclusion rule, md:68) the minimum-AIC model is the patient's selected fit (the reference implementation's documented model-choice rule; the paper's own 'five groups' assignment is not printed). The per-patient growth rate constant g is the risk score - the paper's risk scale is log(g), a monotone transform of g (Pearson r = -0.72 with survival time; log(d) is not predictive, r = -0.218), and higher g means faster regrowth, i.e. treatment failing - and the call is the paper's binary risk group, the upper vs lower 50% of log(g) above/below the cohort median (mortality hazard 5.14, 95% CI 3.10-8.52), carried over as the training cohort's median of g. A patient whose selected model is the pure-decay form has no growth constant, so the paper's log(g) is undefined and the patient gets no risk (the paper presents the nadir min and time-to-nadir tmin as surrogates of g for such evaluation, eqs (5A)/(6A)); patients with fewer than the paper's three datapoints, a first marker value of 0 or negative, or no model with a significant g or d get no prediction, with the reason in note. The paper's own software was the commercial Sigmaplot 9.0 (curve-fitting settings unpublished; the code URL in the paper is a web Cox calculator); the wrapper fits with minpack.lm using the settings of the Stein-group reference implementation tumgr 0.0.4 (starts at 0.00511 day-1, bounds [0, 1], Levenberg-Marquardt control maxiter = maxfev = 1000, factor 0.01), which implements the identical regression-growth equations but is not called directly because its gdphi model and its all-parameters-significant selection rule differ from the paper. The paper has no landmark and no per-patient survival probability (its Pearson r, Cox hazard ratio and Kaplan-Meier plots are cohort-level associations), so the wrapper fits the draws up to the benchmark's landmark in both fit and predict and writes no probability of its own: TxResBench converts the risk score.
methods.licence: wrapper calls minpack.lm (GPL-3), the same Levenberg-Marquardt nonlinear least-squares engine the Stein-group reference implementation tumgr 0.0.4 uses; nothing from the paper (commercial Sigmaplot 9.0) is included

methods.description: The five-band ordinal subgroup rule of Ko et al. (Br J Cancer 2005;93(2):195-199, DOI 10.1038/sj.bjc.6602687; 76 eligible of 103 pooled patients with advanced pancreatic adenocarcinoma on fixed-dose-rate gemcitabine +/- low-dose cisplatin): per patient, the maximum per cent decline of serum CA19-9 from the baseline (pretreatment) value achieved at any point during treatment is binned into five ordered subgroups - no decline / 0-25% decline / 26-50% decline / 51-75% decline / >75% decline (Table 2; the Methods print the top band as '76-100% decline'); the five subgroups had strongly increasing median survival (4.31 / 6.02 / 7.04 / 7.55 / 12.00 months) and median TTF (1.35 / 3.36 / 3.60 / 3.80 / 6.00 months) with overall log-rank chi-square 31.20 (df=4, P<0.001) survival and 50.34 (df=4, P<0.001) TTF, and no sustained-decline requirement ('confirmation by two measurements spaced at least 28 days apart' was not required). The wrapper takes one marker (the per-draw serum CA19-9 value), takes the baseline as the last draw on or before baseline_max_day, takes the deepest decline as the minimum value over the draws after the baseline up to the landmark, and writes risk = the signed per-cent change at that deepest draw (100*(deepest value - baseline)/baseline; a decline is negative, so higher = more likely failing; the quantity the paper's per-cent change is of) and call 1 when the maximum decline is at most call_cutoff_decline (default 25.0%, so the 'no decline' and '0-25% decline' bands are called failing - the paper's own binary Table 3 finding, '>25% decline?': median survival 9.61 vs 4.64 months, log-rank 24.07 P<0.001) and call 0 when the decline is deeper; it writes no probability (the paper defines none; TxResBench converts the risk). Band boundaries and the call cutoff are fixed published/paper-derived constants: the wrapper learns nothing from the training outcomes and is a subclass of the paper's rule.

methods.description: A per-patient binary call of whether a patient on immunotherapy will experience disease progression (RECIST 1.1 or clinical), from three ctDNA features obtainable early in the treatment course: [1] ctDNA detection at the pre-treatment draw, [2] ctDNA detection at the first on-treatment draw (the paper's P2, a median of one cycle in, before imaging/clinical progression), [3] the absolute change in %eVAF from P1 to P2 (Ruiz-Torres et al., medRxiv 2025, DOI 10.1101/2025.01.27.25321198; 16 R/M HNSCC patients on ICB, 13 in the machine-learning analysis; reported 88% accuracy, precision 80%, recall 100%, F1 89%, AUC 0.89, median lead time 25 days (range 0-168) before imaging-detected progression, and the P1->P2 %eVAF increase as the most impactful feature, Figure 3A-B). The paper names no implementation, no hyperparameters, no seed and no cut-off - 'We applied a machine learning model (random forest)' is the whole statement (the research's own published npj code repository holds a figure script only, and the npj version dropped the ML analysis), so the wrapper reproduces the model as a random-forest BINARY classifier on the three features with the named package's defaults (scikit-learn RandomForestClassifier, n_estimators 100, gini, max_features sqrt, bootstrap, class_weight none), random_state from the call's seed, fitted on the training patients on the failure label with the best-RECIST-PD reference mapping (progressive_disease, else no_response, else progression by the first horizon, else death by the first horizon - the paper's only label is the event of progression, and the benchmark carries the other three outcomes through the same score); risk = the forest's P(progression) (higher = treatment more likely failing) and call = 1 when risk >= call_threshold (0.5, the sklearn decision boundary - the paper publishes no threshold). The paper's evaluation protocol (80/20 split, stratified 5-fold CV with metrics per fold, 1000 bootstrap repetitions) is its internal validation of the reported metrics, not a property of the model, and is not reproduced: the benchmark's own out-of-sample evaluation carries it, and the reported cohort statistics are reproduced as text in run.json. Differences from the paper, all because it publishes no code: feature [2] is defined by the paper conditionally on the progression event (the pre-progression sample); prospectively the wrapper takes the most recent draw in (baseline_max_day, landmark_day] as P2 (the paper does not state which sample enters when several exist); a patient with no usable P1 or P2 draw is abstained with the reason in note (the paper excludes such patients from its 13-patient analysis set); an undetectable sample's %eVAF enters feature [3] as the benchmark's value 0 (the paper does not state how an undetectable sample enters the change); patients without a pre-treatment sample or never ctDNA-positive are excluded by the paper, and the wrapper cannot detect 'never' at the landmark, so it gives the patient the score the three features produce.
methods.licence: the preprint is CC BY 4.0 and publishes no analysis code (the only availability statement is 'All the data relevant to this work is included in this manuscript.'; the same research's published version - npj Precision Oncology 2025;9:298, DOI 10.1038/s41698-025-01084-4 - publishes the repository which holds a figure script only and no classifier; the ML analysis is absent from the published version entirely), so this wrapper is original code re-expressing the published model with the scikit-learn 1.5.2 random forest (BSD-3-Clause), the standard Python RF implementation, pinned as the stand-in for the paper's unnamed 'random forest'

methods.description: Random-forest classification of patients by recurrence from the week-3 (single post-treatment) tumour immune parameters, the analysis in Huang et al. (Nat Med 2019, neoadjuvant pembrolizumab in resectable melanoma; Extended Data Fig. 3c). The paper names no implementation, no hyperparameters and publishes no performance, so the wrapper fits a Breiman random forest (R randomForest, the canonical 'random forest analysis', on package defaults: n_trees 500 trees, mtry floor(sqrt(p)), nodesize 1) on the per-patient vector of the last post-baseline value of every marker passed (the benchmark's draws up to the landmark stand in for the paper's week-3 sample; missing values are filled with the training median, the na.roughfix default). The paper's recurrence label is the recurrence-free-survival end point, so the primary classifier is fitted on the training progression outcome (fallback death), and the same model form is fitted on the other outcome the training data carry (death, no_response, progressive_disease) because TxResBench scores all four. risk is the primary forest's class probability (higher = more likely failing) and call is its class at a 0.5 cutoff (1 = recurrence = treatment judged failing); risk_<outcome> is each outcome's own forest's probability. The paper's published output, the ranking of the parameters by importance as mean +/- s.d. over 1,000 forest refits, is computed at fit for the primary classifier and recorded in the fit report (randomForest permutation importance). The paper's own n = 21 cohort, its 33-parameter flow panel and its per-patient data are not published, so every difference is a wrapper choice recorded in the README.

methods.description: The per-timepoint gene-signature classifier of the RNA-Seq arm of van Doorn CLR, Eckold C, Ronacher K, et al., "Transcriptional profiles predict treatment outcome in patients with tuberculosis and diabetes at diagnosis and at two weeks after initiation of anti-tuberculosis treatment", eBioMedicine 2022;82:104173, doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2022.104173: from the genome-wide whole-blood expression vector of one sample, the paper (Supplementary Information and Figure S9) splits the RNA-Seq data 60/40 with the R package caret, selects a per-timepoint gene signature with Recursive Feature Elimination using repeated cross-validation (n = 10), fits a weighted model with the glmnet method (weights 1/frequency * 0.5, repeated CV n = 10) and predicts the held-out test set, reporting the test ROC AUC (diagnosis 0.625, week two 0.667, month six 0.615, month two 0.8667). The wrapper re-implements that pipeline for the benchmark: each patient's query sample is the latest on-treatment draw on or before the landmark (the paper's fixed diagnosis/week 2/month 2/month 6 timepoints have no day clock in the benchmark; the paper's four per-timepoint models collapse into the benchmark's one landmark query - a recorded deviation); the features are the DESeq2-normalized expression values as the dataset reports them (no log, no scaling); the paper's low-expression filter (<50 counts across all samples) is applied as the training-side removal of markers that are zero or never finite for every training query draw; RFE (recursive elimination with repeated 10-fold cross-validation, n = 10 repeats, ranking by |standardized coefficient| of the weighted glmnet, the best size by the resampled accuracy) selects the signature; the final model is the weighted glmnet (glmnet's package defaults where the paper states none: alpha = 1, standardize = TRUE, 100-lambda path) with weights 1/frequency * 0.5 (frequency = the class's share of the training labels, the reading of the paper's verbatim formula - its meaning is not stated, '?'), the lambda chosen by the repeated-CV accuracy; the wrapper writes risk = p_no_response (or, when the training data give no response outcome, the probability of the next failure label the same procedure was applied to) - the per-patient P(poor outcome) of the paper, in the benchmark's failure orientation; the paper's 60/40 split and its reported AUCs are the paper's evaluation protocol, carried by the benchmark's own folds, and are not reproduced; no cutoff is published and none is invented, so no call is written.

methods.description: The RFE-RF model of van Doorn et al. (eBioMedicine 2022;82:104173): a Random Forest classifier of a binary treatment-outcome label (the paper's good vs poor tuberculosis treatment outcome = cured vs died / failed / relapsed) built on the values of a gene subset selected with Recursive Feature Elimination (caret rfe, K = 10-fold cross-validation on the class-balanced dataset, randomForest variable importance) and then fitted on the selected markers' values at one fixed timepoint (the paper's diagnosis, week-two, month-two and diagnosis-minus-week-two delta signatures), with the two classes balanced first (random down-sampling of the majority class, or SMOTE from the DMwR package). The paper evaluates the classifier by leave-one-out cross-validation and reports ROC AUC (diagnosis 8-gene pooled AUC 0.815, week-two 22-gene 0.834, month-two 14-gene 0.791, delta 7-gene 0.849; external Indian validation of the diagnosis signature 0.749). The wrapper applies the same pipeline on the benchmark's markers: per marker the value at the patient's last on-treatment draw on or before the landmark (params timepoint 'landmark', the paper's week-two/month-two instances; 'baseline' reproduces the diagnosis instance), optionally the baseline-minus-timepoint delta (params features 'delta', the paper's delta signature; the supplement prints the opposite sign - immaterial to the trees, recorded), then RFE selects the marker subset and a randomForest (ntree 500, mtry floorsqrt by default) is fitted on the class-balanced training data and saved for prediction. The label is the harness failure outcome standing in for the paper's response group (no_response = SD or PD; when absent progressive_disease, else the event-by-horizon label of the first horizon), the failure class is coded 1, risk = P(failure) from the forest vote fraction and p_no_response / p_progressive_disease carry the own probabilities of the per-outcome pipeline fits, so risk is failure-oriented by construction. A patient missing a selected marker's value at the model's draws gets no prediction with the reason in note - the paper defines no imputation. The paper's RFE sizes, forest tuning, seeds and down-sampling draws are not published, so the wrapper's sizes grid, defaults and seed management are recorded choices, and the LOOCV used by the paper as its evaluation report is not reproduced at fit (the benchmark's own evaluation calls the trained model out-of-sample): each difference is in the README and run.json
