methods.description: The RNN variant of the SHERLOC framework of Mamann et al. (bioRxiv 2026.06.04.730097) for overall survival from the landmark: the patient's longitudinal ctDNA profile is read as a sequence of per-visit feature vectors (in the paper, 17 gene-level ctDNA VAFs + 4 panel-level aggregated features = 21 channels at each of the T clinical timepoints baseline to C4D1), batch-normalized along the timestep axis, processed by a single-layer recurrent neural network (Elman, torch.nn.RNN; input size = hidden size = number of channels, one layer, batch_first, nonlinearity = the torch default 'tanh', RNN.py:32-37), and the terminal hidden state is fused with per-timestep representations of a frozen genomic-interaction encoder (MLP pretrained with the Cox partial-likelihood on solid-biopsy VAF data, frozen after pretraining, 2 dimensions per timestep; the paper uses the external MSK-CHORD cohort, 22,068 patients) and with baseline clinical covariates; the concatenation is dropped out at 0.4 and passed to a single linear layer with sigmoid output whose value is the Cox log-risk fed to pycox's CoxPH, trained by the negative log-partial likelihood (lr 0.005, batch 50, up to 256 epochs, early stopping patience 20, 20% validation split). The wrapper refits it per survival outcome of the training data (death first - the paper's OS, then progression), rebases the outcome times to the benchmark's landmark (the paper's OS from the final on-treatment ctDNA collection), resolves the sequence to the patient's visits up to the landmark (baseline slot = last baseline visit, then the most recent on-treatment visits, at most n_timepoints = 4 slots; the paper's evaluability rule requires all configured timepoints, md:1404-1408) and writes the paper's native outputs: the sigmoid log-risk (risk, monotone in the Cox log-risk) and per-horizon failure probabilities from the Breslow baseline-hazard survival curve. The frozen genomic-interaction encoder cannot be reproduced as published (MSK-CHORD is not redistributed, scripts/data/msk_chord/README.md:1-17), so the wrapper pretrains the same MLP architecture on the training cohort itself - the paper's transfer-learning step is replaced by an in-cohort pretraining (recorded deviation); the marker set is data-driven (the paper derives its channel count from the data, d_input = train_ds[0][0].shape[0], train_DL.py:287-289), so the wrapper take whatever markers a unit carries as the channels.

methods.description: The paper's method 9, 'RNN-GRU' (van Delft et al., Heliyon 2022;8(10):e10932; NSCLC immunotherapy, non-response at 6 months after treatment initiation, 281/412 non-responders, md:114): a gated recurrent unit (GRU) recurrent neural network fed with one serum tumour marker's regular time series (the paper fits each of CYFRA 21.1, CEA, CA-125, NSE and SCC separately; the research's best validation result uses CYFRA, sensitivity 38.6% at specificity 100%). The measurements of the first six weeks are log-transformed, interpolated with a monotone Hermite (PCHIP) spline onto a 7-day grid, transformed back with the natural exponential (removing any negative interpolation results) and log-transformed again (T1 step 1-5); the network is 3 GRU layers of 32, 16 and 1 units with 10% dropout and recurrent dropout in the first two layers, and a final fully connected sigmoid layer (md:55), outputting the class probability of non-response, which is thresholded at an ROC-derived 95% specificity on the training cohort (md:27, md:41). The wrapper reimplements that classifier in the Python Keras 3 API (keras 3.10.0 on tensorflow-cpu 2.20.0; the paper's R keras/tensorflow versions are not stated); the training configuration (optimizer, loss, epochs, batch size, sequence start/end, seed) is not published - the wrapper's declared readings are method_params (optimizer adam, binary cross-entropy, 150 epochs with early stopping, batch 32, grid days 0-42 in 7-day steps) and are recorded in run.json and the README. The wrapper takes one marker, uses the draws on or before the landmark within the paper's -7..+49 day window with the paper's 5/30-day consecutive-gap filter and its inclusion criteria (at least 3 values, at least one between day 28 and day 49, min_draws 3); it writes the network's probability of non-response as risk (higher = failing) and the 95%-specificity call; a patient it cannot score gets no prediction, with the reason in note. It fits the label no_response when it has two classes, else progressive_disease, else progression by the first horizon (params label).

methods.description: The diffCIRI17 model of Wei et al. (J Immunother Cancer 2023;11:e006788; 123 + 99 patients with advanced NSCLC on anti-PD-1/PD-L1 with or without chemotherapy): a random survival forest (randomForestSRC, the paper's stated software) on the per-patient DIFFERENCE (subtraction) of the measured plasma concentrations of the 17 feature cytokines between the 6-week (edt) and baseline (pre) draws, predicting overall survival (the Cytokine-based ICI Response Index, CIRI = the 'predicted risk of prognosis', higher = worse), with the paper's hyperparameters (1000 trees, node size 3, logrank split rule; mtry at the package default) and a binary high/low-risk call from the 1-year Youden-optimized cut-off of the training set ('a predicted CIRI score higher than the cut-off was defined as the high-risk group with poor treatment response and poor prognosis'). The wrapper fits the RSF on the training patients event-free at the landmark, on death when the training data give overall survival and on progression otherwise, takes the pre draw as the last draw on or before baseline_max_day and the edt draw as the last draw before the landmark, writes the ensemble mortality as risk and the high-risk group as the call (1 = treatment judged failing), and no probability of its own - TxResBench converts the risk. Missing cycle values are handled by randomForestSRC's own na.action="na.impute" (the paper states no missing rule); the paper reports no numeric performance for diffCIRI17.

methods.description: The European LeukemiaNet 2020 Table-4 milestones (Hochhaus et al., Leukemia 2020): a per-patient molecular-response call from the BCR-ABL1 transcript level on the International Scale (IS, percent) at the ELN milestones of 3, 6 and 12 months of TKI treatment - 3 months optimal <=10%, warning >10%, failure >10% if a second value >10% confirms it within 1-3 months; 6 months optimal <=1%, warning >1-10%, failure >10%; 12 months optimal <=0.1%, warning >0.1-1%, failure >1% - plus the any-time row (optimal <=0.1%, warning >0.1-1% or loss of MMR from a previous <=0.1% value, failure >1%). The wrapper writes the BCR-ABL1 % IS value at the evaluated milestone as risk (raw percent, the quantity the thresholds are applied to) and call 1 for the ELN failure category, 0 for optimal or warning; it writes no probability. The paper states the milestones in months and gives no day-level conversion, so the wrapper maps them onto the benchmark's day scale with month_days = 365.25/12 (the package's own month conversion): milestone_select 'next' (default) evaluates the milestone whose evaluation band the landmark belongs to - the 3-month row's band runs to the 6-month evaluation so its 1-3-month confirmation window is honored, and after the 12-month milestone the any-time row is used - while a landmark within milestone_tol_days of a milestone day evaluates that milestone with the value at the milestone day ('exact' instead falls back to the any-time row). The paper's non-marker failure criteria (BCR-ABL1 kinase-domain resistance mutations, high-risk additional chromosome abnormalities) cannot be evaluated from a BCR-ABL1-only input and are not part of the call.

methods.description: The PSA-progression and PSA-response reporting criteria of the Prostate Cancer Clinical Trials Working Group 3 (PCWG3; Scher HI et al., J Clin Oncol 2016;34(12):1402-1418, DOI 10.1200/JCO.2015.64.2702; the criteria are the PCWG2 criteria retained verbatim - 'PCWG3 retains the PCWG2 criteria for PSA progression'). The wrapper takes the serial serum PSA trajectory of a castration-resistant prostate cancer patient on treatment (one marker, ng/mL, no transform), and at a landmark day makes a per-patient call: PSA progression per PCWG3 Table 5, confirmed from the draws available by the landmark; it writes risk = the guideline's PSA-response reporting metric, the percent change from baseline (rise or fall, negative = decline) at the assessment moment (the last PSA draw by the benchmark's landmark, standing in for the guideline's fixed 12-week reporting point) - the quantity the guideline records, no probability exists in the guideline and none is written. The call is the Table 5 delay/prevent rule: after a decline from baseline, the first PSA increase that is >=25% AND >=2 ng/mL above the nadir and is confirmed by a second value >=3 weeks later (a confirmed rising trend); with no decline from baseline, a >=25% AND >=2 ng/mL increase from the baseline beyond 12 weeks. The guideline's open points are fixed by declared wrapper choices (see README): the nadir is the running minimum of the on-treatment draws observed so far; the decline vs no-decline branch is decided on the whole observed on-treatment series (minimum < baseline); 'beyond 12 weeks' is strictly >84 days; 'continues to rise' confirmation is a later value >= the first qualifying value at >=21 days; the progression date is the first qualifying value; baseline PSA below the assay's detection limit (value 0 per the contract) makes the percent change undefined and the patient not evaluable. PCWG3 defines NO numeric PSA-decline/response threshold (the common >=50% decline criterion is not in the text: '50%' appears only as the historical note that the increase requirement was reduced from 50% to 25%; Table A1 records 'No FDA drug approvals on the basis of: PSA declines'), so only the progression call and the percent-change reporting metric are written; 'Recording the duration of PSA decline of little value' (Table 5). Differences from the guideline, all declared: the benchmark's landmark truncates the series (at predict the contract ignores draws after it), so the call is 'PSA progression per PCWG3 confirmed by day L' and a rise that would be confirmed after the landmark is not called; the guideline stresses the call is a reporting event, not necessarily a reason to stop treatment ('standards for reporting PSA progression date may not indicate a need to stop treatment'; 'in the case of an isolated PSA rise after an initial decline', PCWG3 advises continuing therapy) while the benchmark reads call 1 as treatment judged failing; and PCWG3's fixed 12-week reporting point is replaced by the benchmark's landmark when it differs. Nothing is fitted (the 25% / 2 ng/mL / 3 weeks / 12 weeks numbers are the guideline's constants), and the guideline publishes no analysis code, so the rule is implemented from the guideline text (fetched full text, PMC4872347).

methods.description: A per-patient binary call of the short-term treatment outcome (STO) - whether the patient will have a positive treatment response (IMWG >= PR: sCR/CR/VGPR/PR) or a non-response (MR/SD/PD) at the next assessment time point - from a Random Under-Sampling Boosting (RUSBoost) ensemble trained on a wide feature matrix of serial immune biomarkers with the baseline clinical score R-ISS and cytogenetic abnormalities (Xiong Y, Xu J, Li B, et al., J Transl Med 2026;24:543, DOI 10.1186/s12967-026-07946-0; 662 newly diagnosed multiple myeloma patients on PI-/IMiD-based induction, biomarkers assessed at baseline and every two treatment cycles, per-cycle sequential tasks 'variables from each assessment point were used to predict the subsequent response', 5-fold CV, learning rate 0.1 and 100 learning cycles, cost matrix penalising misclassification of positive responses, optional Welch's two-sample t-test feature selection at p < 0.05, forward-backward then column-mean imputation; reported F1 0.71-0.75 per cycle vs 0.63/0.64/0.32 for R-ISS and 0.85 for the cycle-independent task vs 0.47 for R-ISS; no analysis software or code is published, so every unstated mechanical detail is a documented wrapper decision). The wrapper maps the paper's procedure onto the benchmark's single landmark query as the paper's CYCLE-INDEPENDENT (pooled) task: the feature vector holds, per marker, the value at the baseline draw (day <= baseline_max_day) and at the latest draw up to the landmark (the paper's 'variables from each assessment point... data available up to the previous assessment time point'; the tidy marker space carries no treatment-cycle clock, so the per-cycle breakdowns are not reproduced and the value of each marker at its two assessment slots stands in for the paper's wide per-cycle slots); missing slots are imputed by the paper's forward-backward fill (missing current value from the baseline value and vice versa) then training column means; the label is the benchmark's no_response (best RECIST response SD or PD - the paper's non-response class; MR is not expressible in RECIST) and, when the training data lacks it, progressive_disease then progression and death by the first horizon (recorded); the ensemble is imbalanced-learn 0.12.4 RUSBoostClassifier (the canonical random-under-sampling AdaBoost, decision stumps, SAMME) with the paper's learning rate 0.1 and 100 learning cycles, sampling_strategy auto, replacement false, the paper's cost matrix as per-sample weights (samples whose true response is positive get cost_misclassify_positive, the others 1 - the higher penalty for treating a responsive patient as non-responsive), the call's seed for the sampling randomness, and the benchmark's cov_* columns (R-ISS, cytogenetics) appended to the feature matrix as the paper's clinical-score channel whenever the dataset carries them (covariates optional: a cohort without cov_* runs on the marker features alone and the run.json records the divergence - the paper's X always includes R-ISS and cytogenetics, whose benchmark channel is the generic cov_* track; the gate's covariate-free world and its row-count contract require the optional declaration, following the keras-lstm-longitudinal-cvd precedent); risk = the ensemble's P(non-response) (1 - P(positive response), higher = treatment more likely failing), call = 1 when risk >= call_threshold 0.5 (the binary decision boundary - the paper publishes no threshold); optional feature selection (feature_selection_p 0.05) runs the paper's Welch's t-test between the positive- and non-response training groups per feature with retention at p < 0.05 - the wrapper's default is the full feature set (the paper's unselected models, which it reports as comparable or superior from Cycle 4 onward and as more robust under attrition). Differences from the paper, all because it publishes no analysis code and no per-patient outputs: the paper's 5-fold cross-validation is its internal evaluation of the reported metrics (reproduced as text in run.json, not run); the cycle-specific models, the cycle-to-day mapping, the ELISA row-wise L2 normalisation (a cross-platform integration step whose platform assignment is not stated), the exact feature-vector column names and the cost-matrix values are all unstated and are recorded as the wrapper's readings; the benchmark's own out-of-sample evaluation carries the evaluation.
methods.licence: the paper is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 and publishes no analysis code (no code-availability statement; only 'The datasets... are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.'; no software, package, function or version is named anywhere - verified by grep; job.code empty), so this wrapper is original code re-expressing the published procedure with the pinned open-source standard RUSBoost implementation imbalanced-learn 0.12.4 (MIT; built on scikit-learn 1.5.2, BSD-3-Clause) as the stand-in for the paper's unnamed 'RUSBoost algorithm'

methods.description: The rapid virological response (RVR) classification rule of Feng et al. (BMC Gastroenterology 2014;14:47, DOI 10.1186/1471-230X-14-47; NCT01140997: 32 genotype 1b chronic hepatitis C patients of 48 pharmacokinetics participants on 48 weeks of peginterferon alpha (type Y peginterferon alpha-2b 90/135/180 ug or peginterferon alpha-2a 180 ug, weekly) plus weight-based ribavirin, then 24 weeks of follow-up): 'RVR was defined as undetectable HCV RNA in a sensitive assay (lower limit of detection <= 50 IU/ml) at week 4 of therapy and maintained up to the end of treatment [7].' (md:43), scored against SVR (undetectable HCV RNA, <50 IU/mL, 24 weeks after treatment cessation, md:43 - week 72 from the first dose) by sensitivity/specificity/accuracy/PPV/NPV (paper reported: 0.286/1.000/0.531/1.000/0.423 in Table 4, md:143 - the Results text prints 0.229/1.000/0.500/1.000/0.407, md:111, and the per-patient calls are not tabulated, so neither set is verifiable from the publication). The wrapper takes one marker (the per-draw serum HCV RNA result, IU/mL; the qualitative undetectable/detectable state is read from the dataset's __detected / __lod rows, 0-coded non-detects, a 0/1 status feature, or - only when the data carries no detection call at all - the level against detection_threshold, default the training median of the last baseline values, a documented stand-in for the assay's unpublished 'undetectable' cut), maps the paper's week-4 visit to the marker draw closest to day 28 (week4_days) among the draws after the baseline window and on or before the landmark within draw_tolerance_days (default +-14, ties to the later draw; the paper defines no tolerance), and applies the rule: call = 1 when the criterion draw or ANY later on-treatment draw up to min(end of treatment, day 336 = week 48, eot_day; landmark) is detectable (not RVR = the paper's RVR-negative side = predicted non-SVR, treatment judged failing), call = 0 otherwise (RVR = undetectable at week 4 and maintained). It writes risk = log1p of the strongest marker level over that window (criterion + maintenance draws; the quantity the per-draw detection calls threshold; the paper defines no per-patient score, TxResBench converts the risk) and the 0/1 call, no probability. A patient with no marker draw within tolerance of the week-4 visit by the landmark gets no prediction with the reason in note. At a landmark before the end of treatment the maintenance condition is evaluated on the draws seen (a partial evaluation, recorded); the week-72 SVR draw is never used (spec leakage trap). The paper's EVR rule is NOT implemented - the paper prints no EVR definition (md:134, md:144 only) and the standard EVR criterion is not substituted (spec deviation 'the EVR criterion cannot be written down'). Nothing is fitted (fixed rule; the fallback detection threshold only reads training marker LEVELS, never outcomes).

methods.description: The per-patient low/high serum sCD8 subgroup call of Siemiatkowska A et al., 'Low on-treatment levels of serum soluble CD8 (sCD8) predict better outcomes in advanced non-small cell lung cancer patients treated with atezolizumab' (Cancer Immunol Immunother 2023;72(6):1853-1863, DOI 10.1007/s00262-023-03377-8; PMID 36688998, PMC9870198; 42 advanced NSCLC patients on second-line atezolizumab 1200 mg IV Q3W within the Polish national drug program, prospective single-centre, Poznan 2019-2020): serum soluble CD8 (sCD8, ng/mL, sandwich ELISA, MyBioSource MBS016364) was measured at baseline and at the end of cycles 1-4 (n = 173 samples); the end-of-cycle-2 level (sCD8.2) was the earliest serial timepoint separating patients with durable disease control (>= SD at 12 months from the start of ATEZO) from those without (median 3.76 vs 9.68 ng/mL, p < 0.001, md:109/md:117); ROC analysis with the Youden index against the durable-disease-control label selected the cutoff 4.09 ng/mL (AUC 0.928, 95% CI 0.785-0.988, p < 0.001, sensitivity 75.0% [34.9-96.8%], specificity 96.2% [80.4-99.9%]; low n = 7 vs high n = 27 of the 34 classified, md:117), and the subgroups were compared by Kaplan-Meier/log-rank and univariable/multivariable Cox: high sCD8.2 (> 4.09 ng/mL) had median PFS 4.4 months (95% CI 3.0-6.0) and median OS 14.4 months (7.3-20.9), low sCD8.2 (<= 4.09 ng/mL) reached neither (log-rank PFS p < 0.001, OS p = 0.007, md:122/md:125); univariable low-vs-high HRs 0.140 [0.039-0.495] p = 0.002 (PFS) and 0.104 [0.014-0.777] p = 0.027 (OS), PFS-adjusted HR 0.061 [0.012-0.304] p < 0.001 (md:127, Table 2). The wrapper writes risk = the raw sCD8.2 concentration in ng/mL (exactly the quantity the cutoff applies to; higher = worse) and call = 1 for high sCD8.2 (> 4.09 ng/mL, the paper's high-risk group = treatment judged failing) and 0 for low sCD8.2 (<= 4.09 ng/mL); it writes no probability (the paper defines none per patient - spec output.projection - so TxResBench converts the risk); a patient without a usable on-treatment draw by the landmark gets no prediction with the reason in note (the paper's incomplete sampling: 34 of 42 classified, md:117/md:163; no imputation stated). The cutoff was derived in the authors' own sample and is kept as the published constant (params cutoff_ng_ml; nothing is learned from the training outcomes, fitted false); the KM/log-rank and Cox HRs are cohort-level evaluation quantities, reported as printed; sCD8.2 is mapped to the benchmark's landmark by the corpus fixed-pair convention (the paper's Q3W schedule implies ~6 weeks / ~day 42 but prints no day number, md:35/md:102).

methods.description: SCOPE (Hussain et al. 2024, npj Digital Medicine; 7:202): a transformer encoder with continuous sinusoidal time embeddings, two causal-masked self-attention layers over a fixed 28-day-period grid of the marker trajectories, a shared prediction head that forecasts the next period's marker values (the pre-training objective), and one independent Cox proportional-hazards head per survival outcome (progression, death) fitted on the frozen pre-trained network (the paper's two-step pre-train/fine-tune; the released example's non-linear emission heads, dropout 0.1, hidden 16, K = 1 rollout window, include-baseline and include-last head inputs). The wrapper resamples the benchmark's draws onto the paper's 28-day periods (last draw in the period, forward-filled, with the observed/mask channel), standardizes log1p marker values and the baseline covariates with the training fold, and writes the progression head's Cox linear predictor as risk and the death head's as risk_death: the Cox score is only meaningful through its ordering (the paper states its absolute value is not meaningful), so no probability is invented and the package converts the per-outcome risks into the event probabilities. Differences from the paper, all recorded: the data are the benchmark's serial blood markers rather than the MM trial's 39-lab panel, the marker transform is log1p plus training z-scores rather than the paper's clinical-normal-range sigmoid (alpha_j/beta_j are the MM labs' reference ranges, absent from the released code), the treatment channel A(t) is dropped because the benchmark contract carries no treatment schedule, the 12 adverse-event heads are not fitted (no AE outcome in the contract; the response outcomes take the progression head's score), and the probabilities of progression/death come from the package's risk-to-probability conversion.

methods.description: The two-sided 15% serial tumour-marker trend rule of Gogas H, Lofts FJ, Evans TRJ, Daryanani S & Mansi JL, 'Are serial measurements of CA19-9 useful in predicting response to chemotherapy in patients with inoperable adenocarcinoma of the pancreas?' (Br J Cancer 1998;77(2):325-328, DOI 10.1038/bjc.1998.50; 39 patients with inoperable adenocarcinoma of the pancreas, 27 male / 12 female, median age 60 years, 18 metastatic / 21 locally advanced, on ECF chemotherapy - continuous-infusion 5-FU 200 mg m-2 day-1 with bolus epirubicin 50 mg m-2 and cisplatin 60 mg m-2 on day 1, repeated every 21 days for up to six cycles): serum CA19-9 measured at baseline and before each cycle (md:106-107); the rule (verbatim, md:127-130) 'A rise or fall in the tumour marker was defined as a greater than 15% increase or decrease in the marker on two consecutive occasions 3 weeks apart. A plateau in the tumour marker was defined as a less than 15% decrease or increase on two occasions.' and the per-patient trend call (decrease / plateau / progressive rise; 13 (36.2%) / 7 (19.4%) / 16 (44.4%) of the 36 classified patients, md:179-184), scored against WHO-criteria CT response (a >15% decrease is 'positive' for a response to treatment, a >15% increase 'positive' for progressive disease, md:131-134; Table 1: fall sensitivity 67% 4/6, specificity 69% 20/29, PPV 30% 4/13, NPV 87% 20/23 for partial response; rise sensitivity 86% 6/7, PPV 37% 6/16 for progressive disease, md:214-235) and against overall survival (median 333 / 253 / 185 days for decrease / plateau / progressive rise; >15% decrease vs >15% increase P = 0.001, md:200-211). The wrapper takes one marker (the per-draw serum CA19-9 value; required_markers LOINC 24108-3), reads the baseline as the last marker draw on or before baseline_max_day (the paper's baseline sample before cycle 1, md:106-107), and applies the rule to the consecutive marker occasions after the baseline up to the benchmark landmark, the decision day: per pair the percent change 100*(v_t - v_{t-1})/v_{t-1} in the paper's raw u ml-1 units (no log transform is described, md:127-130), classified rise (> +15%), fall (< -15%) or plateau (|change| <= 15%), and the per-patient trend call as progressive rise if ANY pair is a rise, else decrease if any pair is a fall, else plateau (the paper does not state how mixed trajectories combine - the wrapper's reading, recorded as a deviation; consistent with 'the remaining 16 (44.4%) patients had a progressive rise', md:179-184, and with all 13 decrease patients' reductions being seen during the first three cycles, md:181-183, md:337-340). It writes risk = the trend class as an ordered code - 0 decrease, 1 plateau, 2 progressive rise; higher = more likely failing, the paper's own ordering (median survival 333/253/185 days, md:200-205; fall 'positive' for response, rise 'positive' for progressive disease, md:131-134) - and call = 1 for the progressive-rise class (the paper's 'a greater than 15% increase was considered to be "positive" with regard to the detection of progressive disease', md:131-133; 0 for decrease and plateau). It writes no probability: the paper defines none per patient (only cohort-level sensitivity/specificity/PPV/NPV and KM medians + rank-test P values), so TxResBench converts the risk. A patient without a baseline marker value, without a marker draw after the baseline by the landmark, or whose serial series contains a non-positive or missing value (0 is the benchmark's below-detection encoding) gets no prediction with the reason in note: the percent change divides by the previous occasion's value and the paper states no handling for a zero or non-measurable previous value (its 3 patients with CA19-9 remaining < 37 u ml-1 throughout were 'non-contributory' and 'excluded from further analysis', md:168-177 - a research-cohort exclusion the wrapper records in run.json but does not gate on, since the benchmark runs the rule on whatever marker values the dataset carries and the rule itself, md:127-130, states no such condition). The paper's Table-1 evaluation of the three trend calls against WHO CT response (md:139-143, md:214-235) and its survival description (Kaplan-Meier medians per class; 'higher than 15% decrease vs >15% increase' and 'reduction or plateau vs serial rise' contrasts, md:200-211; the paper's 'Wilcoxon rank test', md:160-161, reported as both the log-rank and the Peto-Peto rho=1 test) are reproduced at FIT on the training patients and reported in run.json, not in the predictions; the paper's norm < 37 u ml-1 (md:110-111) and its concomitant-bilirubin check (md:112-126) are data-quality notes, not rule inputs.

methods.description: The per-patient three-class serological response classification (SeR = serological remission, SeS = serological stable/unknown significance, SeP = serological progression) of Buma AIG et al. (Cancers 2025;17(22):3647, DOI 10.3390/cancers17223647; 256 advanced NSCLC patients with clinical AND radiological disease control at 3 months, ICI-containing treatment, Radboudumc + NKI, March 2013 - January 2023): the serial serum tumor markers (STM) Cyfra 21.1 (ug/L; reference range 0.0-1.9), CEA (ug/L; 0.0-5.0) and CA-125 (U/mL; 0.0-35.0), all routinely available measurements during ICI-containing treatment on a Roche Cobas 6000/8000/Pro system (md:36), were visualized per patient and subclassified by two investigators blinded to treatment outcomes into 12 recurring dynamics grouped as: persistently normalized levels (SeR; dynamics A-B), stable levels or dynamics of unknown significance (SeS; C-H), increasing levels (SeP; I-L), based on the STM concentration over time with respect to the marker's upper reference limit and the height of the level within the patient (md:51) - a combined per-patient classification then takes the worst available individual class under the importance SeR < SeS < SeP, using the available individual classifications only when not all STMs were measured (md:51); the combined classification was associated with PFS and OS (median PFS 10.8 / 8.3 / 6.9 months and median OS NR / 29.7 / 16.5 months for SeR/SeS/SeP, log-rank significant, md:157-163; multivariable Cox HR 1.563 (95% CI 1.039-2.353) PFS and HR 2.726 (95% CI 1.682-4.418) OS for the combined classification, md:173). The paper publishes NO numeric decision boundaries - the classification is a two-investigator visual judgement ('identification of the recurring dynamics and subclassification into the three serological response patterns was based on initial eyeballing observations and could therefore be considered subjective', md:188) and no analysis code (R 4.4.2 / SPSS 29 are the statistics environment only, md:41), so the wrapper implements the rule as its own algorithmic reading, verified against the Figure 2 dynamics (which the wrapper extracted from the published figure) and recorded in the README and run.json: per marker, over the patient's draws up to the benchmark landmark (the paper's window runs to 7 days after the 2-year treatment period for durable responders or to the progression date - outcome-side information a prediction at the landmark does not have, a recorded adaptation), the pattern is SeP when the final measurement is at least growth_ratio (1.3) x the trajectory's minimum AND ends clearly above the reference limit (rise_end_high 1.2 x), i.e. the marker ends rising well above the limit (dynamics I-L); SeR when the final measurement is at or below remit_margin (0.8) x the reference limit AND the trajectory reached at least the reference limit at some point - the marker remitted into the normal range (dynamics A-B; an elevated-then-normalized series; this excludes the flat never-elevated series, dynamic C, which the authors classified as SeS); and SeS otherwise (stable, oscillation, unknown significance - the remaining dynamics). A marker with fewer than min_draws_marker (3) measurements - the paper's evaluability criterion, md:26 - is unavailable for that patient, and the patient's combined class is the worst-wins class over the available markers only (a patient with no classifiable marker gets no prediction, with the reason in note). The reference limit is the paper's published reference range per STM (params ulns) when the marker is identified by name as Cyfra 21.1 / CYFRA 21-1 / CK-19 / cytokeratin 19 fragment antigen, CEA / carcinoembryonic antigen, or CA-125 / cancer antigen-125 / MUC16 (the name the benchmark's matched features carry per dataset); a marker whose name identifies no STM (e.g. the benchmark's synthetic M1/M2 markers) uses the patient's own baseline value as the within-patient reference limit - 'the height of the STM level itself within each patient' (md:51) - the wrapper's recorded fallback (markers of an unknown scale cannot use the paper's published reference range). The wrapper writes risk = the combined ordinal class (0 = SeR, 1 = SeS, 2 = SeP), exactly the quantity the combined call thresholds, and call = 1 when the combined class is SeP (serological progression = treatment judged failing, the group with the worst PFS/OS, md:157-163) and 0 for SeR/SeS; no probability is written (the paper defines no per-patient probability or risk score - its median survivals, log-rank p values and multivariable Cox HRs are cohort-level results, reported in run.json as reported, not fitted). Fitted false: nothing is learned from the training outcomes; every boundary is the wrapper's published reading (params), chosen to reproduce the paper's 12-dynamics assignment (README, 'the numeric boundaries'), and the paper's own model requires no fitting - it is a fixed rule the authors state is directly usable in practice ('For clinical practice, however, this visual classification can already be used at present and does not require complex algorithms.', md:188). Recorded deviations from the paper: (1) the numeric boundaries are the wrapper's (the paper's are visual and subjective, md:188; not verifiable); (2) the draw window is truncated at the benchmark's landmark (the paper's window end is outcome-dependent, md:36); (3) the benchmark's 0-with-detection-flag encoding of a value below the detection limit is treated as the reported 0 (a level below the reference limit and the trajectory's minimum, the corpus below-threshold convention); (4) a marker with fewer than 3 measurements is treated as unavailable for that patient (the paper's cohort excluded such patients, md:26, and defines no fallback); (5) the paper's multivariable Cox adjustment set, the HR reference category and the log-rank p values are in Supplemental Tables S12-S21, not retrieved - not reproduced, recorded as reported.

methods.description: The two-protein serum alteration panel of Steenbuck et al. (Research Square preprint, DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-5977022/v1, posted 2025-02-13; 22 breast cancer patients on neoadjuvant EC x4 -> paclitaxel x4, 11 pathological complete remission (PCR = ypT0) / 11 non-PCR, md:100-101): per patient, 'patient-specific alterations between pre-NACT and two cycles of NACT' (md:595) of serum N-cadherin (CDH2; UniProt P19022) and c-Met (MET; UniProt P08581) - the t0 (pre-NACT) to t1 (after the second NACT cycle) change of the log2-transformed, MSStatsTMT-normalised TMT-based serum intensities (md:263-264, md:1544-1545) - evaluated by receiver operating characteristic analysis against the binary pathological response label: 'We then used these longitudinal values to generate a receiver-operator curve (ROC) to assess their performance in discriminating eventual PCR from non-PCR (Fig. 3e). ROC analysis yielded an area under the curve (AUC) > 0.93...' (md:596-599; abstract 'AUC 0.93', md:110). The wrapper takes exactly the two markers of the panel (required_markers, match all: UniProt P19022 CDH2 and P08581 MET - the method IS this fixed pair), computes the per-patient delta per marker as the raw difference value(t1) - value(t0) on the log2-TMT intensity scale (the paper's only published t1-vs-t0 quantity definition is the log2 intensity ratio, Table 4 note md:644-645, which is this difference on the log2 scale - the delta operator itself is unpublished, '?', so the wrapper records its own), and writes as risk the mean of the two per-marker deltas, each aligned to the failure direction (higher = more likely non-PCR): at fit the wrapper orients each marker's contribution by the training fold's rank separation of the delta between the failure and the non-failure groups (the Mann-Whitney U statistic, which is the basis of the ROC AUC; pROC 1.18.0's roc default direction='auto' takes the orientation with AUC >= 0.5, R/roc.R:142 - the paper's own evaluation is direction-orienting), falling back on the paper's published directions (CDH2 LogFC +0.27 and MET LogFC -0.32 in PCR, md:626-630; the Fig. 3c-d narrative md:584-593) when the training labels cannot orient a marker; the combination is the wrapper's declaration (the paper prints 'a two-protein panel (N-cadherin, c-Met)', md:1279, and 'as protein classifiers', md:1547, but NO combination rule - no weights, no equation, no per-protein curves, '?'), recorded as a deviation: an equal-weight raw mean of the two direction-aligned deltas on the shared log2-TMT unit (the paper's own Fig. 3c-d panels and Table 4 put both proteins on this one scale; no standardization, no regression, no PLS-DA score - the paper's PLS-DA is a separate 398-protein global overview, md:270-272/md:535-538). The paper defines NO operating cutoff, NO per-patient call and NO probability (AUC only, no CI, md:598), so the wrapper writes risk only - no call, no own probability; the survey/roster group is response-call but the contract classification is static-risk, one score at the landmark, recorded as a deviation (the c3-two-spot-delta-roc / plasma-delta-response-roc / episcore-composite-roc resolution). t0 = the marker's last draw on or before baseline_max_day; t1 = the marker's draw closest to the paper's after-second-EC-cycle point (cycle2_day 42 = 2 x 21-day q3w EC cycles, within cycle2_tolerance_days 14 to cover the q2w variant at day 28 and draw-day jitter) after baseline and at or before the landmark; the t2 (after six cycles) draw is NEVER substituted (it carries the separate CEP192/BCHE/SHBG panel, md:877-890). A patient without both markers' t0/t1 pairs gets no prediction, with the reason in note (the 398-protein core proteome is 'free of missingness', md:523-524, so the paper defines no imputation or fallback, '?'); a below-detection value of 0 participates as 0 and no floor is invented. The ROC/AUC evaluation itself (the paper's 'AUC > 0.93') is a cohort-level statistic the benchmark analysis produces - the wrapper computes the deterministic score only (the paper's exact pROC call is unpublished, '?').

methods.description: The shared-random-effects (shared-parameter) joint model of a repeated blood marker and time to progression or death, illustrated in Example 4.12 (ACTG Protocol 175, repeated log10 CD4 counts) of Robert M. Elashoff, Gang Li and Ning Li, Joint Modeling of Longitudinal and Time-to-Event Data (Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2016; DOI 10.1201/9781315374871): a linear mixed-effects model of the log marker with a subject-specific intercept and slope, whose distribution is taken from a flexible class of smooth densities (the seminonparametric SNP class of Gallant & Nychka 1987, degree snp_degree, relaxing the commonly used normality assumption), is linked to a Cox proportional-hazards event submodel through those shared subject-specific parameters (piecewise-constant baseline hazard); the parameters are fitted by maximum likelihood (Gauss-Hermite quadrature) on the training patients, conditional on being event-free at the landmark, and a patient's prediction is the Section-4.6-style dynamic quantity P(T <= landmark + h | T > landmark, draws to the landmark) for the first benchmark horizon, written as risk (higher = more likely failing). The wrapper writes no own probability columns and no call; one marker at a time; when the joint model cannot be estimated it falls back to a Cox model on the covariates alone (constant_ok). Differences from the monograph: the specific SNP degree, the piecewise baseline hazard, the log1p marker transform (the paper analyses log10 CD4; a log of a zero non-detect is undefined), the time scale and the landmark-conditional prediction are wrapper choices, because the monograph's model chapter is not part of the supplied copy and the book names no fitting software.

methods.description: SHERLOC - Shared and Exclusive Representations of Longitudinal ctDNA data - the proposed model of Mamann et al. (bioRxiv 2026.06.04.730097) for overall survival from the landmark: the patient's longitudinal ctDNA matrix (in the paper, 17 gene-level VAFs + 4 panel-level features = 21 channels at each of the T clinical timepoints baseline to C4D1) is read by two temporal encoders - one single temporal-kernel filter (Linear(T,1)) shared across the gene-level channels with batch normalization and sigmoid, and one feature-specific 2-dim temporal linear representation (Linear(T,2)) per panel-level feature, batch-normalized over the concatenated 2*d_agg dims; the shared-kernel and feature-specific representations are fused with per-timestep representations of a frozen genomic-interaction encoder (MLP pretrained with the Cox partial-likelihood on solid-biopsy VAF data, frozen after pretraining, 2 dimensions per timestep; the paper uses the external MSK-CHORD cohort, 22,068 patients) and with baseline clinical covariates, all batch-normalized before concatenation (order: shared-kernel, feature-specific, clinical, frozen); the concatenation is dropped out at 0.4 and passed to a single linear layer with sigmoid output whose value is the Cox log-risk fed to pycox's CoxPH, trained by the negative log-partial likelihood (Adam lr 0.005, batch 50, up to 256 epochs, early stopping patience 20, 20% validation split). The wrapper refits it per survival outcome of the training data (death first - the paper's OS, then progression), rebases the outcome times to the benchmark's landmark (the paper's OS from the final on-treatment ctDNA collection), resolves the sequence to the patient's visits up to the landmark (baseline slot = last baseline visit, then the T-1 most recent on-treatment visits, at most n_timepoints = 4 slots; the paper's evaluability rule requires all configured timepoints, md:1404-1408) and writes the paper's native outputs: the sigmoid log-risk (risk, monotone in the Cox log-risk) and per-horizon failure probabilities from the Breslow baseline-hazard survival curve. The frozen genomic-interaction encoder cannot be reproduced as published (MSK-CHORD is not redistributed, scripts/data/msk_chord/README.md:1-17), so the wrapper pretrains the same MLP architecture on the training cohort itself - the paper's transfer-learning step is replaced by an in-cohort pretraining (recorded deviation); the marker set is data-driven (the paper derives its input dimensions from the data, d_input = train_ds[0][0].shape[0], train_DL.py:289-291), so the wrapper takes whatever markers a unit carries as the channels: every marker enters the shared temporal-kernel branch, and the feature-specific panel branch is active only for the markers carrying the paper's four panel-aggregate names (_max_of_AF, _mean_of_AF, _cfDNA_conc, _n_kl; recorded convention).

methods.description: The per-sample signal-appearance call of Keup et al. (Cells 2021;10(2):212, DOI 10.3390/cells10020212; 27 HR+ HER2- metastatic breast cancer patients; 3-monthly staging time points TP0/TP1/TP2 across a treatment duration of about 9 months; CTC mRNA and EV mRNA multi-marker RT-qPCR with the AdnaTest TNBC Panel prototype (17 transcripts each) and cfDNA targeted NGS with a customized QIAseq Targeted DNA Panel (17 genes); no published analysis code): for ONE binary liquid-biopsy parameter (one of the paper's 51 - 17 CTC mRNA, 17 EV mRNA overexpression signals, 17 cfDNA gene variants; the appearance call is per parameter, so the wrapper takes exactly one marker), the appearance of the parameter at a staging time point t is defined as [parameter NOT present at the immediately preceding staging time point t-1] AND [present at t]; an appearance is a progressive-disease (PD) call at t, no appearance is a stable-disease (SD) call, and the paper validates the rule on the 54 samples of the two consecutive pairs TP0->TP1 / TP1->TP2 labelled by the staging result at the current point (17 PD / 37 SD; md:354) with sensitivity/specificity/accuracy, a two-tailed Fisher's exact test (p < 0.05, SPSS 11.5) and Holm-Bonferroni alpha = 0.05 (md:75, md:83) - its finding: EV_ERCC1_appearance sens 0.1765, spec 0.9730, acc 0.7222, rank 1 by the sum (md:190), p = 0.03 and significant even after Holm-Bonferroni (md:175, md:275; 'the appearance of EV_ERCC1 significantly correlated with disease progression' in 97% specificity / 18% sensitivity, md:257). The wrapper reads the parameter's binary state per draw (the marker's <marker>__detected companion row when the data has it, else the value above 0 - the paper's signals are binary by construction and the upstream numeric thresholds are not in the paper, refs [21]/[22], so no threshold is invented; the research's 1.3% VAF limit of detection, md:263, is a detection-probability statement, not a call cutoff), evaluates the appearance at the patient's most recent usable on-treatment staging draw on or before the landmark against the draw immediately before it (the reference is the immediately preceding draw, NOT the research baseline - a parameter present at t-2, absent at t-1 and present at t IS an appearance at t, md:79/md:106), and writes the 0/1 call (1 = appearance = PD call - the paper's polarity, PD is the failure class, md:30) plus as risk the parameter's measured value at the call draw (max(value, 0) - the quantity the presence state is thresholded from; the paper defines no per-patient score and no probability, so none is written and the benchmark converts the risk). It saves a model (the fixed rule and the parameter) and abstains with the reason in note when the patient has no on-treatment draw state by the landmark, when there is no draw before the call draw, or when the call draw carries no measured value (the paper evaluates only samples with all parameters characterized, md:97, and defines no fallback).

methods.description: The serial progression/response metabolomic biomarker of Rattner et al. (Oncotarget 2022;13:61-72, DOI 10.18632/oncotarget.28165; the NCIC-CTG CO.20 third-line cetuximab +/- brivanib mCRC trial, N=188; discovery n=68, validation n=120): an OPLS-DA discriminant model on the per-metabolite change-from-baseline features of the Week 1 plasma GC-MS metabolome separates radiographic progression (PD) from partial response (PR) - 'After filtering by VIP>1 and p-value <0.05, a parsimonious model consisting of 21 metabolites was generated' - and every post-treatment sample is then read through the model as a SIMCA-P 'S-score' (0-1), classified serially: 'PD was defined as 2 consecutive S-scores >0.7. PR was defined as 2 or more scores <0.4.' with 0.4<S-score<0.7 designated SD (intermediate; the 21-metabolite model is the Week-1 delta model only - Weeks 4 and 12 did not yield a stable model, and the paper does not track the biomarker serially). SIMCA-P+ 15.0 is commercial (no source; no model file, coefficient set, S-score formula or data published; job.code empty), so the wrapper refits the recipe in available tooling: ropls OPLS-DA (1 predictive component, 1 orthogonal by default, mean-centered and unit-variance scaled - the paper's component count and scaling are not published, declared readings) on change-from-baseline vectors at each patient's first post-baseline draw by the landmark (the Week 1 analog), with the paper's two-stage filter (preliminary model, VIP > vip_cutoff, then a two-sided univariate test at p < p_cutoff between the PR and PD classes - the test's identity is not published, the wrapper uses Wilcoxon rank-sum by default), then a refit on the surviving metabolites. The S-score is written as the OPLS-DA's continuous class prediction (the PD dummy, coded 1 for PD) clipped to [0,1] - the SIMCA construct is not defined mathematically in the paper, so this is the wrapper's declared substitute; it preserves the paper's observed ordering (PD 0.7-1.0, response 0.0-0.66). The discriminant classes are the paper's: training patients with no_response == 0 (best response CR/PR; the trial had no CRs - the 'PR' side) vs progressive_disease == 1 (the 'PD' side); the SD patients (no_response 1 and progressive_disease 0) are excluded from the fit and scored afterwards, exactly as the paper applied the model to its 22 SD patients. The serial rule is applied to the S-score sequence of the patient's post-baseline draws by the landmark: call 1 when n_consecutive_pd consecutive scores exceed s_pd_cutoff (the paper's PD/futility call), call 0 when n_scores_pr or more scores are below s_pr_cutoff (the paper's PR call) and also for the intermediate band (the paper's SD, 'neither progression nor response'; the binary contract call collapses it onto the non-failing side - the paper distinguishes SD from futile). risk = the per-patient summary of the S-score sequence (mean by default, the paper defines no per-patient score; higher = more progression-like), minimal at 0 and maximal at 1. Missing/below-detection values follow the paper: 'Missing values were replaced with the minimum quantitative value in the data set.' - per marker, the training minimum of the quantitative (detected, positive) values is fitted on the training fold and replaces missing rows and non-detects (value 0 or <marker>__detected 0) in both fit and predict; the delta is then defined for every metabolite. A patient with no baseline draw, or fewer than two post-baseline draws by the landmark, gets no prediction with the reason in note (the serial rule needs at least two S-scores; the validation cohort required baseline plus at least two other time points). The wrapper writes no probability (the paper defines none; TxResBench converts the risk) and does not use covariates (arms pooled, age/sex unassociated). Differences from the published pipeline, each declared: the paper's internal-control + median-fold-change normalization and ComBat batch correction and the 5-sample PCA outlier exclusion (criterion unstated) are upstream of the benchmark frame - the values arrive normalized and no batch column exists, so neither is reproduced; the model is always refit per training fold (the 21-metabolite set and the fitted coefficients are not published).

This wrapper reimplements the published OPLS-DA recipe with ropls (Bioconductor, CeCILL licence) and the published serial S-score rule; the wrapper source is distributed under the repository's licence

methods.description: The authors' unpublished scikit-learn-based multistep machine-learning pipeline that calls pathological complete response (pCR, 0% residual viable tumour at resection) versus non-pCR after neoadjuvant radiochemotherapy plus PD-L1 blockade in microsatellite-stable locally advanced rectal cancer, from the 5-feature integrated plasma signature - the LC-MS/MS metabolites phosphatidylcholine and cholest-5-en-23-yn-3beta-ol plus the DIA-MS proteomes APBB1IP, OLFM4, DNAJC19 - measured at baseline, postradiotherapy and postimmunotherapy (Xu J et al., Research Square preprint v1 2025, DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-5509842/v1; 50 patients, 117 plasma samples, 20 pCR / 30 non-pCR; reported cohort-level 'model predictive ability' = accuracy 0.954 by repeated group-to-group validation of the baseline and postradiotherapy cohorts and 0.877 for the postimmunotherapy validation). The wrapper fixes the published endpoint of that pipeline - the 5-feature integrated signature (md:395-397, the sixth of the six listed feature combinations, md:398-400) - and fits a scikit-learn random forest on the benchmark training patients' failure label (no_response, else progressive_disease, else progression or death by the first horizon - the paper's pCR/non-pCR response label's benchmark counterpart), using per marker the baseline value, the last value on or before the landmark and their change and relative change (the paper does not state whether the features enter as single-stage values or as change scores, '?'); risk = P(failure) from the forest (higher = treatment more likely failing) and call = 1 when risk >= call_threshold (0.5, the classifier's decision boundary - the paper publishes no cutoff).

methods.description: The 10-year cardiovascular-disease (CVD) event classifier of Zhao, Feng, Wu, Lupu, Wilke, Wells, Denny and Wei (Scientific Reports 2019;9:717, DOI 10.1038/s41598-018-36745-x; VUMC Synthetic Derivative, 109,490 individuals, 9,824 cases) on LONGITUDINAL (per-one-year-slice) EHR features, reproduced as a benchmark static-risk method: 'we extracted each year value of each feature and concatenated the temporal values from all patients into a two-dimensional matrix for a classifier (e.g. LR, RF, GBT)' (md:560-563), a scikit-learn random forest ('LR, RF, and GBT were implemented with Python Scikit-Learn 0.19.1', md:580-581) with n_estimators=100 and the other hyperparameters tuned on the paper's Supplementary Table 3 grid (max_depth [3, None], max_features ['auto', 3, 10], min_samples_split [2, 3, 10], bootstrap [True, False], criterion ['gini', 'entropy']) by 'a grid search with 10-fold stratified cross-validation on the training set to select the best model with the maximum AUROC' (md:584-586); the paper reports RF longitudinal AUROC 0.761 +/- 0.010 / AUPRC 0.246 +/- 0.012 (Supplementary Table 1). The wrapper builds one wide row per patient from the draws up to the landmark: over n_slices (default 7 - the paper's seven one-year calendar slices of its 2000-2006 observation window) equal-width bins across the history window, the per-slice min/max/median/SD of every passed marker (md:453-457) plus a per-slice measured indicator (the paper's per-slice binary diagnosis/medication indicators applied to marker presence: the benchmark's marker frame carries no codes), with the paper's preprocessing in order - outlier removal > 5 SD from the training mean (md:429-430), a slice without a measurement filled by the patient's closest-date measurement (md:456-458), a marker the patient never had measured filled with the training median (the paper's group-median imputation, md:430-431) - the cov_* columns when the run passes them (the paper's demographic features and EHR length, the latter as the patient's distinct-draw-day count on the benchmark's day axis). It is trained on the benchmark's first available failure label (no_response, else progressive_disease, else progression, else death by the first horizon - the paper's binary case/control label's benchmark counterpart; run.json records which), and writes the fitted probability P(failure) from RandomForestClassifier.predict_proba as risk (the paper's own output object; TxResBench converts it into the four per-outcome probabilities). methods.description: The Functional Principal Component Random Forest (FPCRF) baseline as adapted by Mamann et al. (bioRxiv 2026.06.04.730097) for overall survival from the landmark: the patient's longitudinal ctDNA profile (in the paper, 17 gene-level VAFs + 4 panel-level aggregated features = 21 features at each of the T clinical timepoints baseline to C4D1) is treated feature by feature as a functional object on the paper's fixed 0.75-month grid and reduced by FPCA with 2 components per feature (42 scores); a Random Survival Forest fitted on the scores ranks them by sklearn permutation importance and the top 20 are kept; the selection is z-scored and reduced by PCA to 10 components; the PCA scores are concatenated with baseline clinical covariates and the frozen per-timestep genomic-interaction embeddings (2 dims per timestep, 2T flattened) and fed to a sksurv CoxnetSurvivalAnalysis with an Elastic Net penalty (l1_ratio 0.5), whose alpha is chosen by the paper's two-step procedure (regularisation path with 20 alphas, then a 4-fold KFold grid search with fit_baseline_model=True for the Breslow baseline). The wrapper refits the pipeline per survival outcome of the training data (death first - the paper's OS, then progression), rebases the outcome times to the benchmark's landmark (the paper's OS from the final on-treatment ctDNA collection), resolves the trajectory to the patient's visits up to the landmark (baseline slot = last baseline visit, then the T-1 most recent on-treatment visits, at most n_timepoints = 4 slots; the paper's evaluability rule requires all configured timepoints), and writes the paper's native outputs: the Cox linear predictor (risk, higher = worse) and per-horizon failure probabilities from the Breslow baseline-hazard survival curve. The frozen genomic-interaction encoder cannot be reproduced as published (MSK-CHORD is not redistributed, scripts/data/msk_chord/README.md:1-17), so the wrapper pretrains the same MLP architecture on the training cohort itself - the paper's transfer-learning step is replaced by an in-cohort pretraining (recorded deviation); the marker set is data-driven (the paper's 17-gene + 4-panel feature set is its assay application; the pipeline is per-feature identical for the gene and panel blocks), so the wrapper takes whatever markers a unit carries as the features.

(bioRxiv 2026.06.04.730097) for overall survival from the landmark: per patient, the longitudinal ctDNA profile (in the paper, 17 gene-level VAFs + 4 panel-level aggregated features x T clinical timepoints baseline to C4D1) is flattened into a feature matrix together with per-timestep embeddings of a frozen genomic-interaction encoder (an MLP pretrained with the Cox partial-likelihood on solid-biopsy data, 2 dims per timestep - in the paper 22,068 MSK-CHORD patients, not redistributed), and sksurv's CoxnetSurvivalAnalysis is fitted on it with the paper's two-step lambda selection: a 20-alpha solution path (alpha_min_ratio 0.001, max_iter 5000) followed by a 4-fold KFold grid search over that path, error_score 0.5, the concordance index as score; the refit has fit_baseline_model=True so the Breslow baseline survival function is available. The three penalties are the SAME function and pipeline, only l1_ratio differs (ridge 1e-5, lasso 1.0, elastic net 0.5), so they are ONE method with the params.penalty switch (default elastic_net = the paper's config default and the Table 3 method). The wrapper refits it per survival outcome of the training data (death first - the paper's OS, then progression), rebases the outcome times to the benchmark landmark (the paper's OS is from the final on-treatment ctDNA collection), resolves the matrix to the patient's visits up to the landmark (baseline slot + the T-1 most recent visits, at most n_timepoints = 4; the paper's evaluability rule requires all configured timepoints) and writes the paper's native outputs: the Cox linear predictor (risk, higher = higher risk) and per-horizon failure probabilities from the Breslow baseline survival function. Clinical covariates are NOT model features: the paper text mentions concatenated baseline clinical characteristics c but the code's _build_feature_matrix never selects the cln_* columns (code wins, recorded deviation); they are used only for the encoder's pretraining clinical branch (covariates optional). methods.description: The Random Survival Forest baseline of SHERLOC (Mamann et al., bioRxiv 2026.06.04.730097), the framework that models overall survival from the landmark (the time of the final on-treatment ctDNA collection) in metastatic nonsquamous NSCLC on atezolizumab-based therapy: the flattened longitudinal ctDNA channel matrix (the paper: 21 channels - 17 gene-level VAFs and 4 panel-level features - x 4 protocol timepoints) concatenated with the frozen 2-dimensions-per-timestep genomic-interaction embeddings (the authors pretrain an MLP_SolidBiopsy encoder with a Cox loss on the 22,068-patient pan-cancer MSK-CHORD cohort, which is not redistributed, so the same architecture is pretrained here on the benchmark's training patients' baseline channel values with the paper's pretraining hyperparameters and fixed seed 1), fed to sksurv.ensemble.RandomSurvivalForest (log-rank splitting, Nelson-Aalen cumulative hazards at the terminal nodes averaged into the ensemble CHF), tuned by GridSearchCV over n_estimators [50, 100] x min_samples_split [2, 6] with 4-fold KFold, error_score = 0.5, RandomSurvivalForest(random_state = 1) - exactly the authors' scripts/train_ML.py method 'RSF'; the risk is sksurv's predict = the sum of the estimated ensemble cumulative hazard function over the distinct training event times (no sign flip: higher = higher risk, failure-oriented by construction) and no probability or call is written (the paper's survival function exists only for its own IBS evaluation; the benchmark converts the risk per outcome). Deviations recorded: the benchmark's marker set replaces the paper's fixed 21 channels (the gene/panel split and the 4 panel-level aggregates are not recoverable from a general marker set, and the authors' code concatenates the gene and panel blocks into one flat vector before the forest, so the split is computationally irrelevant); the paper's text says the unified feature vector also concatenates baseline clinical characteristics c but the published code's _build_feature_matrix never selects the cln_* columns - code wins; the paper's protocol visits become the patient's draws by the benchmark landmark (baseline token + latest T-1 on-treatment draws, carry-forward padding, 0 for a marker cell missing at a token day); the benchmark's own training fold and the call's seed replace the paper's 100-x-70/30 Monte Carlo cross-validation; the paper's endpoint is overall survival from the landmark, with progression-free survival as the fallback when the training data has no OS; covariates are declared none (never used, by either the paper's code or the encoder's extracted 2-dim representation).

methods.description: The survival support vector machine (sSVM) that Wu et al. fitted with the scikit-survival package (v0.17.2, exactly as named in the paper) to predict minimal-residual-disease risk of disease progression after chemoradiotherapy/radiotherapy (CRT/RT) in inoperable localized NSCLC: 'For each time point, a machine learning model was constructed employing survival support vector machine (sSVM, scikit-survival package, v0.17.2) algorithm [12] on the extracted neomer profiles.' (md:52), where each time point's model is cross-sectional on ONE plasma sample per patient ('A total of 97 plasma samples... were collected from the 44 patients to develop MRD prediction models', md:52) with the 1759 neomer features of that sample as X ('The neomer features were profiled as the ratio of neomer-detecting reads over the total reads and the read count of each of the 1758 neomers.', md:50; count = read counts as profiled, no scaling, no selection, no transform - md:50, and sksurv does not scale) and the patients' progression-free survival as the outcome (the paper calls the output 'MRD risk' for disease progression, md:79, and validates with 'Kaplan-Meier curves of progression-free survival', md:121), and the every-sample risk scores converted to a binary high-/low-risk MRD status 'by choosing a cutoff value to ensure 90% specificity' (md:57; 'the selection of the cut-off value was determined at 90% specificity of the training set', md:79). The paper names NO sSVM class, kernel or hyperparameter (md:52 - scikit-survival 0.17.2 exports five survival-SVM classes) and publishes no analysis code (data on request, md:195; job.code = []), so the wrapper pins the presumed linear class sksurv.svm.FastSurvivalSVM with the package's own defaults (alpha=1, rank_ratio=1.0, fit_intercept=False, optimizer 'avltree', max_iter=20, tol=None; sksurv/svm/survival_svm.py:848-854; random_state from the call's seed) - every one of these is a wrapper-documented assumption recorded in run.json, never a paper fact. The 90%-specificity cutoff is computed on the fit call's training cohort risk scores (the paper's per-training-set reading, md:79; the md:57 pooled-LOOCV-scores alternative is recorded as unresolved), against the training patients with no observed progression (the negatives of the paper's specificity; the paper's MRD status is a call on progression). The paper's evaluation procedure (one model per time point TP1/TP2/TP3, leave-one-out cross-validation over 39/33/25 samples, md:57) is not the task's: the benchmark supplies one landmark call and its own train/test folds, and the wrapper implements the model - the sSVM plus the training-set 90%-specificity cutoff - not the LOOCV loop (recorded difference). In the benchmark each marker column of the wide profile is one measurement marker; per patient X is the values of all markers at the patient's most recent draw after baseline_max_day and at or before the landmark (the benchmark has no TP1/TP2/TP3 visit label; the time-point model stands in for the 'at the landmark' model, the same substitution the wrapper adopts whenever a protocol visit has no benchmark counterpart; one sample per patient per fitted model, exactly as in the paper, so a sample whose draw lacks any marker of the fitted set is abstained rather than imputed - the paper defines no imputation); risk = the sSVM risk score (higher = higher risk for rank_ratio=1, sksurv/svm/survival_svm.py:864-893 with the sign flip at:886-888) and call = the paper's MRD high-risk flag (1 = risk >= the training 90%-specificity cutoff), so risk and call are failure-oriented by construction; no probability is written by the method (the sSVM is not a probabilistic model) - TxResBench converts the risk per outcome. The outcome the model is fitted on is the paper's endpoint, progression-free survival; the other outcomes are served by that conversion, and a call is written only when a high-/low-risk call exists (progression). The wrapper is deterministic for a given seed (sksurv resolves tied survival times by a random shuffle, sksurv/svm/survival_svm.py:729-745; the wrapper seeds it from the call's seed - the paper states no seed, '?').

methods.description: The paper's 10-gene whole-blood immunotranscriptome sparse-PLS (sPLS) classifier of clinical benefit (CB) to anti-PD-(L)1 immune checkpoint inhibitor monotherapy in metastatic urothelial cancer - van Wilpe S, Croci D, Fonseca Costa SS, et al., JCI Insight 2025;10(5):e186062, DOI 10.1172/jci.insight.186062 - a supervised classifier of the on-treatment whole-blood transcriptome into predicted CB vs predicted N-CB (CB = radiological and clinical PFS at or beyond 6 months from treatment initiation, md:30/md:107; 42 CB / 51 N-CB of 93 patients, md:30; 79 patients with paired baseline and on-treatment RNA-seq, split into discovery n = 29 / test n = 29 / validation n = 21, md:48/md:65/md:141; reported performance discovery AUC 0.86, test AUC 0.84, validation AUC 0.77, sensitivities/specificities for detecting N-CB, md:9/md:62/md:151). The paper publishes no analysis code (job.code = []; the gene-expression analysis ran on the proprietary LITOSeek platform of Novigenix SA, md:145) and names no sPLS package ('we employed the sparse partial least squares method', md:165), so this wrapper re-implements the published recipe on the published panel: per patient, for the 9 nameable panel genes (CD86, CEBPA, CLC, PDXK, PTTG1, RAD51, SMPD3, SCARF1, TOX; the 10th gene is an unnamed noncoding RNA that cannot be represented, a recorded deviation; required_markers match all), the value at the earliest on-treatment draw by the landmark and the BL-to-OT change (the paired design of the DEA that selected the panel, md:160/md:165; the OT expression is the discrimination object of the discovery analyses, md:57; the paper never states the per-patient model input, '?' - this is the wrapper's declared choice), a standard sparse-PLS classifier (the wrapper's own implementation of sPLS - NIPALS deflation with soft-thresholded loadings, keep_genes features per component, default 2; the paper's 10/15/20-feature reduction operated on the discovery-cohort DEG list, which is not a benchmark input; the panel is the paper's final feature selection) plus a binomial logistic of the paper's CB label (derived from the training PFS at the 6-month horizon) on the sPLS component(s) - the number of components is chosen by the paper's own resampling scheme, repeated 3-fold cross-validation with 10 iterations (md:165), by the mean fold AUC of the risk against the training CB label among 1..ncomp_max components (default 1: the most parsimonious reading; the paper states no component count), giving P(CB) per patient. Outputs: risk = p_no_response = P(N-CB) = 1 - P(CB) (failure-oriented; the paper's reported sensitivities/specificities are for detecting N-CB, md:9/md:151, and the wrapper records the named inversion of the CB probability on which the 55% cutoff is stated, md:167; p_no_response is the declared mapping of the paper's 6-month PFS-based failure class onto the benchmark's closest response outcome, the paper's label not being a RECIST SD/PD call; the other outcomes' probabilities are the package's conversions of the risk) and call = 1 (treatment judged failing, predicted N-CB) when P(CB) < cutoff, call = 0 when P(CB) >= cutoff (the boundary is fixed as predicted CB for P(CB) >= 0.55, per the paper's 55% classification cutoff on the CB probability, md:167). The fitted sPLS model, its components, coefficients and every probability are the wrapper's, not the paper's; each difference from the paper is listed in the README and in run.json.

methods.description: Two-stage Bayesian joint model (Phillips et al., medRxiv 2024.07.02.24309776; authors' code COVID-joint-model-CoP, commit fb48446) for one serial blood marker: stage 1 fits the authors' hierarchical Bayesian log-linear mixed model of the marker (per-patient random intercept and strictly negative random slope with correlation, covariate effects on both, Student-t(4) measurement error, weakly informative priors, the authors' Stan model verbatim), stage 2 fits one survival::coxph per sampled trajectory on the landmark-conditional start-stop data with the time-varying covariate = the predicted true marker value 7 days before t (the paper's exposure-to-report gap), the paper's per-imputation structure and asymptotic-MLE draws of the coefficients, and stage 3 turns the per-draw Breslow baseline into the conditional event probability P(T <= horizon | T > landmark) - the paper's OWN output is per-individual VE_i(t) = 1 - exp(gamma A_i(t-7) + zeta) versus a control arm, which the benchmark's single-arm design replaces by the hazard (the arm effect, the site strata, the assay-specific outlier rules and the post-outcome informative-censoring covariates are dropped or disabled; the paper's 60,000 trajectories are thinned to 800 by default; new patients are scored through the stage-1 random effects conditioned on their observed draws up to the landmark). The wrapper writes the progression and death conditional event probabilities by every horizon (risk = the first horizon's progression probability) and abstains with a note for a patient without an on-treatment marker draw by the landmark or with fewer than two draws; one fit serves both survival outcomes (progression from pfs, death from os).

Its 16 inputs are the risk factors significant in the authors' univariate logistic regression (P < 0.01, md:170-174): the post-CRT serum CEA category (<=2 vs >2 ng/mL; the cutoff from the cohort median 2.2 ng/mL, md:165-167) plus 15 clinical variables (gender, age, tumour location, chemotherapy regimen, clinical T, clinical N, TNM stage, tumour grade, anemia, diarrhea, urinary symptoms, dermatitis, leukopenia, RT dose, RT-surgery interval); in the benchmark these arrive as the marker's last on-treatment draw before the landmark (the paper's single post-CRT measurement ~6-10 weeks after CRT, md:132-133) and the cov_* clinical columns; covariates is declared optional, so when a dataset's patients table carries the cov_* clinical track the wrapper fits the paper's 16-input model, and with the track absent it fits the marker category alone, a documented fallback (the paper defines no marker-only model, so that fit is recorded in run.json as a deviation). The paper publishes no code (STATISTICA is proprietary; availability is data-only, md:737-738), so the wrapper refits the published specification with scikit-learn's MLPClassifier (hidden_layer_sizes=(4,), activation logistic, solver 'sgd' - the multilayer backpropagation algorithm of md:79-81), fitted on the training patients whose harness outcome no_response (best RECIST SD or PD - the closest benchmark analogue of the paper's non-pCR residual-tumour class) is known; the wrapper fits P(no response) directly, so risk = p_no_response = the network's probability and is failure-oriented by construction, the flip of the paper's stated P(pCR) (md:138-139) - the paper's label is pathological (ypT0N0) and the benchmark carries RECIST response, a recorded difference. Everything the paper leaves unspecified - activation functions, learning rule/rate, momentum, epochs, error function, stopping, weight initialisation (all '?' per the spec), input standardisation (?, md:187-321), the classification probability cutoff behind its indices (?, md:148-150), and the membership of the pre-CRT CEA (significant in Table 2, md:407-411, but absent from the 16-variable Results list md:170-174 and from Table 5's VSR top-5) - is the wrapper's documented choice, made once and recorded in run.json and the README; no scikit-learn default is presented as a paper fact. methods.description: Per-patient prediction of pathological complete response (pCR: 'the absence of malignant cells in primary tumors and nodes (ypT0N0) in the resected specimen following neoadjuvant CRT', Huang C-M et al., Sci Rep 2020;10:12555, DOI 10.1038/s41598-020-69345-9; training cohort n = 236, 56/180 pCR/non-pCR, Table 3 testing AUROC 0.72 / accuracy 0.84, n = 71; validation Table 4 AUROC 0.74, n = 34) from the k-nearest-neighbour classifier of the paper: 'The KNN model predicts new samples by using training samples; the process entails a majority vote on the outcome of points that are k-nearest to the new sample.' (md:70-71), fitted in STATISTICA 13.0 on the 16 significant risk factors (P < 0.01 univariate, md:170-174): gender, age, tumor location, chemotherapy type, clinical T stage (T2/T3/T4), clinical N stage (N0/N1/N2), TNM stage (II/III), tumor grade, post-CRT CEA ('Post-CRT CEA (ng/mL) <= 2 / > 2', cut-off 2 ng/mL from the cohort median 2.2 ng/mL, md:165-167), anemia, diarrhea, urinary symptoms, dermatitis, leukopenia, radiation therapy dose and the radiation-to-surgery interval. The paper publishes no code (STATISTICA 13.0 is proprietary, md:157; job.code = []) and never states k, the distance metric, the vote weighting, the feature encoding or the classification cutoff (all '?'), so the wrapper refits the described majority-vote classifier on the benchmark training patients with its own recorded choices (k selected by 5-fold CV on the training fold, Euclidean distance on the encoded and standardised features, ordered categories as ordinal codes, 0/1 factors as 0/1, age z-scored; the CEA cut-off fixed at the published 2 ng/mL) and writes, per patient, the vote fraction of the failure class (non-pCR = the harness no_response label) as risk and p_no_response, plus call = 1 when the majority vote is non-pCR (treatment judged failing). Covariates optional (benchmark track D1): with the covariate track on, the paper's 15 clinical covariates are resolved from its cov_* columns by name and missing ones are left out (coverage recorded); with the covariate track off, the wrapper drops the paper's covariate terms and keeps the marker part of the classifier - the benchmark main-track rule - and records the deviation. The paper's 16-variable enumeration excludes pre-CRT CEA (md:170-174), so the wrapper uses the CEA draw during treatment up to the landmark (the paper's post-CRT measurement, 'Approximately 6-10 weeks after completing CRT... before surgery', md:132-133) only; patients without that draw or with an unreadable paper covariate get no prediction with a note (the paper's complete-case cohorts, md:93-99).

(md:737-738) - and the wrapper uses only numpy and pandas from the base image)

methods.description: The multiple logistic regression (MLR) that Huang et al. (Scientific Reports 2020;10:12555, doi:10.1038/s41598-020-69345-9) fitted in STATISTICA 13.0 (md:157) to predict pathological complete response (pCR = ypT0N0 in the total-mesorectal-excision specimen, md:128-129) after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (training n = 236, 56 pCR / 180 non-pCR; validation n = 34, 7/27, Table 1 md:338-344). Its inputs are the risk factors significant (P < 0.01) in the authors' univariate logistic regression (md:170-174): the post-CRT serum CEA category (<=2 vs >2 ng/mL; cutoff from the cohort median 2.2 ng/mL, md:165-167) plus 15 clinical variables (gender, age, tumour location, chemotherapy regimen, clinical T stage, clinical N stage, TNM stage, tumour grade, anemia, diarrhoea, urinary symptoms, dermatitis, leukopenia, RT dose, RT-surgery interval); in the benchmark these arrive as the marker's last on-treatment draw at or before the landmark and the dataset's cov_* columns. The paper publishes no code (STATISTICA is proprietary; availability is data-only, md:737-738) and no model table, so the wrapper refits the described multiple logistic regression - maximum likelihood by Fisher scoring with an intercept - on the training patients whose harness outcome no_response (best RECIST SD or PD, the closest benchmark analogue of the paper's non-pCR residual-tumour class) is known; risk = p_no_response = the fitted P(no response), failure-oriented by construction, the flip of the paper's stated P(pCR) (md:138-139). Covariates are declared optional because the benchmark runs methods with the covariate track or without it (the common arena has covariates off): with the cov_* track the wrapper fits the paper's 16-variable model; with no track it fits the post-CRT CEA category alone, a benchmark-mode fallback the paper does not define, recorded in run.json and the README as a deviation. Every choice the paper does not state is the wrapper's and is recorded in run.json and the README: the coding of the multi-level categoricals (0/1 dummies as given, one-hot with alias-dropping for character columns), the estimation details (MLE via Fisher scoring; STATISTICA's are not published,?), and no probability cutoff - the paper never states the one behind its sensitivity/PPV/accuracy (Tables 3-4, md:148-150) - so no call is written and the benchmark's analysis derives its own.
